knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Based Radius Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical three-way contraction, retention, and expansion rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose thresholds \(0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1\), factors \(0<\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}<1<\gamma_{\mathrm{inc}}\), and a maximum radius \(\Delta_{\max}>0\). Given \(\Delta_k\), an agreement ratio \(\rho_k\), and a trial step \(s_k\), set \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}\Delta_k\) if \(\rho_k<\eta_1\); set \(\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\gamma_{\mathrm{inc}}\Delta_k,\Delta_{\max}\}\) if \(\rho_k\geq\eta_2\) and the trial step is boundary-active; and set \(\Delta_{k+1}=\Delta_k\) otherwise. Accept the trial point exactly when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\); otherwise retain \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radius contracts below the lower ratio threshold, expands up to its cap for very good boundary-active steps, and is retained otherwise; the lower threshold also determines trial-point acceptance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update produces \(0<\Delta_{k+1}\leq\Delta_{\max}\), with contraction for poor agreement, capped expansion for very good boundary-active steps, and retention in all remaining cases.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical discrete threshold radius update
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(0<\Delta_k\leq\Delta_{\max}\), let \(s_k\) be the trial step, and let \(\rho_k\) be its agreement ratio.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The canonical three-branch discrete update used in a Euclidean trust-region method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\Delta_{k+1}=\begin{cases}\gamma_c\Delta_k,&\rho_k<\eta_c,\\\Delta_k,&\eta_c\leq\rho_k\leq\eta_e\text{ or }\|s_k\|_2<\Delta_k,\\\min\{\gamma_e\Delta_k,\Delta_{\max}\},&\rho_k>\eta_e\text{ and }\|s_k\|_2=\Delta_k,\end{cases}\] where \(0<\gamma_c<1<\gamma_e\) and \(0<\eta_c<\eta_e<1\). The Nocedal-Wright canonical instance is \((\gamma_c,\gamma_e,\eta_c,\eta_e)=(1/4,2,1/4,3/4)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold-based update contracts the radius after poor agreement, retains it after intermediate agreement, and expands it after strong agreement only when the step is boundary-limited. Expansion is capped by a maximum radius. The canonical numerical factors are one-quarter for contraction and two for expansion, with ratio thresholds one-quarter and three-quarters.
assumptions_latex: The boundary test uses the same norm as the trust-region constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed piecewise recurrence defines a classical threshold-based radius update.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The update is \(\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\theta_k\Delta_k,\Delta_{\max}\}\) with \(\theta_k\in\{\gamma_c,1,\gamma_e\}\), except that the cap is immaterial in the first two branches.
special_cases_latex: With \(\gamma_c=1/4\), \(\gamma_e=2\), \(\eta_c=1/4\), and \(\eta_e=3/4\), the recurrence is Algorithm 4.1's radius rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: If the trial step lies strictly inside the region, the radius is not expanded.
The cap preserves \(\Delta_{k+1}\leq\Delta_{\max}\).
boundary_notes: Floating-point implementations normally replace exact boundary equality with a tolerance.
Acceptance and contraction thresholds may be chosen independently in other variants.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Delta>0\), let \(\rho\) be an agreement ratio, and fix \(0<\eta_1\leq\eta_2<1\) and \(0<\gamma_1\leq\gamma_2<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: BTR-style graded control using ranges of admissible updates rather than one fixed multiplier per class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graded radius-update family is the set-valued map \[\mathcal U(\Delta,\rho)=\begin{cases}[\Delta,\infty),&\rho\geq\eta_2,\\[\gamma_2\Delta,\Delta],&\eta_1\leq\rho<\eta_2,\\[\gamma_1\Delta,\gamma_2\Delta],&\rho<\eta_1.\end{cases}\] A radius sequence belongs to this family if \(\Delta_{k+1}\in\mathcal U(\Delta_k,\rho_k)\) for every \(k\). With a cap \(\Delta_{\max}\), replace each interval by its intersection with \((0,\Delta_{\max}]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graded update does not prescribe one contraction or expansion factor. It permits a range of next radii based on the quality class: nondecrease after strong agreement, limited contraction or retention after ordinary acceptance, and mandatory bounded contraction after rejection. Any selection from the corresponding interval is a member of the family.
assumptions_latex: When a finite cap is imposed, the selected interval must remain nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal U\) defines the graded radius-update family and \(\Delta_{k+1}\in\mathcal U(\Delta_k,\rho_k)\) defines its admissible sequences.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For unsuccessful iterations, the multiplier \(\Delta_{k+1}/\Delta_k\) belongs to \([\gamma_1,\gamma_2]\); for ordinary successful iterations it belongs to \([\gamma_2,1]\); for very successful iterations it belongs to \([1,\infty)\).
special_cases_latex: Selecting interval endpoints yields discrete update variants.
Choosing \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2\) forces a single contraction multiplier after rejection.
immediate_consequences_latex: Rejection gives \(\Delta_{k+1}<\Delta_k\).
Strong agreement gives \(\Delta_{k+1}\geq\Delta_k\) before application of any external cap.
boundary_notes: The cited family does not require a boundary-active step before allowing radius increase.
Additional lower and upper safeguards can narrow the admissible intervals.

children.title: Interpolated Radius Updates
children.top_down_role: Radius changes selected through interpolation of agreement or model information.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolated Radius Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius selection by safeguarded interpolation of agreement-dependent target multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose knots \(-\infty<r_0<r_1<\cdots<r_q<\infty\) and positive multipliers \(g_0,\ldots,g_q\). Let \(g:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty)\) be piecewise affine with \(g(r_i)=g_i\), constant outside \([r_0,r_q]\), and clipped to \([\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]\), where \(0<\gamma_{\min}\leq1\leq\gamma_{\max}\). Given the agreement statistic \(\rho_k\), update \(\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\Delta_{\max},\max\{\Delta_{\min},g(\rho_k)\Delta_k\}\}\). Thus neighboring target multipliers are interpolated continuously while explicit radius and multiplier safeguards are enforced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Piecewise-affine interpolation maps agreement ratios to radius multipliers, after which multiplier and absolute-radius safeguards are applied.
assumptions_latex: The knot sequence is strictly increasing and all target multipliers are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_{k+1}\in[\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\) and \(g(\rho_k)\in[\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]\).
review_flags: no authoritative locator supplied for this interpolation formulation
interpolation knots and extrapolation conventions are policy-dependent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is internally defined and fits the interpolated-update leaf, but the knot construction, constant extrapolation, and safeguard convention are policy choices without an authoritative citation. children.title: Continuous Radius Updates
children.top_down_role: Radius policies varying smoothly with graded agreement information.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Radius Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General continuous mapping from model agreement to a safeguarded radius multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}\to[\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]\) be continuous, where \(0<\gamma_{\min}<1<\gamma_{\max}\), and choose thresholds \(\eta_1<\eta_2\) such that \(g(r)<1\) for \(r<\eta_1\), \(g(r)=1\) for \(r\in[\eta_1,\eta_2]\), and \(g(r)>1\) for \(r>\eta_2\). Given agreement statistic \(\rho_k\), set \(\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\Delta_{\max},\max\{\Delta_{\min},g(\rho_k)\Delta_k\}\}\). The update varies continuously with \(\rho_k\) except where the absolute radius bounds become active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous safeguarded function converts agreement into contraction, retention, or expansion multipliers and then clips the resulting radius to fixed bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is continuous and takes values in \([\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]\).
The stated contraction, retention, and expansion sign conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The radius update is safeguarded and is continuous in \(\rho_k\) wherever neither absolute bound is active.
review_flags: no authoritative locator supplied for the continuous-update family
the plateau requirement selects one particular continuous regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuous multiplier map is mathematically coherent and the algorithm content kind is appropriate, but the plateau and transition conditions select a particular continuous-update family for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Graded-Update Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Bounds and fallback regimes for interpolated or continuous radius changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Graded-Update Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform multiplier and absolute-radius bounds for graded update maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a graded radius policy propose \(\widehat\Delta_{k+1}=g(\rho_k)\Delta_k\). It is safeguarded when constants \(0<\gamma_{\min}\leq1\leq\gamma_{\max}<\infty\) and \(0<\Delta_{\min}<\Delta_{\max}<\infty\) are fixed, \(g(r)\in[\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]\) for every admissible agreement value \(r\), and the implemented update is \(\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\Delta_{\max},\max\{\Delta_{\min},\widehat\Delta_{k+1}\}\}\). These conditions prevent a single update from changing the radius by an unbounded factor and keep every implemented radius positive and finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graded policy is safeguarded by bounded multipliers and clipping to positive finite radius limits, preventing unbounded one-step changes or radius collapse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_{k+1}\in[\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\) and the unclipped multiplier is uniformly bounded.

children.title: Radius Safeguard System
children.top_down_role: Scale-selection and safeguarding mechanisms for reliable region management.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capped, positive, boundary-aware radius safeguards
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\widehat\Delta>0\), \(0<\Delta_0\leq\widehat\Delta\), and suppose an unsafeguarded radius proposal is \(\widetilde\Delta_{k+1}>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional radius management with positivity, a global upper cap, and a boundary-activity condition for expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A radius safeguard system consists of \[0<\Delta_k\leq\widehat\Delta,\qquad \Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\widehat\Delta,\widetilde\Delta_{k+1}\},\] together with the expansion gate \[\Delta_{k+1}>\Delta_k\ \Longrightarrow\ \rho_k>\eta_e\ \text{ and }\ \|s_k\|_k=\Delta_k.\] For a contraction proposal \(\widetilde\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_k\Delta_k\), require \(0<\underline\gamma\leq\gamma_k\leq\overline\gamma<1\). These conditions preserve a positive finite scale, prevent unbounded expansion, and allow expansion only when the current region constrained a strongly agreeing step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeguarded radius remains positive and no larger than a prescribed maximum. Contraction factors are bounded away from zero and one, so one update neither annihilates the radius nor fails to contract. Expansion is gated by both strong model agreement and an active trust-region boundary, because an interior step does not show that a larger region would have permitted more progress.
assumptions_latex: The boundary condition uses the norm defining the current trust region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cap, contraction-factor bounds, and expansion gate define the radius safeguard system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The cap is the projection \(\Delta_{k+1}=\Pi_{(0,\widehat\Delta]}(\widetilde\Delta_{k+1})\) for positive proposals, with the upper endpoint included.
special_cases_latex: Algorithm 4.1 uses \(\gamma_k=1/4\), expansion proposal \(2\Delta_k\), and cap \(\widehat\Delta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: By induction, \(0<\Delta_k\leq\widehat\Delta\) for every finite \(k\).
No interior trial step triggers expansion.
boundary_notes: A strictly positive numerical floor is an implementation safeguard but changes asymptotic behavior and is not imposed here.
Approximate boundary tests should use a stated tolerance in finite precision.

children.title: Radius Initialization

knowledge_statements.title: Radius Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible starting-radius requirements for a safeguarded trust-region iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix radius safeguards \(0<\Delta_{\min}<\Delta_{\max}<\infty\). A valid initialization selects \(\Delta_0\in[\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\) before the first trust-region subproblem is solved. If a characteristic problem scale \(d_0>0\) is available, a scale-aware initialization may use \(\Delta_0=\min\{\Delta_{\max},\max\{\Delta_{\min},\tau d_0\}\}\) for a prescribed dimensionless \(\tau>0\). The mathematical requirement is positivity and compatibility with the imposed bounds; the particular scale estimator and value of \(\tau\) belong to the implementation policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The initial radius must be positive and satisfy its safeguards; a characteristic problem scale may be multiplied by a dimensionless factor and clipped to those bounds.
assumptions_latex: When scale-aware initialization is used, \(d_0>0\) and \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_0\in[\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\).

source_refs.locator: 6.1 The Basic Trust-Region Algorithm p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adaptive choice of the initial trust-region radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Procedure for selecting an initial trust-region radius by repeatedly testing model agreement, retaining successful scales, and optionally shifting the initial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\) and an arbitrary \(\Delta_0^{(0)}\), evaluate \(f_0\) and \(g_0\), and initialize \(i=j=0\), \(f_{\min}=f_0\), and \(\Delta_0^{\max}=0\). At each trial, compute \(d_0^{(i)},m_0^{(i)},f_0^{(i)},\rho_0^{(i)}\). If \(|\rho_0^{(i)}-1|\leq\mu_1\), set \(\Delta_0^{\max}\leftarrow\max\{\Delta_0^{\max},\Delta_0^{(i)}\}\). If additionally \(j\leq j_{\max}\) and \(f_0^{(i)}<f_{\min}\), set \(f_{\min}\leftarrow f_0^{(i)}\) and \(\sigma\leftarrow\Delta_0^{(i)}/\|g_0\|\). While \(i\leq i_{\max}\), choose \(\tau^{(i)}\) by the prescribed update rule for \(|\rho_0^{(i)}-1|>\mu_1\), for \(|\rho_0^{(i)}-1|\leq\mu_2\), or otherwise, set \(\Delta_0^{(i+1)}=\tau^{(i)}\Delta_0^{(i)}\), and increment \(i\). After the trial loop, if \(j\leq j_{\max}\) and \(f_{\min}<f_0\), replace \(x_0\) by \(x_0-\sigma g_0\), increment \(j\), and restart; otherwise return \(\Delta_0=\max\{\Delta_0^{(i)},\Delta_0^{\max}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from an arbitrary trial radius. Repeatedly compute a trial step and its model-agreement ratio, retain the largest radius whose ratio is sufficiently close to one, and update the radius using the prescribed ratio-dependent scaling rule. Record improving trials for a bounded number of restarts; after the trial loop, shift the initial point along the negative gradient and restart when such an improvement exists. Otherwise, return the larger of the final trial radius and the largest well-agreeing radius.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ and }\Delta_0^{(0)}\text{ are given, and }f_0=f(x_0),\ g_0=\nabla f(x_0)\text{ are computable}
d_0^{(i)},m_0^{(i)},f_0^{(i)},\rho_0^{(i)},\tau^{(i)}\text{ are computed by the prescribed trial and update formulas}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_0=\max\{\Delta_0^{(i)},\Delta_0^{\max}\}\text{ after at most the prescribed trial and restart limits}

children.title: Radius Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower and upper safeguards governing admissible region sizes.

knowledge_statements.title: Radius Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant lower and upper safeguards for implemented trust-region radii.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose constants \(0<\Delta_{\min}<\Delta_{\max}<\infty\). A radius sequence is bounded by the safeguard system when \(\Delta_k\in[\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\) for every implemented iteration \(k\). For any proposed radius \(\widehat\Delta_{k+1}>0\), the projection update \(\Delta_{k+1}=\min\{\Delta_{\max},\max\{\Delta_{\min},\widehat\Delta_{k+1}\}\}\) preserves this invariant. The upper bound limits excessively large local models, while the optional positive lower implementation bound prevents numerical underflow; convergence analyses may instead permit radii to approach zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clipping every proposed radius to fixed positive lower and finite upper bounds preserves the radius invariant, although theoretical analyses often omit a positive lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_{k+1}\in[\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\).

children.title: Radius Recovery
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms for restoring useful region scales after poor updates or degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Radius Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded restoration after an invalid, nonfinite, or numerically unusable radius proposal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\Delta_{\min}<\Delta_{\max}<\infty\), a recovery factor \(\gamma_{\mathrm{rec}}\in(0,1)\), and a valid previous radius \(\Delta_k\). If a proposed \(\widehat\Delta_{k+1}\) is finite and positive, use its projection onto \([\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\). Otherwise reject the invalid proposal and set \(\Delta_{k+1}=\max\{\Delta_{\min},\gamma_{\mathrm{rec}}\Delta_k\}\). Recompute the trial step within the recovered trust region before evaluating acceptance. This recovery rule restores a finite admissible radius without accepting a step generated under an invalid radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invalid radius proposal is discarded, replaced by a contracted safeguarded radius, and followed by recomputation of the trial step before acceptance is considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recovery yields \(\Delta_{k+1}\in[\Delta_{\min},\Delta_{\max}]\) and requires a new trial step.
review_flags: no authoritative locator supplied for this numerical recovery convention
recovery triggers and recomputation policies are implementation-dependent

children.title: Trust-Region Metric Geometry
children.top_down_role: Interaction between variable scaling, changing metrics, and restricted-step geometry.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Section 4.5, Scaling and Trust Regions in Other Norms

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric geometry of a trust region
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta_k>0\), and let \(\|\cdot\|_k\) be a norm, possibly varying with \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional restricted-step geometry, including Euclidean, polyhedral, and ellipsoidal trust regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The trust-region metric geometry at iteration \(k\) is the norm ball \[\mathcal B_k=\{x_k+s:\|s\|_k\leq\Delta_k\}.\] If \(S_k\) is nonsingular and \(\|s\|_k=\|S_k^{-1}s\|_2\), then \[\mathcal B_k=x_k+\{s:s^TS_k^{-T}S_k^{-1}s\leq\Delta_k^2\}=x_k+S_k\{w:\|w\|_2\leq\Delta_k\}.\] Thus a Euclidean ball in scaled coordinates \(w=S_k^{-1}s\) is an ellipsoid in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trust-region geometry is the ball of the chosen step norm centered at the current iterate. A nonsingular change of variables converts a Euclidean ball in scaled coordinates into an ellipsoid in the original coordinates, with metric matrix given by the inverse-transpose times the inverse of the scaling matrix. The norm therefore determines which directions count as long or short.
assumptions_latex: For the ellipsoidal representation, \(S_k\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B_k\) and its scaled-coordinate representation define the trust-region metric geometry.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(M_k=S_k^{-T}S_k^{-1}\succ0\), the ellipsoidal norm is \(\|s\|_{M_k}=\sqrt{s^TM_ks}\).
special_cases_latex: \(S_k=I\) gives the Euclidean ball.
The \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms give cross-polytope and box geometries rather than ellipsoids.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing the norm can change the Cauchy point, eigenpoint, and model minimizer even when the model and radius are fixed.
Variable rescaling and ellipsoidal trust-region geometry are mathematically equivalent.
boundary_notes: A positive-semidefinite singular metric defines a seminorm and an unbounded cylinder, not a norm-bounded trust region.
Metric choice alone does not guarantee model fidelity in the resulting region.

notation.meaning: Nonsingular scaling map from scaled to original steps.

children.title: Scaling Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Preselected and iteration-dependent metric families.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed and iteration-dependent trust-region scaling regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, let \(s=S_kw\), and let \(m_k(x_k+s)=f(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TH_ks\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear variable scalings for quadratic trust-region models; both preselected and iteration-dependent regimes are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scaling regime is a sequence \(\{S_k\}\) defining \[\|s\|_k=\|S_k^{-1}s\|_2,\qquad \|S_k^{-1}s\|_2\leq\Delta_k.\] In scaled coordinates, \[g_k^{(s)}=S_k^Tg_k,\qquad H_k^{(s)}=S_k^TH_kS_k,\] and \[m_k(x_k+S_kw)=f(x_k)+(g_k^{(s)})^Tw+\tfrac12w^TH_k^{(s)}w.\] The regime is fixed when \(S_k=S\) for all \(k\), diagonal when every \(S_k\) is diagonal, and adaptive when \(S_k\) depends on the current iterate, model, or preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaling regime is a fixed or varying sequence of nonsingular coordinate transformations. It defines the trust-region norm through the inverse scaling. Gradients transform by the transpose scaling and model Hessians by congruence. A fixed scaling uses one transformation throughout; a diagonal scaling changes variable units independently; an adaptive scaling may follow current curvature or preconditioning information.
assumptions_latex: The quadratic model uses a symmetric \(H_k\).
The same \(S_k\) is used consistently in the coordinate transformation, model, and trust-region constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed norm and transformed model quantities define the family of fixed, diagonal, and adaptive scaling regimes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The original-variable constraint is \(s^TS_k^{-T}S_k^{-1}s\leq\Delta_k^2\).
special_cases_latex: \(S_k=I\) is the unscaled regime.
A constant diagonal \(S\) represents preselected typical variable sizes.
A preconditioner-derived \(S_k\) gives an iteration-dependent regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: Model values are invariant under the consistent substitution \(s=S_kw\).
Scaling changes the feasible geometry without changing the represented original-space quadratic.
boundary_notes: Singular scalings are excluded.
Unboundedly ill-conditioned scaling sequences may destroy uniform metric equivalence even though each individual \(S_k\) is nonsingular.

notation.meaning: Gradient and Hessian representation in scaled coordinates.

children.title: Fixed Scaling
children.top_down_role: Trust-region metrics selected before iteration-dependent information is incorporated.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region geometry induced by one iteration-independent positive-definite scaling matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular and fixed for all iterations. The fixed-scaled trust region at iteration \(k\) is \(\mathcal{T}_k=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert Ds\rVert_2\leq\Delta_k\}\). Equivalently, with \(M=D^{\mathsf T}D\succ0\), it is the ellipsoid \(\mathcal{T}_k=\{s:s^{\mathsf T}Ms\leq\Delta_k^2\}\). Because \(D\) is independent of \(k\), only the scalar radius changes the region between iterations; the metric orientation and relative axis lengths remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed scaling uses one nonsingular matrix at every iteration, producing ellipsoidal trust regions whose size changes with the radius but whose metric geometry remains constant.
assumptions_latex: \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and independent of \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert Ds\rVert_2\leq\Delta_k\) is equivalent to \(s^{\mathsf T}D^{\mathsf T}Ds\leq\Delta_k^2\), with a fixed positive-definite metric.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Cauchy Point Calculation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimizes the linear model over the current diagonally scaled trust region and then minimizes the quadratic model along the resulting feasible ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(m_k(p)=f_k+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp\), first choose
\[
p_k^{\mathrm s}\in\arg\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\{f_k+g_k^Tp:\|Dp\|\leq\Delta_k\}.
\]
Next choose
\[
\tau_k\in\arg\min_{\tau>0}\{m_k(\tau p_k^{\mathrm s}):\|\tau Dp_k^{\mathrm s}\|\leq\Delta_k\},
\]
and set \(p_k^{\mathrm c}=\tau_kp_k^{\mathrm s}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First minimize the linear model over the current diagonally scaled trust region. Then minimize the quadratic model along the feasible positive ray generated by that solution. The resulting scaled ray point is the generalized Cauchy point.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is positive diagonal and fixed during the calculation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k^{\mathrm c}=\tau_kp_k^{\mathrm s},\quad p_k^{\mathrm s}\in\arg\min_{\|Dp\|\leq\Delta_k}(f_k+g_k^Tp),\quad \tau_k\in\arg\min_{\substack{\tau>0\\\|\tau Dp_k^{\mathrm s}\|\leq\Delta_k}}m_k(\tau p_k^{\mathrm s}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Powell–Yuan trial step and predicted reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the constrained quadratic trial step, differentiable merit function, reductions, null-space projection, and the two feasibility-reduction regimes used by the method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let d_k solve \[\min_{d\in\mathbb R^n}\phi_k(d):=g_k^Td+\tfrac12d^TB_kd\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \|c_k+A_k^Td\|_2\le \xi_k,\ \|d\|_2\le\Delta_k.\] Define \[P_k(x)=f(x)-\lambda(x)^Tc(x)+\sigma_k\|c(x)\|_2^2,\qquad \lambda(x)\in\arg\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\|g(x)-A(x)\lambda\|_2,\] with the minimum-norm least-squares solution, \(Ared_k=P_k(x_k)-P_k(x_k+d_k)\), \(\bar d_k=\bar P_kd_k\), and \(\bar P_k=I-A(x_k)A(x_k)^+\). The predicted reduction is \[\begin{aligned}Pred_k={}&-(g_k-A_k\lambda_k)^Td_k-\tfrac12d_k^TB_k\bar d_k\\&+[\lambda(x_k+d_k)-\lambda_k]^T\!\left(c_k+\tfrac12A_k^Td_k\right)\\&+\sigma_k\bigl(\|c_k\|_2^2-\|c_k+A_k^Td_k\|_2^2\bigr).\end{aligned}\] If \(\|c_k\|_2-\|c_k+A_k^Td_k\|_2>0\), then \(\sigma_k\) can be increased, if necessary, so that \[Pred_k\ge\tfrac12\sigma_k\bigl(\|c_k\|_2^2-\|c_k+A_k^Td_k\|_2^2\bigr).\] If the norm difference is zero, then \(d_k\) minimizes \(\phi_k\) over the intersection of the trust region and \(\ker(A_k^T)\), \(Pred_k=\phi_k(0)-\phi_k(d_k)\), and \[Pred_k=0\iff g_k-A_k\lambda_k=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trial step minimizes the quadratic model subject to a linearized-feasibility bound and a trust region. Actual reduction is measured with Fletcher's differentiable merit function, while predicted reduction combines projected quadratic decrease, multiplier variation, and squared constraint reduction. Strict linearized constraint reduction permits the penalty to be raised until the stated positive lower bound holds. With zero constraint-norm reduction, the step is the null-space trust-region minimizer, and predicted reduction vanishes exactly when the projected stationarity residual vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \lambda(x)\text{ is the minimum-norm solution of }\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\|g(x)-A(x)\lambda\|_2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}\|c_k\|_2>\|c_k+A_k^Td_k\|_2\Rightarrow Pred_k\ge\frac12\sigma_k(\|c_k\|_2^2-\|c_k+A_k^Td_k\|_2^2)\text{ after increasing }\sigma_k\text{ if needed},\\ \|c_k\|_2=\|c_k+A_k^Td_k\|_2\Rightarrow Pred_k=\phi_k(0)-\phi_k(d_k),\quad Pred_k=0\iff g_k-A_k\lambda_k=0.\end{cases}

children.title: Adaptive Scaling
children.top_down_role: Trust-region metrics adjusted using evolving problem or model information.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-dependent metric scaling for smooth trust-region models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\Delta_k>0\), and let \(D_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be a symmetric positive-definite scaling matrix chosen using information available at iteration \(k\). An adaptively scaled trust region is \[\mathcal T_k=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|D_ks\|_2\leq\Delta_k\}.\] To prevent degeneration of the changing geometry, require constants \(0<d_-\leq d_+<\infty\), independent of \(k\), such that \[d_-I\preceq D_k\preceq d_+I\qquad\text{for every }k\geq0.\] The rule producing \(D_{k+1}\) may use current derivative or curvature information, but it must preserve these uniform bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive scaling chooses the trust-region metric from current iteration information while imposing iteration-independent lower and upper spectral bounds that prevent the metric from degenerating.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
The scaling rule preserves \(d_-I\preceq D_k\preceq d_+I\) for fixed constants \(0<d_-\leq d_+<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regions \(\mathcal T_k=\{s:\|D_ks\|_2\leq\Delta_k\}\) use an adaptive metric that remains uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean metric.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Transition Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform safeguards for transitions between consecutive trust-region metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_k,D_{k+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive-definite scaling matrices. A safeguarded scaling transition satisfies fixed constants \(0<\sigma_-\leq1\leq\sigma_+<\infty\) such that, for every \(s\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\sigma_-\|D_ks\|_2\leq\|D_{k+1}s\|_2\leq\sigma_+\|D_ks\|_2.\] Equivalently, \[\sigma_-^2D_k^2\preceq D_{k+1}^2\preceq\sigma_+^2D_k^2.\] Thus one transition cannot make the measured norm of any step arbitrarily smaller or larger relative to the preceding metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeguarded transition bounds the change between consecutive scaled norms by fixed factors, preventing a single metric update from abruptly collapsing or enlarging the measured size of a step.
assumptions_latex: The constants \(\sigma_-\) and \(\sigma_+\) are positive and independent of \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_-\|D_ks\|_2\leq\|D_{k+1}s\|_2\leq\sigma_+\|D_ks\|_2\) for every \(s\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: uniform lower and upper transition factors

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform equivalence class of changing trust-region metrics
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{\|\cdot\|_k\}_{k\geq0}\) be norms on \(\mathbb R^n\). For ellipsoidal metrics, write \(\|x\|_k=\|S_k^{-1}x\|_2\) with nonsingular \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional changing metrics used in convergence analysis; equivalence constants must be uniform over iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \(\{\|\cdot\|_k\}\) belongs to a uniformly Euclidean-equivalent changing-metric class if there exists \(\kappa_{une}\geq1\), independent of \(k\), such that \[\frac1{\kappa_{une}}\|x\|_k\leq\|x\|_2\leq\kappa_{une}\|x\|_k\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n\text{ and }k\geq0.\] For \(\|x\|_k=\|S_k^{-1}x\|_2\), a sufficient class condition is \[\frac1{\kappa_{scb}}\leq\sigma_{\min}(S_k)\leq\sigma_{\max}(S_k)\leq\kappa_{scb}\qquad\text{for every }k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing trust-region norms are uniformly equivalent when one iteration-independent constant compares every one of them with the Euclidean norm in both directions. For ellipsoidal norms generated by scaling matrices, uniform lower and upper singular-value bounds are sufficient. This prevents trust regions from flattening without bound in one direction or expanding without bound in another as iterations proceed.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\|\cdot\|_k\) is a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\).
The constants \(\kappa_{une}\) and \(\kappa_{scb}\), when used, do not depend on \(k\).
Every ellipsoidal scaling matrix \(S_k\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed two-sided norm comparison defines the changing-metric equivalence class, and the singular-value bounds give a sufficient membership condition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exist constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\) independent of \(k\) such that \(c\|x\|_2\leq\|x\|_k\leq C\|x\|_2\) for all \(x,k\).
For metric matrices \(M_k=S_k^{-T}S_k^{-1}\), uniform equivalence is equivalent to uniform positive lower and finite upper spectral bounds on \(M_k\).
special_cases_latex: Any fixed norm sequence \(\|\cdot\|_k\equiv\|\cdot\|_*\) is uniformly equivalent in finite dimension.
Uniformly bounded diagonal scalings with diagonal entries bounded away from zero satisfy the condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Trust regions cannot asymptotically collapse or become unbounded in a direction relative to their stated radii.
Euclidean step lengths and metric step lengths control each other uniformly over all iterations.
boundary_notes: Individual norm equivalence at each iteration is insufficient if its constants diverge with \(k\).
The condition is sufficient for the cited convergence framework but may be relaxable along only the generated gradient, step, and negative-curvature directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Equivalent Norms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform equivalence of an iteration-indexed norm family to a reference norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a fixed norm on \(X\), and let \(\{\|\cdot\|_k\}_{k\geq0}\) be norms on \(X\). The family is uniformly equivalent to \(\|\cdot\|\) if there exist constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\), independent of \(k\), such that \[c\|s\|\leq\|s\|_k\leq C\|s\|\qquad\text{for every }s\in X\text{ and }k\geq0.\] Consequently, the balls satisfy \(\{s:\|s\|\leq r/C\}\subseteq\{s:\|s\|_k\leq r\}\subseteq\{s:\|s\|\leq r/c\}\) for every \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A changing family of norms is uniformly equivalent to a reference norm when common positive comparison constants work for every vector and every iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\|s\|\leq\|s\|_k\leq C\|s\|\) uniformly in \(s\) and \(k\).

children.title: Weakly Equivalent Norms
children.top_down_role: Changing-metric regimes governed by less restrictive norm comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Equivalent Norms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise, but not necessarily uniform, equivalence of changing norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space with reference norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and let \(\|\cdot\|_k\) be a norm for every \(k\geq0\). The family is weakly equivalent to the reference norm if, for each \(k\), there exist numbers \(0<c_k\leq C_k<\infty\) satisfying \[c_k\|s\|\leq\|s\|_k\leq C_k\|s\|\qquad\text{for every }s\in X,\] without requiring \(\inf_k c_k>0\) or \(\sup_k C_k<\infty\). Hence each individual metric has the same topology as the reference metric, although the comparison may degenerate along the iteration sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each changing norm is equivalent to the reference norm separately, but its comparison constants may deteriorate without any iteration-independent bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_k\|s\|\leq\|s\|_k\leq C_k\|s\|\) for each fixed \(k\), with no uniform bound required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criticality-weighted comparison of changing norms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition comparing a reference norm with iteration-dependent norms; the lower comparison may degenerate as the criticality measure approaches zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) and \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_k\) be norms on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). There exist constants \(\kappa_{\mathrm{low}}>0\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{up}}>0\), and a criticality measure satisfying \(\pi(x_k)\in[0,1]\), such that for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(k\ge 0\), \[\kappa_{\mathrm{low}}\pi(x_k)\lVert x\rVert_k\leq\lVert x\rVert\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{up}}\lVert x\rVert_k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every iteration, the reference norm is at most a uniform multiple of the iteration-dependent norm. Its lower comparison is weighted by the current criticality measure and can therefore weaken or vanish when that measure is small or zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_{\mathrm{low}}\pi(x_k)\lVert x\rVert_k\leq\lVert x\rVert\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{up}}\lVert x\rVert_k\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(k\geq0\)

knowledge_statements.title: Changing-Metric Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of step-size and convergence statements under uniform metric equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\{\|\cdot\|_k\}\) is uniformly equivalent to a reference norm \(\|\cdot\|\), with \(c\|s\|\leq\|s\|_k\leq C\|s\|\). For every sequence \(s_k\in X\), \[\|s_k\|_k\to0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\|s_k\|\to0.\] Moreover, if \(\|s_k\|_k\leq\Delta_k\), then \(\|s_k\|\leq\Delta_k/c\); conversely, \(\|s_k\|\leq\Delta_k/C\) implies \(\|s_k\|_k\leq\Delta_k\). Therefore shrinking trust-region radii force shrinking steps in the reference geometry, and metric trust-region balls admit uniform inner and outer reference-norm bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform norm equivalence transfers vanishing-step statements and traps every changing-metric trust region between fixed multiples of reference-norm balls.
assumptions_latex: \(c\|s\|\leq\|s\|_k\leq C\|s\|\) for all \(s\in X\) and \(k\), with \(0<c\leq C<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|s_k\|_k\to0\iff\|s_k\|\to0\), with the stated uniform ball inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Geometry-Reflecting Trust Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust regions induced by norms whose unit balls reflect weighted, block, or polyhedral problem structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_k>0\), and let \(P_k\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and contain \(0\) in its interior. Its Minkowski functional \(\gamma_{P_k}:\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,\infty)\), defined by \[\gamma_{P_k}(s)=\inf\{t>0:s\in tP_k\},\] is a norm, and the corresponding trust region satisfies \[\mathcal T_k=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\gamma_{P_k}(s)\leq\Delta_k\}=\Delta_kP_k.\] Examples include \(\gamma_{P_k}(s)=\|D_ks\|_1\) for an invertible \(D_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\); \(\gamma_{P_k}(s)=\max_{1\leq j\leq q}\|D_{k,j}s_j\|_{p_j}\) for a fixed block decomposition \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_q)\), exponents \(1\leq p_j\leq\infty\), and injective block maps \(D_{k,j}\); and \(\gamma_{P_k}(s)=\|A_ks\|_\infty\) for a matrix \(A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\) with trivial nullspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem-geometry-reflecting trust region is a scaled unit ball of a norm chosen to represent weighted, block, or polyhedral structure.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and contains \(0\) in its interior.
Every linear map used in a displayed norm representation is injective on its stated domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T_k=\{s:\gamma_{P_k}(s)\leq\Delta_k\}=\Delta_kP_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure-sensitive norm trust region
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\) is the current iterate, \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) is a trial step, \(\Delta_k>0\), and \(D_k\) is a nonsingular scaling matrix chosen from problem structure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic trust regions defined by scaled polyhedral norms; more general gauges require separate assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem-geometry-reflecting trust region is a set \[\mathcal T_k(\Delta_k)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:\|D_kp\|_{\mathsf s}\leq\Delta_k\},\qquad \mathsf s\in\{1,\infty\},\] where the scaling \(D_k\) and norm are selected to represent known anisotropy, block scaling, or coordinatewise step restrictions. Its unit set is centrally symmetric, convex, closed, bounded, and contains the origin in its interior. Equivalently, it is the inverse image under \(D_k\) of a scaled cross-polytope when \(\mathsf s=1\), or a scaled box when \(\mathsf s=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem-geometry-reflecting trust region consists of all steps \(p\) whose scaled \(\ell_1\) or \(\ell_\infty\) norm is at most \(\Delta_k\). The nonsingular scaling \(D_k\) encodes known coordinate or block anisotropy. Thus the region is a cross-polytope or box in scaled coordinates and is a closed, bounded, centrally symmetric convex neighborhood of zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T_k(\Delta_k)=\{p:\|D_kp\|_{\mathsf s}\leq\Delta_k\}\) is the structure-sensitive trust region used to restrict the local-model step.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(z=D_kp\), \(\mathcal T_k(\Delta_k)=D_k^{-1}\{z:\|z\|_{\mathsf s}\leq\Delta_k\}\).
For \(\mathsf s=\infty\), membership is equivalent to \(|(D_kp)_i|\leq\Delta_k\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: \(D_k=I\) gives the ordinary \(\ell_1\) or \(\ell_\infty\) trust region.
Diagonal \(D_k\) gives coordinate-scaled absolute-value bounds.
immediate_consequences_latex: The region is compact, so every continuous local model attains a minimum on it.
Nonsingular scaling makes its induced norm equivalent to the Euclidean norm in finite dimensions.
boundary_notes: This definition does not cover asymmetric regions or unbounded gauges.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonally Scaled Trust-Region Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an ellipsoidal trust region for a quadratic local model and records the source's sufficient boundedness condition for iteration-dependent diagonal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m_k(p)=f_k+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp\), with \(\|\cdot\|\) the Euclidean norm. A positive diagonal matrix \(D_k=\operatorname{diag}(d_{k,1},\ldots,d_{k,n})\) defines the scaled trust-region subproblem
\[
\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}m_k(p)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \|D_kp\|\leq\Delta_k.
\]
Large \(d_{k,i}\) shorten the ellipsoid in sensitive coordinate directions, whereas smaller entries permit longer steps in less-sensitive directions. The scaling may vary with \(k\); the source states that most of the chapter's trust-region theory continues to apply, with minor modifications, provided
\[
0<d_{\mathrm{lo}}\leq d_{k,i}\leq d_{\mathrm{hi}}<\infty\qquad\forall k,i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal scaling changes a Euclidean trust region into an ellipsoid. Larger diagonal entries restrict movement in sensitive coordinates. If the scaling changes between iterations, the source qualifies its theoretical transfer by requiring all diagonal entries to remain uniformly bounded above and away from zero.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the stated variable-scaling transfer: }0<d_{\mathrm{lo}}\leq d_{k,i}\leq d_{\mathrm{hi}}<\infty\quad\forall k,i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal T_k=\{p:\|D_kp\|_2\leq\Delta_k\};\quad \text{under uniform positive bounds on }D_k,\text{ most of the referenced trust-region theory applies with minor modifications.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Form and Spherical Rescaling of the Diagonal-Metric Cauchy Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the scaled linear-model solution and feasible ray length, then records the equivalent spherical trust-region model under a diagonal change of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(g_k\neq0\), \(D\succ0\) is diagonal, \(\Delta_k>0\), and \(\|\cdot\|=\|\cdot\|_2\). Then
\[
p_k^{\mathrm s}=-\frac{\Delta_k}{\|D^{-1}g_k\|_2}D^{-2}g_k,
\]
and
\[
\tau_k=\begin{cases}
1,&g_k^TD^{-2}B_kD^{-2}g_k\leq0,\\[2mm]
\min\!\left\{\dfrac{\|D^{-1}g_k\|_2^3}{\Delta_k g_k^TD^{-2}B_kD^{-2}g_k},1\right\},&g_k^TD^{-2}B_kD^{-2}g_k>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(p_k^{\mathrm c}=\tau_kp_k^{\mathrm s}\). With \(\widetilde p=Dp\), the scaled subproblem is equivalently
\[
\min_{\|\widetilde p\|_2\leq\Delta_k}\left[f_k+(D^{-1}g_k)^T\widetilde p+\tfrac12\widetilde p^T(D^{-1}B_kD^{-1})\widetilde p\right].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonzero gradient and a positive diagonal metric, the scaled linear-model solution and its optimal feasible quadratic-model ray length have explicit formulas. The substitution p-tilde = Dp converts the ellipsoidal subproblem into a Euclidean-ball trust-region subproblem with transformed gradient D inverse g and transformed Hessian D inverse B D inverse.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Non-Euclidean Trust Regions and the Infinity-Norm Box Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records common non-Euclidean trust-region geometries and the box form induced by the infinity norm in a bound-constrained quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Trust regions may be defined by \(\|p\|_1\leq\Delta_k\), \(\|p\|_\infty\leq\Delta_k\), or, for positive diagonal \(D\), by \(\|Dp\|_1\leq\Delta_k\) or \(\|Dp\|_\infty\leq\Delta_k\). For a feasible iterate \(x_k\geq0\), the infinity-norm bound-constrained subproblem
\[
\min_p m_k(p)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_k+p\geq0,\quad \|p\|_\infty\leq\Delta_k
\]
has the equivalent box constraints
\[
x_k+p\geq0,\qquad -\Delta_ke\leq p\leq\Delta_ke.
\]
Hence it is a bound-constrained quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trust regions can use the 1-norm or infinity norm, with or without positive diagonal scaling. For a nonnegativity-constrained problem, an infinity-norm trust region combines with feasibility to give coordinatewise lower and upper bounds, making the model subproblem a bound-constrained quadratic program.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is positive diagonal when a scaled norm is used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{p:x_k+p\geq0,\ \|p\|_\infty\leq\Delta_k\}=\{p:x_k+p\geq0,\ -\Delta_ke\leq p\leq\Delta_ke\},\quad\text{so the model subproblem is a bound-constrained QP.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First- and second-order trust-region fidelity hierarchy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(x\in S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(0<\Delta\leq\Delta_{\max}\), and \(B(x;\Delta)=\{y:\|y-x\|_2\leq\Delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth finite-dimensional models, organized into the fully linear and fully quadratic accuracy levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The trust-region model fidelity hierarchy consists of two nested accuracy specifications. A \(C^1\) model is first-order faithful on \(B(x;\Delta)\) when constants independent of \(x\) and \(\Delta\) satisfy \[|f(y)-m(y)|\leq\kappa_{ef}\Delta^2,\qquad \|
abla f(y)-
abla m(y)\|\leq\kappa_{eg}\Delta.\] A \(C^2\) model is second-order faithful when \[|f(y)-m(y)|\leq\kappa_{ef}\Delta^3,\quad \|
abla f(y)-
abla m(y)\|\leq\kappa_{eg}\Delta^2,\quad \|
abla^2f(y)-
abla^2m(y)\|\leq\kappa_{eh}\Delta\] for every \(y\in B(x;\Delta)\). A model class occupies a level when an appropriate model exists uniformly for every admissible center and radius and can be certified or produced by a uniformly finite model-improvement procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fidelity hierarchy has a first-order level, with function and gradient errors of orders \(\Delta^2\) and \(\Delta\), and a second-order level, with function, gradient, and Hessian errors of orders \(\Delta^3\), \(\Delta^2\), and \(\Delta\). The constants are uniform over admissible centers and radii, and the model class must admit a uniformly finite certification or improvement procedure.
assumptions_latex: For the first-order level, \(f\in C^1\) and \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the relevant balls.
For the second-order level, \(f\in C^2\) and \(\nabla^2 f\) is Lipschitz on that neighborhood.
The constants \(\kappa_{ef},\kappa_{eg},\kappa_{eh}>0\) do not depend on \(x\), \(\Delta\), or \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed scale-dependent inequalities define the fully linear and fully quadratic levels of the model-fidelity hierarchy.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The order-two level strengthens the order-one level by controlling one additional derivative and improving the powers of \(\Delta\) in the lower-order errors.
special_cases_latex: Exact first- or second-order Taylor models satisfy the corresponding local orders under Lipschitz derivative assumptions.
Well-poised polynomial interpolation and regression models can furnish these fidelity classes.
immediate_consequences_latex: Shrinking \(\Delta\) forces the model derivatives to approach the corresponding objective derivatives at the stated rates.
boundary_notes: Membership of a model class does not imply that every member is accurate at every center and radius.
Stochastic or probabilistic fidelity is outside this deterministic hierarchy.

notation.meaning: Uniform function, gradient, and Hessian error constants.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), current point \(x_k\), step \(p\in\mathbb R^n\), radius \(\Delta_k>0\), vector \(g_k\in\mathbb R^n\), and symmetric \(B_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A local quadratic model of \(f\) at \(x_k\) is the map \[m_k(p)=c_k+g_k^Tp+	frac12p^TB_kp,\qquad \|p\|\leq\Delta_k,\] where \(c_k\) approximates \(f(x_k)\), \(g_k\) approximates \(

abla f(x_k)\), and a second-order Taylor model when also \(B_k=

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local trust-region representation is a quadratic function of the step \(p\), consisting of a constant, a linear term \(g_k^Tp\), and a symmetric curvature term \(p^TB_kp/2\), used only for steps inside the radius \(\Delta_k\). \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\) and \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) give the second-order Taylor model.
immediate_consequences_latex: The model gradient and Hessian in step coordinates are \(\nabla m_k(p)=g_k+B_kp\) and \(\nabla^2m_k(p)=B_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General trust-region iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic local optimization framework; it does not guarantee discovery of a global minimizer and permits variations in problem class, norm, model construction, and trial-step computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To seek a local minimizer of \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), a trust-region method maintains iterates \(x_k\), local models \(m_k\), radii \(\Delta_k>0\), and trust regions \(\mathcal T_k=\{x_k+s:\|s\|\leq\Delta_k\}\). At iteration \(k\), it chooses a trial step \(s_k\) in the trust region that gives sufficient model decrease and evaluates \(f(x_k+s_k)\). When \(m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)>0\), it compares actual and predicted reductions through \(\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)}\). If \(\rho_k\) is sufficiently positive, the trial point is accepted as the next iterate; otherwise it is rejected. An unsuccessful ratio causes \(\Delta_k\) to decrease, while a successful ratio permits the radius to increase or remain unchanged. The framework is local and provides no guarantee that the attained local minimizer is globally best.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region method repeatedly builds a local model around the current iterate, restricts a sufficiently model-decreasing trial step to a norm ball, and compares the objective decrease actually achieved with the decrease predicted by the model. A sufficiently positive agreement ratio permits acceptance of the trial point; inadequate agreement leads to rejection and a smaller region, while successful agreement permits the radius to grow or stay fixed. The procedure seeks a local solution and does not guarantee a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)};\quad \rho_k\ \text{sufficiently positive}\Rightarrow x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\quad \rho_k\ \text{not sufficiently positive}\Rightarrow x_{k+1}=x_k\ \text{and}\ \Delta_{k+1}<\Delta_k.

knowledge_statements.title: Taylor Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-p Taylor approximation used as a local trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(p\)-times continuously differentiable near \(x_k\), where \(p\geq1\). The order-\(p\) Taylor model at \(x_k\) is \[T_{k,p}(s)=f(x_k)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}\nabla^jf(x_k)[s]^j.\] If \(\nabla^pf\) is locally Lipschitz and the segment \(\{x_k+ts:0\leq t\leq1\}\) remains in that neighborhood, then \[f(x_k+s)-T_{k,p}(s)=O(\|s\|^{p+1})\qquad\text{as }s\to0.\] A trust-region method assesses or minimizes this model only over its prescribed region of trial steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The order-p Taylor model truncates the derivative expansion after degree p; if the p-th derivative is locally Lipschitz, its local value error is of order p+1.
assumptions_latex: The segment \(\{x_k+ts:0\leq t\leq1\}\) remains in that neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition on a domain that excludes zeros of the affine denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth function $c:D\to\mathbb R$ is conic if and only if there exist a quadratic function $p$ and an affine function $\ell$ such that $\ell(x)\neq0$ for every $x\in D$ and $c(x)=p(x)/\ell(x)^2$ for every $x\in D$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth function is conic exactly when, on its domain, it is the ratio of a quadratic function to the square of a nonzero affine function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Collinear-scaling representation of a conic local model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation, stationarity equation, admissibility boundary, and minimizer formula for the conic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $1+b^Td\neq0$, define
\[
c(d)=f(x_k)+\frac{g_k^Td}{1+b^Td}+\frac12\frac{d^TA_kd}{(1+b^Td)^2},\qquad \widetilde d=\frac{d}{1+b^Td}.
\]
The inverse change is $d=\widetilde d/(1-b^T\widetilde d)$ whenever $1-b^T\widetilde d\neq0$, and in the transformed coordinate
\[
c(\widetilde d)=f(x_k)+g_k^T\widetilde d+\tfrac12\widetilde d^TA_k\widetilde d.
\]
Moreover, $\nabla c(d)=0$ if and only if $g_k+A_kd/(1+b^Td)=0$. If $A_k$ is invertible and $1+b^TA_k^{-1}g_k\neq0$, the stationary step is
\[
d_*=-\frac{A_k^{-1}g_k}{1+b^TA_k^{-1}g_k}.
\]
If additionally $A_k\succ0$, this admissible stationary step corresponds to the unique minimizer of the transformed quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic local model becomes an ordinary quadratic model after the collinear change of variables d-tilde = d/(1+bᵀd). Away from the singular affine hyperplane, stationarity is equivalent to a linear equation in the transformed step. If the curvature matrix is invertible and the resulting step is admissible, the stationary step has the displayed closed form; positive-definite curvature makes it the unique transformed-model minimizer.
assumptions_latex: A_k\text{ is invertible for the closed-form stationary step}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(d)=f(x_k)+g_k^T\widetilde d+\tfrac12\widetilde d^TA_k\widetilde d,\quad \nabla c(d)=0\iff g_k+\frac{A_kd}{1+b^Td}=0,\quad d_*=-\frac{A_k^{-1}g_k}{1+b^TA_k^{-1}g_k}

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\) is a real Hilbert space, \(g_k\in X\), and \(\mathcal B_k:X\to X\) is a bounded self-adjoint linear operator.

It is completely specified by its center value, linear coefficient, and curvature operator. The operator may be stored explicitly or accessed only through its action on vectors, and it may represent exact, updated, sampled, or projected curvature.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secant-curvature trust-region model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable, \(s_{k-1}=x_k-x_{k-1}\), and \(y_{k-1}=\nabla f(x_k)-\nabla f(x_{k-1})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic smooth unconstrained optimization using a symmetric Hessian approximation in a quadratic trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A quasi-Newton trust-region model is \[m_k(p)=f(x_k)+\nabla f(x_k)^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp,
\qquad \|p\|\leq\Delta_k,\] where \(B_k=B_k^T\) is an approximation to \(\nabla^2f(x_k)\) obtained from previous iterates and gradients by a quasi-Newton update. For an unmodified secant update based on the most recent displacement, the defining interpolation condition is \[B_ks_{k-1}=y_{k-1}.\] Positive definiteness is optional for a trust-region model; indefinite approximations, such as those produced by SR1, remain admissible because the step is restricted to a bounded region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-Newton trust-region model replaces the exact Hessian in the quadratic model by a symmetric matrix updated from previous steps and gradient differences. A standard secant update makes the new approximation map the latest displacement \(s_{k-1}\) to the latest gradient change \(y_{k-1}\). Unlike a line-search direction matrix, the model matrix need not be positive definite because the trust-region subproblem remains bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at the points defining \(y_{k-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic model with updated secant curvature \(B_k\) is a quasi-Newton trust-region model.
equivalent_formulations_latex: An inverse update uses \(H_ky_{k-1}=s_{k-1}\) when \(H_k=B_k^{-1}\) exists.
special_cases_latex: BFGS maintains positive definiteness when its curvature condition holds.
SR1 may produce an indefinite \(B_k\), which is admissible in a trust region.
immediate_consequences_latex: The model uses curvature information without evaluating the exact Hessian.
boundary_notes: The secant equation alone does not select a unique update.
Skipped or damped updates may replace the exact secant condition by a safeguarded variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic trust-region model and transformed quadratic representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains the explicit rational model and transformed subproblem. The convergence claims are not promoted because their hypotheses are absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a current point x, let f=f(x), g=\nabla f(x), A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n} be a Hessian approximation, a\in\mathbb R^n, D be a scaling matrix, and \Delta>0. On the domain 1-a^Ts>0, the conic trust-region subproblem is
\[
\min_s\; f+\frac{g^Ts}{1-a^Ts}+\frac12\frac{s^TAs}{(1-a^Ts)^2}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|Ds\|\le\Delta.
\]
Under the associated conic parameterization, it can be written as
\[
\min_w\; f+g^TJw+\frac12w^TBw
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
s=\frac{Jw}{1+h^Tw},\quad \|Ds\|\le\Delta,
\]
where 1+h^Tw\ne0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic trust-region model replaces the ordinary quadratic local model by a rational expression defined only where its conic denominator is positive. Under the associated conic change of variables, the objective becomes quadratic in the transformed variable w while the scaled trust-region constraint remains imposed on the original step s.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\text{ is a Hessian approximation},\quad a\in\mathbb R^n,\quad \Delta>0
J,h,B\text{ are the associated conic-model parameters}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\|Ds\|\le\Delta}\left(f+\frac{g^Ts}{1-a^Ts}+\frac12\frac{s^TAs}{(1-a^Ts)^2}\right)\quad\text{admits the stated quadratic representation in }w

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Curvature Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic models represented through a symmetric curvature-action oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\mathcal B_k:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a linear self-adjoint operator available through products \(v\mapsto\mathcal B_kv\). The matrix-free quadratic model is \[m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12\langle s,\mathcal B_ks\rangle.\] Its gradient with respect to \(s\) is \[\nabla m_k(s)=g_k+\mathcal B_ks.\] Consequently, model values, gradient actions, and Krylov subproblem iterations can be computed without assembling a curvature matrix. If \(f\) is twice differentiable at \(x_k\) and \(\mathcal B_kv=\nabla^2f(x_k)v\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), this is the exact-Hessian quadratic model in operator form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature is represented by products with a self-adjoint linear operator, allowing model values, gradients, and Krylov trust-region computations without storing a Hessian matrix.
assumptions_latex: The ambient space is \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its Euclidean inner product.
The oracle returns \(\mathcal B_kv\) for every requested \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12\langle s,\mathcal B_ks\rangle\) and \(\nabla m_k(s)=g_k+\mathcal B_ks\).

notation.meaning: model gradient vector at the current point

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature-action quadratic model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(g_k\in\mathbb R^n\), \(B_k=B_k^T\), and an oracle returns \(\mathcal O_k(v)=B_kv\) for requested vectors \(v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-scale finite-dimensional trust-region models evaluated and minimized through matrix-vector products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix-free curvature model is the quadratic \[m_k(p)=c_k+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp,
\qquad \|p\|\leq\Delta_k,\] together with an access contract that supplies \(B_kv\) for arbitrary requested \(v\) without requiring assembly or storage of the entries of \(B_k\). The quadratic term is evaluated as \(p^T\mathcal O_k(p)/2\), and Krylov iterations generate their residuals and search directions using only calls to \(\mathcal O_k\), vector operations, and inner products. For Newton curvature, an action may be exact or approximated by a gradient difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free curvature model is an ordinary symmetric quadratic trust-region model equipped only with a vector-product oracle for its curvature matrix. Model values and Krylov subproblem iterations use products \(B_kv\), inner products, and vector operations, so the matrix entries need not be formed or stored. With Newton curvature, the products can be exact Hessian-vector products or gradient-difference approximations.
assumptions_latex: The oracle satisfies \(\mathcal O_k(v)=B_kv\) for every vector requested by the subproblem solver.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((m_k,\mathcal O_k)\) defines a matrix-free curvature model.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p^TB_kp=\langle p,\mathcal O_k(p)\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For Newton-CG, \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\).
A finite-difference action is \(\mathcal O_k(v)\approx[\nabla f(x_k+hv)-\nabla f(x_k)]/h\).
immediate_consequences_latex: CG-Steihaug iterations require curvature actions but not an explicit factorization.
boundary_notes: An inaccurate action defines an inexact model and requires separate error control.
Matrix-free access does not by itself reduce the number of oracle calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Subspace-Restricted Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of a quadratic local model and Euclidean trust region to a selected search subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(x_k,g_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(B_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(\Delta_k>0\). Choose an integer \(r_k\) with \(1\leq r_k\leq n\), and let \(Q_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r_k}\) satisfy \(Q_k^{\mathsf T}Q_k=I_{r_k}\). Its columns span the search subspace \(\mathcal S_k=\operatorname{range}(Q_k)\), and every restricted step has the form \(s=Q_kz\) for \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{r_k}\). For \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}B_ks\), the restricted model is \[\widehat m_k(z)=m_k(Q_kz)=f(x_k)+(Q_k^{\mathsf T}g_k)^{\mathsf T}z+\tfrac12z^{\mathsf T}(Q_k^{\mathsf T}B_kQ_k)z.\] Because \(Q_k\) has orthonormal columns, \(\|Q_kz\|_2=\|z\|_2\); hence the Euclidean constraint \(\|s\|_2\leq\Delta_k\) is equivalent to \(\|z\|_2\leq\Delta_k\) on \(\mathcal S_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal basis parameterizes the selected search subspace, projects the quadratic model into reduced coordinates, and preserves the Euclidean trust-region radius when the reduced step is lifted.
assumptions_latex: The full-space trust region uses the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat m_k(z)=f(x_k)+(Q_k^{\mathsf T}g_k)^{\mathsf T}z+\tfrac12z^{\mathsf T}(Q_k^{\mathsf T}B_kQ_k)z\), with \(\|Q_kz\|_2=\|z\|_2\).

notation.meaning: orthonormal basis matrix for the search subspace
reduced coordinates of a trial step
quadratic model restricted to reduced coordinates

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subspace-restricted model substitutes \(p=Q_kz\) into the full quadratic model. special_cases_latex: For positive definite \(B_k\), choosing \(\mathcal S_k=\operatorname{span}\{g_k,B_k^{-1}g_k\}\) gives two-dimensional subspace minimization.
Krylov subspaces give iteratively enlarged restricted models.

boundary_notes: Accuracy outside \(\mathcal S_k\) is neither asserted nor assessed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Problem-derived local-model interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(F:X\to Y\) is a problem map, \(\Phi:Y\to\mathbb R\), and the objective has the structured form \(f=\Phi\circ F\), possibly with constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface for importing problem-derived residual, constraint, or regularization structure into trust-region step computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structured local-model interface at \(x_k\) is a tuple \[\mathfrak M_k=(m_k,\mathcal T_k,\mathcal E_k),\] where \(m_k\) is obtained from a local representation of the problem maps, \(\mathcal T_k\) is the admissible trust-region step set, and \(\mathcal E_k\) exposes the quantities required to evaluate \(m_k(p)\), its first-order action, and any curvature action for \(p\in\mathcal T_k\). Consistency at the center requires \(m_k(0)=f(x_k)\) and \(Dm_k(0)=Df(x_k)\) whenever these derivatives exist. The interface specifies the local object supplied to trust-region globalization, not the complete specialized algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured model interface packages a problem-derived local model, its admissible trust-region steps, and evaluation operations for values, first-order information, and curvature actions. It matches the objective value and derivative at the center when those quantities exist. The interface defines what a specialized model supplies to trust-region globalization, without defining the specialized method's full iteration.
assumptions_latex: The evaluator \(\mathcal E_k\) is defined for every \(p\in\mathcal T_k\).
When first-order consistency is claimed, \(f\) and \(m_k\) are differentiable at the center.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak M_k=(m_k,\mathcal T_k,\mathcal E_k)\) is a structured model interface when it satisfies the stated domain and center-consistency conditions.
special_cases_latex: Residual linearization gives the Gauss-Newton interface.
Lagrangian quadratic approximation gives the SQP interface.
immediate_consequences_latex: A trust-region framework can consume different structured models through the same value and derivative-action contract.
boundary_notes: This abstraction does not prescribe acceptance ratios, multiplier updates, or regularization updates.
No single inspected source states this exact interface tuple.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-Squares Models Induced by Residual Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes Gauss–Newton, full Newton, and quadratic-residual-induced objective models, including the convex-model failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_k=m_k^c(x_k)\), \(A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and define \(m_k^f(x_k+s)=\tfrac12\|m_k^c(x_k+s)\|_2^2\). If \[m_k^c(x_k+s)=r_k+A_ks,\] then \[m_k^f(x_k+s)=\frac12\|r_k+A_ks\|_2^2,\] which is the convex quadratic Gauss--Newton model. With \(H_{ik}=\nabla_{xx}m_{ik}^c(x_k)\), the full Newton quadratic model additionally contains \[\frac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_{ik}s^TH_{ik}s.\] If instead \[m_k^c(x_k+s)=r_k+A_ks+\frac12w_k(s,s),\qquad [w_k(u,v)]_i=u^TH_{ik}v,\] then squaring the residual model also produces the cubic term \(\tfrac12\langle A_ks,w_k(s,s)\rangle\) and quartic term \(\tfrac18\|w_k(s,s)\|_2^2\). Because the Gauss--Newton model is convex, it can fail to represent negative curvature; in the stated trust-region setting, convergence to a critical point need not yield second-order criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring an affine residual model gives the convex quadratic Gauss–Newton model. Adding residual-component Hessian contributions gives the full Newton quadratic model. Squaring a quadratic residual model also creates cubic and quartic terms. The convex Gauss–Newton model can hide negative curvature, so the stated trust-region method may converge to a critical point that is not second-order critical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m_k^c(x_k+s)=r_k+A_ks\Rightarrow m_k^f(x_k+s)=\frac12\|r_k+A_ks\|_2^2;\quad m_k^c(x_k+s)=r_k+A_ks+\frac12w_k(s,s)\Rightarrow m_k^f\text{ contains quadratic, cubic, and quartic terms}

knowledge_statements.title: Gauss-Newton Model Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-squares linearization exposed as a quadratic trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and define \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\). At \(x_k\), with \(F_k=F(x_k)\) and Jacobian \(J_k=F'(x_k)\), the Gauss--Newton model is \[m_k^{\mathrm{GN}}(s)=\tfrac12\|F_k+J_ks\|_2^2=f(x_k)+(J_k^{\mathsf T}F_k)^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}J_k^{\mathsf T}J_ks.\] Thus the trust-region interface supplies model gradient \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F_k\), positive-semidefinite curvature \(B_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\), and products with these quantities, while globalization restricts \(s\) to the chosen trust region and evaluates the actual residual at trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize the residual, square its norm, and expose the resulting gradient and positive-semidefinite Gauss–Newton curvature to the trust-region globalization mechanism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F_k\) and \(B_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\succeq0\) define the quadratic Gauss--Newton trust-region model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonlinear least squares, using residual linearization within a trust region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Gauss-Newton model interface at \(x_k\) is \[m_k^{GN}(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2,
\qquad \|p\|\leq\Delta_k.\] Its expanded quadratic form is \[m_k^{GN}(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k\|_2^2+(J_k^Tr_k)^Tp+	frac12p^TJ_k^TJ_kp.\] Thus the interface supplies model gradient \(g_k=J_k^Tr_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and positive-semidefinite curvature \(B_k=J_k^TJ_k\), omitting the residual-weighted second-derivative term in the exact Hessian of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonlinear least squares, the Gauss-Newton interface linearizes the residual as \(r_k+J_kp\) and squares its Euclidean norm. The resulting quadratic has exact objective gradient \(J_k^Tr_k\) and positive-semidefinite curvature \(J_k^TJ_k\). It omits the part of the exact objective Hessian that contains second derivatives of the individual residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_k^{GN}(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2\) is the Gauss-Newton local model supplied to trust-region globalization.
equivalent_formulations_latex: An unconstrained stationary Gauss-Newton step satisfies \(J_k^TJ_kp=-J_k^Tr_k\) when the normal equations are solvable.
special_cases_latex: If every residual is affine, the Gauss-Newton model equals the objective exactly.
If \(r(x_*)=0\), the omitted residual-weighted Hessian term vanishes at \(x_*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(J_k^TJ_k\succeq0\).
Model products can be evaluated using successive actions by \(J_k\) and \(J_k^T\).
boundary_notes: Rank deficiency may make the unconstrained model minimizer nonunique.
Large residuals can make the omitted curvature significant.

children.title: Lagrangian Hessian Model Interface
children.top_down_role: Constrained second-order models entering trust-region SQP and related frameworks.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Hessian Model Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained SQP interface using the current Lagrangian Hessian approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), where \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}c(x)\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\). At an iterate \((x_k,\lambda_k)\), a Lagrangian-Hessian model interface supplies \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\in\mathbb R^n\), \(J_k=Dc(x_k)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and a symmetric matrix \(B_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) approximating \(\nabla^2_{xx}L(x_k,\lambda_k)\). The associated trust-region SQP subproblem is
\[
\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n,\,\|s\|_2\leq\Delta_k}\; f(x_k)+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}B_ks
\quad\text{subject to}\quad c(x_k)+J_ks=0.
\]
Thus, objective curvature is represented by the Lagrangian-Hessian approximation and feasibility by the linearized constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface provides an objective gradient, an explicitly oriented constraint Jacobian, and a symmetric Lagrangian-Hessian approximation for a linearly constrained trust-region SQP model.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) are twice continuously differentiable near \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_k\) supplies the second-order objective term, while \(c(x_k)+J_ks=0\) supplies the first-order feasibility interface.

notation.meaning: constraint Jacobian with rows corresponding to constraint components

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-region SQP Lagrangian model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Minimize \(f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), with \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), Jacobian \(A_k=Dc(x_k)\), multiplier estimate \(\lambda_k\), and Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth equality-constrained nonlinear programming; inequality constraints require an active-set or cone formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Lagrangian Hessian model interface at \((x_k,\lambda_k)\) is the equality-constrained quadratic model \[\min_p\;q_k(p)=f(x_k)+
abla f(x_k)^Tp+	frac12p^TB_kp\quad	ext{subject to}\quad c(x_k)+A_kp=0,\] optionally intersected with \(\|p\|\leq\Delta_k\), where \(B_k\) represents \(
abla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x_k,\lambda_k)\). The interface is exact-curvature when \(B_k=
abla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x_k,\lambda_k)\) and quasi-Newton otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an equality-constrained problem, the interface supplies a quadratic objective model whose curvature approximates the Hessian of the Lagrangian and a linearized constraint equation \(c(x_k)+A_kp=0\). A trust-region SQP method additionally bounds the step. Exact Lagrangian curvature or a symmetric quasi-Newton approximation may be used.
assumptions_latex: Exact curvature requires the relevant functions to be twice differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed linearly constrained quadratic is the Lagrangian Hessian model passed to a trust-region SQP framework.
equivalent_formulations_latex: On the linearized constraint, \(\nabla f(x_k)^Tp\) may be replaced by \(\nabla_x\mathcal L(x_k,\lambda_k)^Tp\) up to a constant determined by feasibility linearization.
special_cases_latex: With no constraints, the model reduces to the ordinary quadratic trust-region model.
A quasi-Newton \(B_k\) gives a quasi-Newton SQP model.
immediate_consequences_latex: Only curvature on feasible tangent directions directly affects the tangential step.
boundary_notes: The definition does not specify a merit function or normal-tangential decomposition.
Inequality-constrained SQP requires additional slackness and active-set conditions.

notation.meaning: Constraint Jacobian at the current iterate.
