knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear, exact-Hessian, and quasi-Newton trust-region models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region subproblem regimes distinguished by the curvature matrix in a Euclidean local model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
m_k(p)=f(x_k)+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp,\qquad \|p\|_2\le\Delta_k,
\]
where \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(\Delta_k>0\). If \(B_k=0\) and \(g_k\ne0\), the unique minimizer is
\[
p_k=-\Delta_k\frac{g_k}{\|g_k\|_2}.
\]
If \(B_k=0\) and \(g_k=0\), every feasible \(p\) minimizes the constant model. If \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), the continuous quadratic model has a global minimizer on the compact Euclidean ball even when \(B_k\) is indefinite. Choosing \(B_k\) as a quasi-Newton approximation instead gives a quasi-Newton trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With zero curvature and a nonzero gradient, minimizing the linear model over a Euclidean trust region gives the negative gradient scaled to the boundary. With zero gradient, the model is constant and every feasible step minimizes it. An exact-Hessian quadratic model still has a global trust-region minimizer when the Hessian is indefinite because the feasible ball is compact. Replacing the Hessian with a secant approximation gives a quasi-Newton trust-region model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of an M-Norm Trust-Region Subproblem to Euclidean Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a positive-definite scaled-norm trust-region quadratic subproblem under an invertible change of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=M^T\succ0\), define \(\|x\|_M=\sqrt{\langle x,Mx\rangle}\), and let \(q(s)=\langle g,s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle s,Hs\rangle\) for \(s\in\mathbb R^n\). If \(M=S^{-T}S^{-1}\) for an invertible \(S\) and \(\bar s=S^{-1}s\), then \(\|s\|_M=\|\bar s\|_2\) and the problem \(\min_{\|s\|_M\leq\Delta}q(s)\) is equivalent to \(\min_{\|\bar s\|_2\leq\Delta}\bar q(\bar s)\), where \(\bar q(\bar s)=\langle S^Tg,\bar s\rangle+\tfrac12\langle\bar s,S^THS\bar s\rangle\). A solution \(\bar s^{\mathrm M}\) is mapped back by \(s^{\mathrm M}=S\bar s^{\mathrm M}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic trust-region problem defined using a symmetric positive-definite M-norm becomes an equivalent Euclidean-norm trust-region problem under an invertible coordinate change, with solutions mapped back by the inverse change of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|s\|_M=\|\bar s\|_2,\quad \bar g=S^Tg,\quad \bar H=S^THS,\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{\|s\|_M\leq\Delta}q(s)=S\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|\bar s\|_2\leq\Delta}\bar q(\bar s)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-region sufficient model-decrease condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a Cauchy-scale predicted-reduction requirement and records sufficient ways to obtain it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quadratic trust-region model \(q^{(k)}\), a step \(s_k\) has sufficient model decrease if, for some \(\beta_1\in(0,1]\), \[q^{(k)}(0)-q^{(k)}(s_k)\ge \beta_1\|g_k\|_2\min\!\left\{\Delta_k,\frac{\|g_k\|_2}{\|B_k\|_2}\right\}.\] The Cauchy point and an exact solution of the trust-region subproblem satisfy this inequality with \(\beta_1=\tfrac12\). More generally, if \(q^{(k)}(0)-q^{(k)}(s_k)\ge\beta_2\bigl(q^{(k)}(0)-q^{(k)}(s_k^c)\bigr)\), then the inequality holds with \(\beta_1=\tfrac12\beta_2\). When \(B_k=0\), the quotient in the minimum is interpreted as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region step is sufficiently accurate when its predicted reduction is at least a fixed fraction of the standard Cauchy-scale bound. Both the Cauchy point and an exact subproblem minimizer attain the bound with factor one half; a step attaining a beta-2 fraction of the Cauchy decrease attains it with factor beta-2 over two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q^{(k)}(0)-q^{(k)}(s_k)\ge\beta_1\|g_k\|_2\min\left\{\Delta_k,\frac{\|g_k\|_2}{\|B_k\|_2}\right\},\quad \beta_1=\tfrac12\ \text{for exact or Cauchy steps, and }\beta_1=\tfrac12\beta_2\ \text{under the fraction-of-Cauchy condition}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Box Representation of an Infinity-Norm Trust Region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise representation of an infinity-norm trust region and its intersection with translated simple bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\Delta\ge 0\),
\[
\|s\|_\infty\le\Delta\iff -\Delta\le s_i\le\Delta\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).
\]
If the step must also satisfy \(l\le x+s\le u\), then its componentwise bounds are
\[
\max\{l_i-x_i,-\Delta\}\le s_i\le\min\{u_i-x_i,\Delta\},\quad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Thus the intersection of the two axis-aligned boxes is again an axis-aligned box, possibly empty when the componentwise lower and upper bounds are inconsistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinity-norm trust region is a box. Intersecting it with translated simple variable bounds gives componentwise lower bounds formed by maxima and upper bounds formed by minima; the intersection is empty if any lower endpoint exceeds its upper endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{s:\|s\|_\infty\le\Delta,\ l\le x+s\le u\}=\prod_{i=1}^n[\max\{l_i-x_i,-\Delta\},\min\{u_i-x_i,\Delta\}],\text{ with the set empty if an interval is inconsistent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spherical-ellipsoidal scaling correspondence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(H=H^T\), and \(\Delta>0\). Define \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertible linear scaling between an ellipsoidal quadratic trust-region problem in \(s\) and a Euclidean-ball problem in scaled coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Euclidean scaling correspondence associated with \(S\) is the bijection \(s=Sw\) between \[\mathcal E_S(\Delta)=\{s:\|S^{-1}s\|_2\leq\Delta\}\quad\text{and}\quad \mathcal B_2(\Delta)=\{w:\|w\|_2\leq\Delta\}.\] Under this bijection, \[q(Sw)=(S^Tg)^Tw+\tfrac12w^T(S^THS)w.\] Thus the scaled data are \(g_S=S^Tg\) and \(H_S=S^THS\), and a vector \(w_*\) globally minimizes the scaled spherical problem if and only if \(s_*=Sw_*\) globally minimizes the original ellipsoidal problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular matrix \(S\) maps the Euclidean radius-\(\Delta\) ball bijectively onto the ellipsoid defined by \(\|S^{-1}s\|_2\leq\Delta\). Substitution \(s=Sw\) transforms the quadratic data to \(g_S=S^Tg\) and \(H_S=S^THS\). Feasibility, objective values, global minimizers, and boundary activity correspond exactly under this change of variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in\mathcal E_S(\Delta)}q(s)=S\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|w\|_2\leq\Delta}\{g_S^Tw+\tfrac12w^TH_Sw\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(M=S^{-T}S^{-1}\succ0\), the ellipsoid is \(\{s:s^TMs\leq\Delta^2\}\).
Given \(M\succ0\), choosing \(S=M^{-1/2}\) converts \(s^TMs\leq\Delta^2\) to \(\|w\|_2\leq\Delta\).
special_cases_latex: For diagonal \(S\), the correspondence rescales individual variables.
For orthogonal \(S\), the region remains spherical and the transformation is a rotation or reflection.
immediate_consequences_latex: Congruence preserves the inertia of \(H\), so \(H\) and \(S^THS\) have the same counts of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues.
boundary_notes: Singular \(S\) does not define a bijective full-dimensional correspondence.
A general non-Euclidean norm ball cannot necessarily be transformed into a Euclidean ball by a linear map.

notation.meaning: Ellipsoidal trust region induced by the nonsingular scaling matrix S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonal Scaling of Nonlinear Least-Squares Trust Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates an ellipsoidal nonlinear least-squares trust region to its multiplier equation and augmented least-squares representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D_k$ be diagonal with strictly positive diagonal entries and consider $\min_p\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2$ subject to $\|D_kp\|\leq\Delta_k$. If $p_k$ is a solution with associated multiplier $\lambda\geq0$, then $(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda D_k^2)p_k=-J_k^Tr_k$. For any fixed $\lambda\geq0$, this equation is equivalent to $p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_p\left\|\begin{bmatrix}J_k\\\sqrt{\lambda}D_k\end{bmatrix}p+\begin{bmatrix}r_k\\0\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2$. Choosing $\operatorname{diag}(D_k^2)=\operatorname{diag}(J_k^TJ_k)$ yields diagonal variable-scaling invariance of the resulting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal metric turns the spherical nonlinear least-squares trust region into an ellipsoid. Its multiplier equation is the normal equation of an augmented least-squares problem, and matching the metric diagonal to the Gauss–Newton diagonal makes the method invariant under diagonal rescaling of the variables.
assumptions_latex: D_k\text{ is diagonal with strictly positive diagonal entries}
\text{For the trust-region implication, }p_k\text{ is a solution and }\lambda\text{ is an associated multiplier}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (J_k^TJ_k+\lambda D_k^2)p_k=-J_k^Tr_k\iff p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_p\left\|\begin{bmatrix}J_k\\\sqrt{\lambda}D_k\end{bmatrix}p+\begin{bmatrix}r_k\\0\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and global optimality characterization for the quadratic trust-region subproblem over a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), a symmetric matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\), consider the Euclidean trust-region subproblem \[\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\ q(s):=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|s\|_2\le\Delta.\] Its feasible set is compact, so a global minimizer exists even when \(B\) is indefinite. A feasible vector \(s_*\) is globally minimizing if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\ge0\) such that \[(B+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g,\qquad B+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda_*(\|s_*\|_2-\Delta)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic over a Euclidean trust-region ball always has a global minimizer, and global minimizers are characterized exactly by the stated scalar-multiplier system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global minimizer exists, and a feasible \(s_*\) is globally minimizing if and only if it satisfies the stated multiplier system for some \(\lambda_*\ge0\).

children.title: Scaled-Euclidean Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Trust-region subproblems posed over ellipsoidal regions induced by scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled-Euclidean Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic trust-region subproblem constrained by an ellipsoid induced by positive-definite scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), symmetric \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), symmetric positive-definite \(W\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\), the scaled-Euclidean trust-region subproblem is \[\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\ g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|s\|_W:=(s^{\mathsf T}Ws)^{1/2}\le\Delta.\] The feasible set is an ellipsoid. Since \(W\succ0\), it is compact, and hence a global minimizer exists for every symmetric \(B\), including indefinite matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled-Euclidean trust-region subproblem minimizes a quadratic over the ellipsoid defined by a symmetric positive-definite scaling matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled subproblem has a nonempty compact feasible set and at least one global minimizer.

children.title: Euclidean Scaling Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Coordinate and metric relationships between spherical and scaled-Euclidean formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Scaling Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact change of variables between ellipsoidal and Euclidean trust-region subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\succ0\) be symmetric and let \(W^{1/2}\) denote its symmetric positive-definite square root. Under the bijection \(z=W^{1/2}s\), the scaled subproblem \[\min_{s^{\mathsf T}Ws\le\Delta^2}g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\] becomes the Euclidean subproblem \[\min_{\|z\|_2\le\Delta}\ \widehat g^{\mathsf T}z+\tfrac12z^{\mathsf T}\widehat Bz,\qquad \widehat g=W^{-1/2}g,\quad \widehat B=W^{-1/2}BW^{-1/2}.\] Feasible points and global minimizers correspond one-to-one through \(s=W^{-1/2}z\), and the two objective values are identical at corresponding points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplication by the square root of the scaling matrix converts an ellipsoidal trust region exactly into a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_*\) solves the scaled problem if and only if \(z_*=W^{1/2}s_*\) solves the transformed Euclidean problem.

children.title: Non-Euclidean Subproblem Geometry Family
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral, block-diagonal, absolute-value, and other non-Euclidean region geometries.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Non-Euclidean trust-region geometry family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\gamma:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty)\) be a norm or a positive-definite quadratic gauge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quadratic subproblems whose feasible region is not restricted to the unscaled Euclidean ball; includes polyhedral and curvature-adapted geometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A non-Euclidean trust-region geometry is the closed region \[\mathcal R_\gamma(\Delta)=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:\gamma(s)\leq\Delta\},\qquad\Delta>0,\] where \(\gamma\neq\|\cdot\|_2\). The associated subproblem is \(\min_{s\in\mathcal R_\gamma(\Delta)}q(s)\). Principal subclasses are polyhedral geometries \(\gamma(s)=\|Ds\|_1\) or \(\|Ds\|_\infty\), ellipsoidal geometries \(\gamma(s)=(s^TMs)^{1/2}\) with \(M\succ0\), and absolute-curvature geometries \(\gamma(s)=(s^T|H|s)^{1/2}\) when \(|H|\succ0\). A block-factor geometry may use \(M=PL|B|L^TP^T\succ0\) from \(H=PLBL^TP^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-Euclidean trust-region geometry replaces the ordinary Euclidean length by another norm or positive-definite quadratic gauge. The feasible region is the corresponding radius-\(\Delta\) ball, and the same quadratic model is minimized over it. This family includes scaled polyhedral balls, ellipsoids, the absolute-Hessian norm, and norms induced by block-indefinite factorizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The geometry-subproblem pair is \((\mathcal R_\gamma(\Delta),\min_{s\in\mathcal R_\gamma(\Delta)}q(s))\) for a declared non-Euclidean gauge \(\gamma\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(M\succ0\) and \(M=S^{-T}S^{-1}\), the ellipsoidal subclass is linearly equivalent to a Euclidean-ball subproblem.
The \(\ell_\infty\) region is the box \(\{s: |[Ds]_i|\leq\Delta\text{ for every }i\}\) when \(D\) is nonsingular diagonal.
special_cases_latex: For nonsingular \(H\), the ideal absolute-curvature norm satisfies \(\|s\|_{|H|}^2=s^T|H|s\).
A block-diagonal absolute-value geometry uses \(M=PL|B|L^TP^T\) and reduces to a structured block-diagonal subproblem.
immediate_consequences_latex: The geometry changes which feasible point is the Cauchy point and which point globally minimizes the same quadratic model.
boundary_notes: If the proposed quadratic gauge matrix is singular, it is not a norm and the region may be unbounded.
Polyhedral norm subproblems do not inherit the Euclidean multiplier characterization without modification.

notation.meaning: Declared norm or positive-definite quadratic gauge defining the region.
Spectral absolute value of a symmetric matrix H.

children.title: General-Norm Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Trust-region subproblems posed using non-Euclidean region norms.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Norm Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic trust-region subproblem over the ball of an arbitrary finite-dimensional norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be any norm on \(\mathbb R^n\). Given \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), symmetric \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\), the general-norm trust-region subproblem is \[\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\ g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|s\|\le\Delta.\] In finite dimensions its feasible ball is compact, so a global minimizer exists. Unlike the Euclidean case, first-order optimality uses the normal cone of the norm ball, and a single shifted system \((B+\lambda I)s=-g\) need not characterize global solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general-norm subproblem minimizes the quadratic model over any norm ball; existence remains automatic, but Euclidean spectral characterizations generally do not.
assumptions_latex: \(\|\cdot\|\) is a norm on finite-dimensional \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem has a global minimizer, while its optimality system must respect the geometry of the chosen norm ball.

children.title: Structured Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Trust-region subproblems whose regions exploit block, polyhedral, or problem-specific structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-separable quadratic models coupled through a structured trust-region constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_r)\), with \(s_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}\), and suppose \(B=\operatorname{diag}(B_1,\ldots,B_r)\). For positive-definite block scalings \(W_i\), a structured trust-region subproblem has the representation \[\min_{s_1,\ldots,s_r}\ \sum_{i=1}^r\left(g_i^{\mathsf T}s_i+\tfrac12s_i^{\mathsf T}B_is_i\right)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{i=1}^r s_i^{\mathsf T}W_is_i\le\Delta^2.\] The objective separates by blocks; only the radius constraint couples them. Consequently, fixing one multiplier for the radius constraint reduces the stationarity equations to independent block systems \((B_i+\lambda W_i)s_i=-g_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block-diagonal curvature and block-scaled geometry separate the quadratic equations, leaving only the trust-region radius to couple the blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a fixed radius multiplier \(\lambda\), the structured stationarity system decomposes into \(r\) independent block equations.

children.title: Geometry-Solver Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between region geometry and applicable solver families.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Solver Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility criterion based on feasibility and norm-appropriate Cauchy decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\) and let the trust region be \(\{s:\|s\|\le\Delta\}\), with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\). A subproblem solver is geometry-compatible with this norm if, for every input, it returns a feasible \(s\) satisfying \[q(0)-q(s)\ge\kappa\,\|g\|_*\min\!\left\{\Delta,\frac{\|g\|_*}{\beta}\right\},\] where \(\kappa>0\) is uniform and \(\beta\ge\sup_{\|u\|\le1}|u^{\mathsf T}Bu|\). Thus both feasibility operations and the sufficient-decrease guarantee are computed in the declared primal-dual geometry, not in an unrelated Euclidean metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible solver enforces the declared norm constraint and achieves uniform Cauchy-type decrease measured using that norm and its dual.
assumptions_latex: The constant \(\kappa\) is independent of the particular subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step is feasible in the chosen geometry and provides the displayed norm-consistent model decrease.

notation.meaning: upper bound on quadratic curvature over the norm unit ball

children.title: Curvature and Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Positive-definite, singular, indefinite, interior, and boundary solution families.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean curvature and boundary regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(s_*\) be a global minimizer of \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\) subject to \(\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\), where \(H=H^T\) and \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean trust-region global solutions classified jointly by Hessian inertia and constraint activity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The curvature-boundary regime of \((H,s_*)\) is defined by the curvature label \[C(H)=\begin{cases}\mathrm{PD},&\lambda_{\min}(H)>0,\\ \mathrm{PSD\!\!-singular},&\lambda_{\min}(H)=0\text{ and }H\succeq0,\\ \mathrm{indefinite},&\lambda_{\min}(H)<0,\end{cases}\] and the activity label \[A(s_*)=\begin{cases}\mathrm{interior},&\|s_*\|_2<\Delta,\\ \mathrm{boundary},&\|s_*\|_2=\Delta.\end{cases}\] An indefinite-interior pair is excluded because an indefinite quadratic cannot attain its global minimum strictly inside the ball. In the positive-definite class the unconstrained minimizer \(-H^{-1}g\) determines activity; in the singular semidefinite class the global solution set may contain both interior and boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Euclidean trust-region problem, curvature is positive definite, singular positive semidefinite, or indefinite according to the smallest eigenvalue of \(H\). A selected global solution is interior or boundary according to whether its norm is below or equal to the radius. Indefinite curvature cannot occur with an interior global minimizer. Positive-definite activity is determined by the unconstrained minimizer, while singular convex problems may have multiple solutions with differing activity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The admissible regime is the pair \((C(H),A(s_*))\), excluding \((\mathrm{indefinite},\mathrm{interior})\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using a global multiplier \(\lambda_*\geq0\), interior activity is equivalent to \(\lambda_*=0\) together with \(\|s_*\|_2<\Delta\); positive multiplier implies boundary activity.
special_cases_latex: If \(H\succ0\) and \(\|H^{-1}g\|_2<\Delta\), the unique solution is interior.
If \(H\succ0\) and \(\|H^{-1}g\|_2\geq\Delta\), the unique solution is on the boundary.
If \(H\) is indefinite, every global solution is on the boundary.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive definiteness of the shifted matrix \(H+\lambda_*I\) implies uniqueness of the global solution.
boundary_notes: The hard case is a refinement of the indefinite-boundary regime and is not identified by this two-label taxonomy.
When \(H\succeq0\) is singular, activity may depend on which global minimizer is selected.

notation.meaning: Constraint-activity label of a selected global minimizer.

children.title: Positive-Definite Curvature Regime
children.top_down_role: Subproblems with locally convex quadratic curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Curvature Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution classification for Euclidean trust-region models with positive-definite curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|s\|_2\le\Delta}g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\) with \(B\succ0\). The quadratic is strictly convex, so the global minimizer is unique. Let \(s_N=-B^{-1}g\). If \(\|s_N\|_2\le\Delta\), then \(s_*=s_N\) and the trust-region multiplier is \(\lambda_*=0\). If \(\|s_N\|_2>\Delta\), then \(\|s_*\|_2=\Delta\) and there is a unique \(\lambda_*>0\) satisfying \[(B+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g,\qquad \|s_*\|_2=\Delta.\] Thus positive-definite curvature permits no hard case or multiplicity of global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive-definite curvature, the solution is uniquely the Newton step when feasible and otherwise a uniquely shifted boundary step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizer is unique and is classified by whether \(\|-B^{-1}g\|_2\) is at most \(\Delta\).

children.title: Singular Curvature Regime
children.top_down_role: Subproblems with degenerate curvature and nontrivial null-space behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Curvature Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution classification for Euclidean trust-region models with positive-semidefinite singular curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|s\|_2\le\Delta}g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\) with \(B\succeq0\) singular. If \(g\in\operatorname{Range}(B)\) and the minimum-norm solution \(s_0=-B^{\dagger}g\) satisfies \(\|s_0\|_2\le\Delta\), then every feasible \(s_0+z\), with \(z\in\ker(B)\), is globally minimizing; the minimizer is interior only when such a point has norm strictly below \(\Delta\). Otherwise the global minimizer is unique, lies on the boundary, and satisfies \[(B+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g,\qquad \lambda_*>0,\qquad \|s_*\|_2=\Delta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular semidefinite curvature allows a null-space family of unconstrained minimizers; otherwise a positive shift produces a unique boundary solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global solutions are either feasible members of \(-B^{\dagger}g+\ker(B)\) or the unique positively shifted boundary solution.

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the curvature matrix
null space of the curvature matrix

children.title: Indefinite Curvature Regime
children.top_down_role: Subproblems exhibiting directions of negative curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Curvature Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies Euclidean trust-region subproblems whose quadratic model has negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|p\|_2\leq\Delta} q(p)\), where \(q(p)=g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), \(B=B^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\Delta>0\). If \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), then every global minimizer \(p_*\) satisfies \(\|p_*\|_2=\Delta\), and every multiplier \(\lambda_*\) satisfying the global primal-dual optimality conditions is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indefinite-curvature regime occurs when the symmetric Hessian has a negative eigenvalue. Every global minimizer then lies on the trust-region boundary, and every optimal norm-constraint multiplier is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\Longrightarrow \|p_*\|_2=\Delta\) and every optimal multiplier satisfies \(\lambda_*>0\).

children.title: Interior Solution Regime
children.top_down_role: Solution families for which the trust-region boundary is inactive.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior Solution Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes global solutions strictly inside a Euclidean trust region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(p)=g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\) over \(\|p\|_2\leq\Delta\), a global minimizer \(p_*\) is interior exactly when \(Bp_*=-g\), \(B\succeq0\), and \(\|p_*\|_2<\Delta\). Equivalently, the primal-dual optimality conditions hold with multiplier \(\lambda_*=0\) and inactive norm constraint. An interior global minimizer can therefore exist only when the unconstrained quadratic is bounded below and its stationary equation has a solution inside the ball. If \(B\succ0\), the interior solution is unique and equals \(p_*=-B^{-1}g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior solution is an unconstrained global quadratic minimizer lying strictly inside the ball; its trust-region multiplier is zero, and it is unique when the Hessian is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|p_*\|_2<\Delta\Longleftrightarrow Bp_*=-g,\ B\succeq0,\ \lambda_*=0\), provided \(p_*\) is globally optimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-interior full-step regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the strict-interior specialization supported by the source. The source also permits equality, in which case the same full step lies on the trust-region boundary and is outside this node's interior-only scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: m_k(p)=f_k+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp.\quad B_k\succ0\ \land\ \|B_k^{-1}g_k\|<\Delta_k\ \Longrightarrow\ p_k^*=-B_k^{-1}g_k\text{ is the unique minimizer of }m_k\text{ over }\{p:\|p\|\leq\Delta_k\},\text{ with }\|p_k^*\|<\Delta_k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the quadratic-model matrix is positive definite and its unconstrained minimizer lies strictly inside the trust-region ball, that point is the unique trust-region solution and is the full step. The equality case is also a full step according to the source, but it lies on the boundary rather than in this interior regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k^*=-B_k^{-1}g_k,\qquad \|p_k^*\|<\Delta_k,\qquad p_k^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|\leq\Delta_k}m_k(p).

children.title: Boundary Solution Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Solution Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes global solutions attaining the Euclidean trust-region radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(p)=g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\) over \(\|p\|_2\leq\Delta\), the boundary regime consists of global minimizers \(p_*\) satisfying \(\|p_*\|_2=\Delta\). Such a point is globally optimal exactly when there exists \(\lambda_*\geq0\) for which \((B+\lambda_*I)p_*=-g\) and \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\). Boundary activity does not by itself imply \(\lambda_*>0\): a zero multiplier is possible when an unconstrained minimizer happens to lie on the sphere. If \(B\) is indefinite, however, positive semidefiniteness of the shifted matrix forces \(\lambda_*>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary solution has norm equal to the radius and satisfies a positive-semidefinite shifted stationarity system. Its multiplier may be zero unless negative curvature forces a positive shift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_*\) is a boundary global minimizer iff \(\|p_*\|_2=\Delta\) and some \(\lambda_*\geq0\) satisfies \((B+\lambda_*I)p_*=-g\) and \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\).

children.title: Subproblem Optimality Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Equivalent structural views supporting analysis, certificates, and solver construction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Euclidean subproblem optimality representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min\{q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs:\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\}\), with \(H=H^T\) and \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic subproblems represented through shifted systems, spectral coordinates, complementarity, or a secular equation where nonsingularity permits it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimality representation is a tuple \((s,\lambda)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \[(H+\lambda I)s=-g,\qquad H+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad \|s\|_2\leq\Delta,\qquad \lambda(\|s\|_2-\Delta)=0.\] The representation family consists of this primal-dual system and its coordinate forms. If \(H=U\operatorname{diag}(\theta_i)U^T\), then \((\theta_i+\lambda)\hat s_i=-\hat g_i\), where \(\hat s=U^Ts\) and \(\hat g=U^Tg\). If \(H+\lambda I\succ0\) and \(\lambda>0\), boundary feasibility becomes the secular equation \[\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\hat g_i^2}{(\theta_i+\lambda)^2}=\Delta^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean trust-region optimum can be encoded by a step and nonnegative shift satisfying a shifted linear system, positive-semidefiniteness, primal feasibility, and complementary activity. Diagonalizing \(H\) gives an equivalent componentwise shifted system. When the shifted matrix is positive definite and the multiplier is positive, the boundary norm condition becomes a scalar secular equation. Singular shifted systems remain in the family but cannot always be represented by the ordinary inverse-based secular formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation family is the set of primal-dual tuples satisfying the displayed shifted-system, semidefiniteness, feasibility, and complementarity relations, together with their valid spectral and secular coordinate forms.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(H+\lambda I\succ0\), \(s=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g\).
In spectral coordinates, positive semidefiniteness is \(\theta_i+\lambda\geq0\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: For an interior solution, \(\lambda=0\), \(Hs=-g\), and \(H\succeq0\).
For a regular boundary solution, \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\) and the secular equation determines the norm constraint.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(H+\lambda I\succ0\), the represented global minimizer is unique.
boundary_notes: At a singular shift, the equation requires \(g\) to lie in the range of \(H+\lambda I\), and null-space components may be needed to meet the boundary.
The inverse-based secular equation omits such singular hard-case solutions unless augmented.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative spectral shift and trust-region multiplier.
Eigenvalues of H in an orthonormal spectral decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Optimality Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality conditions for the Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\Delta>0\). A vector \(p_*\) globally minimizes \(g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\) subject to \(\|p\|_2\leq\Delta\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\geq0\) such that \((B+\lambda_*I)p_*=-g\), \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\), \(\|p_*\|_2\leq\Delta\), and \(\lambda_*(\|p_*\|_2-\Delta)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible step is globally optimal exactly when stationarity, complementary slackness, a nonnegative multiplier, and positive semidefiniteness of the shifted Hessian hold together.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|_2\leq\Delta}(g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp)\) iff the stated primal-dual system has a solution \(\lambda_*\geq0\).

notation.meaning: dual multiplier for the trust-region constraint

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global primal-dual trust-region certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\). Let \(q(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\) and \(B=\{s:\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global optimality certificate for the finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblem, including singular shifted matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal-dual optimality certificate is a pair \((s_*,\lambda_*)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\|s_*\|_2\leq\Delta,\qquad \lambda_*\geq0,\qquad (H+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g,\] \[H+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda_*(\|s_*\|_2-\Delta)=0.\] The primal component is the candidate step and the dual component is the nonnegative multiplier or spectral shift. The certificate is strict when \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\). Singular certificates allow \(H+\lambda_*I\succeq0\) with a nontrivial null space and may correspond to more than one primal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global primal-dual certificate for the Euclidean trust-region subproblem is a feasible step \(s_*\) and a nonnegative multiplier \(\lambda_*\). They must satisfy stationarity through the shifted system, global curvature through positive-semidefiniteness of the shifted Hessian, and complementarity between the multiplier and boundary slack. A positive-definite shifted Hessian makes the certificate strict and the primal solution unique; a singular shifted Hessian can admit multiple certified steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((s_*,\lambda_*)\) is a global primal-dual certificate exactly when it satisfies feasibility, nonnegative duality, shifted stationarity, global semidefinite curvature, and complementarity as displayed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Complementarity may be written \(\lambda_*(\Delta^2-\|s_*\|_2^2)=0\) because \(\lambda_*\geq0\) and \(\|s_*\|_2\leq\Delta\).
If \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\), stationarity is equivalent to \(s_*=-(H+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\).
special_cases_latex: An interior certificate has \(\lambda_*=0\), \(Hs_*=-g\), \(H\succeq0\), and \(\|s_*\|_2<\Delta\).
A positive-multiplier certificate necessarily has \(\|s_*\|_2=\Delta\).
A singular boundary certificate may include a null-space component of \(H+\lambda_*I\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The existence of a strict certificate implies that \(s_*\) is the unique global minimizer.
The semidefinite condition distinguishes the global certificate from ordinary first-order stationarity on the boundary.
boundary_notes: These relations are specific to a Euclidean quadratic trust-region constraint; other norms require different dual objects.
Positive semidefiniteness, rather than only tangent-space second-order conditions, is part of the global certificate.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative trust-region multiplier and spectral shift.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral form of a shifted trust-region system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\). Write \(H=Q\operatorname{diag}(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)Q^T\), where \(Q=[q_1,\ldots,q_n]\) is orthogonal and \(\theta_1\leq\cdots\leq\theta_n\). The associated quadratic model is \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean trust-region subproblems; the displayed inverse formula covers nonsingular shifts, while singular hard-case completion is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[s(\lambda):=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g=-\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{q_i^Tg}{\theta_i+\lambda}q_i,\qquad \lambda> -\theta_1.\] The spectral shifted-system correspondence associates each admissible shift \(\lambda\) with this unique solution of \((H+\lambda I)s=-g\). A trust-region solution represented by a nonsingular shift is obtained when \(\lambda\geq0\), \(H+\lambda I\succeq0\), \(\|s(\lambda)\|\leq\Delta\), and \(\lambda(\Delta-\|s(\lambda)\|)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every shift \(\lambda> -\theta_1\), the shifted matrix is positive definite and the unique shifted-system solution is \(s(\lambda)=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g\). In the eigenbasis of \(H\), its component along \(q_i\) is \(-(q_i^Tg)/(\theta_i+\lambda)\). An admissible trust-region solution additionally satisfies nonnegative-shift, feasibility, positive-semidefiniteness, and complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lambda> -\theta_1\Longrightarrow (H+\lambda I)s(\lambda)=-g,\qquad q_i^Ts(\lambda)=-\frac{q_i^Tg}{\theta_i+\lambda}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[Q^Ts(\lambda)=-\operatorname{diag}\!\left((\theta_i+\lambda)^{-1}\right)Q^Tg.\]
\[\|s(\lambda)\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(q_i^Tg)^2}{(\theta_i+\lambda)^2}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(H\succ0\) and \(\|H^{-1}g\|\leq\Delta\), then \(\lambda=0\) and \(s(0)=-H^{-1}g\).
If the constraint is active and the easy case holds, the required shift is the unique \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\theta_1\}\) satisfying \(\|s(\lambda)\|=\Delta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: On \((-\theta_1,\infty)\), \(\|s(\lambda)\|\) is nonincreasing and tends to zero as \(\lambda\to\infty\).
The eigencomponents having small \(\theta_i+\lambda\) dominate the shifted solution.
boundary_notes: At \(\lambda=-\theta_1\), the inverse formula is undefined; a solution may instead require a pseudoinverse component plus a vector in the leftmost eigenspace.
The correspondence does not by itself assert that every shifted-system solution is globally optimal; the feasibility, complementarity, and semidefiniteness conditions remain necessary.

notation.meaning: Ordered eigenvalues and corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors of the model Hessian.
Solution of the shifted linear system at shift \(\lambda\).

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses primal-dual trust-region conditions in an eigenbasis of the symmetric Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=Q\operatorname{diag}(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)Q^T\), with orthogonal \(Q\), and set \(\gamma=Q^Tg\) and \(z=Q^Tp\). For a multiplier \(\lambda\geq\max\{0,-\theta_1\}\), shifted stationarity is equivalent to \((\theta_i+\lambda)z_i=-\gamma_i\) for every \(i\). If \(\theta_i+\lambda>0\) for all \(i\), then \(z_i=-\gamma_i/(\theta_i+\lambda)\). If equality occurs, solvability requires \(\gamma_i=0\) on the zero-shift eigenspace, while components of \(z\) in that eigenspace are determined by feasibility and complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonalizing the Hessian converts shifted stationarity into independent scalar equations; singular shifted eigenvalues require the gradient to be orthogonal to their eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B+\lambda I)p=-g\Longleftrightarrow (\theta_i+\lambda)z_i=-\gamma_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Shifted-System Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents regular trust-region solutions through a positive-definite shifted linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric \(B\), define \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) whenever \(\lambda\geq0\) and \(\lambda> -\lambda_{\min}(B)\). Then \(B+\lambda I\succ0\), so \(p(\lambda)\) is uniquely defined. It is a global trust-region solution precisely when \(\|p(\lambda)\|_2\leq\Delta\) and \(\lambda(\|p(\lambda)\|_2-\Delta)=0\). Within this regular characterization, \(\lambda=0\) represents a feasible unconstrained minimizer when \(B\succ0\), whereas \(\lambda>0\) requires \(\|p(\lambda)\|_2=\Delta\). A singular shifted Hessian requires a pseudoinverse-plus-nullspace representation and is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the nonnegative shift makes the shifted Hessian positive definite, one uniquely defined shifted solve gives the step. Feasibility and complementary slackness determine whether that step is globally optimal; singular shifts require a separate representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) is optimal iff \(\|p(\lambda)\|_2\leq\Delta\) and \(\lambda(\|p(\lambda)\|_2-\Delta)=0\).

notation.meaning: step generated by the shifted system

children.title: Spectral Shift Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between spectral structure and admissible shifted-system regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Shift Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Links shifted-system definiteness and solvability to the Hessian spectrum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the eigenvalues of symmetric \(B\) be \(\theta_1\leq\cdots\leq\theta_n\), and let \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). The eigenvalues of \(B+\lambda I\) are exactly \(\theta_i+\lambda\). Consequently, \(B+\lambda I\succeq0\) if and only if \(\lambda\geq-\theta_1\), and \(B+\lambda I\succ0\) if and only if \(\lambda> -\theta_1\). At \(\lambda=-\theta_1\), the system \((B+\lambda I)p=-g\) is solvable exactly when \(g\perp\ker(B-\theta_1I)\). When \(\theta_1<0\) and this endpoint is the optimal trust-region shift, the singular correspondence gives the classical hard-case spectral structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a scalar identity shifts every Hessian eigenvalue equally. At the leftmost singular shift, the shifted system is solvable exactly when the gradient is orthogonal to the leftmost eigenspace; this becomes the hard-case structure when that nonnegative endpoint is the optimal trust-region shift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B+\lambda I\succeq0\Longleftrightarrow\lambda\geq-\theta_1\), with endpoint solvability iff \(g\perp\ker(B-\theta_1I)\).

notation.meaning: spectral shift, and a trust-region multiplier when nonnegative and optimal

knowledge_statements.title: Secular-Equation Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar characterization of regular boundary solutions in an eigenbasis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=Q\operatorname{diag}(\theta_i)Q^T\), \(\gamma=Q^Tg\), and \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\theta_1\}\). The regular shifted step is \(p(\lambda)=-Q\operatorname{diag}((\theta_i+\lambda)^{-1})\gamma\). It lies on the trust-region boundary exactly when the secular equation \(\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i^2/(\theta_i+\lambda)^2=\Delta^2\) holds. The left-hand side is continuous and nonincreasing on this interval, and it is strictly decreasing unless \(g=0\). Hence any regular positive-multiplier boundary solution is obtained from the unique admissible root whenever such a root exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the regular boundary case, the multiplier is the admissible root of a scalar norm equation obtained after diagonalizing the Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|p(\lambda)\|_2=\Delta\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\gamma_i^2}{(\theta_i+\lambda)^2}=\Delta^2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secular equation for an active Euclidean trust region
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g\neq0\), and \(\Delta>0\). For \(\lambda> -\lambda_{\min}(H)\), define \(s(\lambda)=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean trust-region subproblems in the nonsingular easy case, with an active trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The secular function is \[\phi(\lambda):=\frac{1}{\|s(\lambda)\|}-\frac{1}{\Delta},\qquad \lambda> -\lambda_{\min}(H).\] A secular-equation characterization of a boundary solution is a root \(\lambda_*\geq\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\) satisfying \(\phi(\lambda_*)=0\), together with \(s_*=s(\lambda_*)\). Then \(\|s_*\|=\Delta\), \((H+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g\), and \(H+\lambda_*I\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The secular equation replaces the vector trust-region boundary condition by the scalar equation \(1/\|s(\lambda)\|-1/\Delta=0\), where \(s(\lambda)\) solves the shifted linear system. A root in the positive-semidefinite shift interval determines both the multiplier and the boundary step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\phi(\lambda_*)=0\Longleftrightarrow\|s(\lambda_*)\|=\Delta,\qquad s_*:=s(\lambda_*).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(q_i^Tg)^2}{(\theta_i+\lambda_*)^2}=\Delta^2.\]
The equation \(\|s(\lambda)\|-\Delta=0\) has the same roots, but its reciprocal form is the standard secular equation used for Newton iteration near spectral poles.
special_cases_latex: If \(H\succ0\) and \(\|H^{-1}g\|<\Delta\), the solution is interior with \(\lambda_*=0\); no boundary secular root is required.
For indefinite \(H\) in the easy case, \(\lambda_*>-\lambda_{\min}(H)>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(g\neq0\), \(\phi\) is strictly increasing and concave on \((-\lambda_{\min}(H),\infty)\).
A root, when present in the admissible interval, is unique.
boundary_notes: In the hard case, the pole associated with the leftmost eigenspace disappears and an admissible root may fail to exist in the open interval.
The definition uses the Euclidean norm; a scaled norm replaces \(I\) by a positive-definite metric matrix.

notation.meaning: Trust-region multiplier obtained as an admissible scalar root.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal-Norm Reformulation of the Secular Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded local conditioning principle for Newton solution of the trust-region secular equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta>0\), and consider \(\lambda>-\lambda_1\) close to \(-\lambda_1\). If \(\phi_1(\lambda)=\|p(\lambda)\|-\Delta\) has the local form \(\phi_1(\lambda)\approx C_1/(\lambda+\lambda_1)+C_2\), with \(C_1>0\), then its strong nonlinearity can make Newton root finding unreliable or slow. Wherever \(\|p(\lambda)\|>0\), the same target equation can be written as \(\phi_2(\lambda)=\Delta^{-1}-\|p(\lambda)\|^{-1}=0\). Near the pole, \(\phi_2(\lambda)\approx\Delta^{-1}-(\lambda+\lambda_1)/C_3\) for some \(C_3>0\), so the transformed residual is nearly linear there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the smallest-eigenvalue pole, the direct norm residual behaves like a reciprocal function and may be poorly shaped for Newton's method. The equivalent reciprocal-norm residual is nearly linear there and is therefore a better root-finding formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_2(\lambda)=\frac1\Delta-\frac1{\|p(\lambda)\|}\approx\frac1\Delta-\frac{\lambda+\lambda_1}{C_3}\quad\text{near }-\lambda_1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secular Newton Approach and Factorization Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded description of a comparatively high-accuracy Euclidean trust-region subproblem procedure for moderate dimension; the factorization counts are typical implementation costs, not complexity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When the trust-region subproblem is sufficiently small that several factorizations are practical, the multiplier characterization can be used to seek a closer approximation to its solution by applying a scalar Newton iteration to identify a multiplier \(\lambda\) whose associated step matches the prescribed radius \(\Delta\). The approach typically uses about three factorizations involving \(B\), compared with one for dogleg and two for two-dimensional subspace minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a moderately sized trust-region subproblem, a scalar Newton iteration can seek the multiplier whose step matches the trust-region radius. This gives a closer subproblem approximation at the typical cost of about three factorizations, versus one for dogleg and two for two-dimensional subspace minimization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotics of the Shifted-System Step Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded spectral properties of the secular-equation step map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{S}^n\), let \((\lambda_j,q_j)\) be an eigenpair of \(B\), and define \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) wherever the inverse exists. Then \(\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\|p(\lambda)\|=0\). Moreover, if \(q_j^Tg\neq0\), then \(\|p(\lambda)\|\to\infty\) as \(\lambda\to-\lambda_j\) through values in the domain of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shifted-system step norm tends to zero as the shift grows. At an eigenvalue pole whose eigenvector has a nonzero gradient component, the step norm diverges.
assumptions_latex: p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\text{ whenever }B+\lambda I\text{ is nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\|p(\lambda)\|=0,\qquad q_j^Tg\neq0\implies\lim_{\substack{\lambda\to-\lambda_j\\B+\lambda I\text{ nonsingular}}}\|p(\lambda)\|=\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Secular Equation for the Trust-Region Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithmic representation for the Euclidean trust-region subproblem, limited in its positive-multiplier branch to nonsingular positive-definite shifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given Euclidean trust-region subproblem data \(B\), \(g\), and \(\Delta>0\), first test whether \(\lambda=0\), together with its corresponding step \(p\), satisfies the cited optimality conditions and \(\|p\|\leq\Delta\). Otherwise, in the branch where \(\lambda>0\) and \(B+\lambda I\succ0\), define \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) and seek \(\lambda\) satisfying \(\|p(\lambda)\|=\Delta\). This is a one-dimensional root-finding problem in \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First test the zero-multiplier case. Otherwise, for a positive multiplier making the shifted Hessian positive definite, solve the shifted system and find the scalar multiplier for which the step norm equals the trust-region radius.
assumptions_latex: B+\lambda I\succ0\text{ in the shifted-system branch}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g,\qquad \|p(\lambda)\|=\Delta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton Update for the Reciprocal-Norm Secular Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded scalar update rule; the subsequent practical implementation is not present in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an iterate \(\lambda^{(\ell)}\) where \(\phi_2\) is differentiable and \(\phi_2'(\lambda^{(\ell)})\neq0\), apply Newton's method to the reciprocal-norm secular residual by setting \[\lambda^{(\ell+1)}=\lambda^{(\ell)}-\frac{\phi_2(\lambda^{(\ell)})}{\phi_2'(\lambda^{(\ell)})}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provided the reciprocal-norm residual has a nonzero derivative at the current multiplier, update the multiplier using the ordinary scalar Newton step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda^{(\ell+1)}=\lambda^{(\ell)}-\frac{\phi_2(\lambda^{(\ell)})}{\phi_2'(\lambda^{(\ell)})}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular and singular augmented eigenvector representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), let \(M\succ0\), let \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\Delta>0\). The trust-region norm is \(\|s\|_M=(s^TMs)^{1/2}\). For a parameter \(\vartheta\in\mathbb R\), define the symmetric pencil \(A(\vartheta)-\mu B\) with \[A(\vartheta)=\begin{pmatrix}H&g\\g^T&\vartheta\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}M&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional ellipsoidal trust-region subproblems; the Euclidean case is recovered with \(M=I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The augmented eigenproblem representation pair consists of: (i) a regular eigenvector \(\binom{s}{1}\) satisfying \[A(\vartheta)\binom{s}{1}=-\lambda B\binom{s}{1},\] whose first block is \((H+\lambda M)s=-g\); and (ii) a singular hard-case eigenvector \(\binom{v}{0}\) satisfying \[A(\vartheta)\binom{v}{0}=-\lambda_1B\binom{v}{0},\] equivalently \(Hv=-\lambda_1Mv\) and \(g^Tv=0\). The controlling parameter is selected so that the regular representation also satisfies \(\lambda\geq0\), \(H+\lambda M\succeq0\), and \(\lambda(\|s\|_M-\Delta)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region shifted system can be embedded in a symmetric generalized eigenproblem of dimension \(n+1\). Eigenvectors with nonzero last component can be normalized to \((s,1)\) and yield the shifted-system step. Eigenvectors with zero last component identify a generalized leftmost-eigenspace direction orthogonal to the gradient, which is the complementary hard-case representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A(\vartheta)\binom{s}{1}=-\lambda B\binom{s}{1}\Longrightarrow (H+\lambda M)s=-g,\quad g^Ts+\vartheta=-\lambda.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The regular eigenvalue is \(\mu=-\lambda\); selecting the leftmost generalized eigenvalue enforces the required semidefinite shifted Hessian.
A zero-last-component eigenvector is precisely a generalized eigenvector of \((H,M)\) that is orthogonal to \(g\).
special_cases_latex: For \(M=I\), the pencil is an ordinary symmetric augmented eigenproblem.
At the hard-case critical parameter, the augmented eigenspace contains both \(\binom{s_{\mathrm{cri}}}{1}\) and vectors \(\binom{v}{0}\) from the leftmost eigenspace.
immediate_consequences_latex: The step and multiplier may be recovered from an extremal generalized eigenpair without explicitly factorizing each shifted Hessian.
The singular member of the pair supplies the eigenspace direction needed to complete a hard-case boundary step.
boundary_notes: A regular eigenvector whose last component is zero cannot be normalized to \(\binom{s}{1}\).
The eigenproblem alone does not impose the trust-region radius; the parameter \(\vartheta\) must be adjusted to satisfy complementarity.

notation.meaning: The augmented symmetric matrix and positive-definite metric matrix defining the pencil.
Regular step-bearing and singular hard-case eigenvector forms.

children.title: Augmented-Matrix Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Trust-region structure represented through enlarged matrix formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Matrix Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearizes the regular trust-region secular equation using a nonsymmetric augmented matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g\neq0\) and \(\Delta>0\), define the augmented matrix \(M_\Delta=\begin{pmatrix}-B&gg^T/\Delta^2\\I&-B\end{pmatrix}\). A scalar \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(M_\Delta\) with eigenvector \((y_1,y_2)\) exactly when \(y_1=(B+\lambda I)y_2\) and \((B+\lambda I)^2y_2=g(g^Ty_2)/\Delta^2\). If \(B+\lambda I\) is positive definite and \(g^Ty_2\neq0\), these relations imply the secular equation \(g^T(B+\lambda I)^{-2}g=\Delta^2\), so \(p=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) is a boundary trust-region candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block augmented matrix linearizes the squared shifted-system equation. Its admissible real eigenvalues satisfy the trust-region secular equation and recover boundary candidates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_\Delta(y_1,y_2)^T=\lambda(y_1,y_2)^T\) yields the secular equation when \(B+\lambda I\succ0\) and \(g^Ty_2\neq0\).

notation.meaning: nonsymmetric augmented matrix of order two n

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block-matrix algebra is internally plausible, but this specialized nonsymmetric linearization has no citation. An inspectable theorem, section, or page supporting the exact block matrix, sign convention, and secular-equation implication is required before the formulation can be relied upon.

children.title: Eigenproblem Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Trust-region structure represented through associated eigenvalue problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenproblem Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies regular boundary multipliers through the rightmost real eigenvalue of an augmented matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_\Delta=\begin{pmatrix}-B&gg^T/\Delta^2\\I&-B\end{pmatrix}\), and suppose the trust-region solution is regular: \(B+\lambda_*I\succ0\) and \(\|p_*\|_2=\Delta\). Then \(\lambda_*\) is the rightmost real eigenvalue associated with the secular branch of \(M_\Delta\), and \(p_*=-(B+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\). Conversely, an eigenvalue \(\lambda\geq\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\) whose eigenvector has nonzero coupling to \(g\), and for which the recovered step has norm \(\Delta\), satisfies the global primal-dual conditions. Singular hard cases require separate treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the regular boundary regime, an admissible rightmost augmented-matrix eigenvalue is the optimal multiplier; solving the associated shifted system recovers the step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_*\) is the admissible rightmost real eigenvalue of \(M_\Delta\), and \(p_*=-(B+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rightmost-real-eigenvalue selection claim is specialized and materially stronger than the elementary augmented-matrix algebra. No source is supplied, and the phrase 'associated with the secular branch' is not formally defined. A precise theorem and locator establishing the selection rule and all regularity hypotheses are required.

children.title: Algebraic Reformulation Selection
children.top_down_role: Computational regimes favoring augmented-matrix or eigenproblem representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Reformulation Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects an exact algebraic representation according to regularity and available matrix operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Euclidean trust-region subproblem, equivalent exact formulations should be selected by the shifted Hessian's regularity. If \(B+\lambda I\succ0\), the shifted system together with the scalar equation \(\|(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\|_2=\Delta\) gives the regular boundary solution. An eigendecomposition of \(B\) converts this equation into the secular sum and is appropriate when spectral data are available. The augmented eigenproblem provides a linearized alternative for locating admissible shifts. If \(B+\lambda I\) is singular, neither inverse-based formula applies; use the pseudoinverse-plus-nullspace hard-case representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use shifted solves or a secular equation in regular cases, an augmented eigenproblem as a linearization, and a pseudoinverse-nullspace representation at the singular hard case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reformulation must preserve \((B+\lambda I)p=-g\), \(B+\lambda I\succeq0\), and the applicable norm and complementarity conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle depends on a specialized augmented-eigenproblem alternative and makes comparative method-selection claims without any citation. A source with a specific locator is needed to confirm the exact equivalences, applicability boundaries, and singular-case selection guidance.

children.title: Trust-Region Hard Case
children.top_down_role: Spectrally degenerate nonconvex subproblems and their dedicated numerical treatment.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral hard case of the trust-region subproblem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|s\|\leq\Delta}g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), where \(H=H^T\), \(\Delta>0\), \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\), and \(E_1=\ker(H-\theta_1I)\). Let \(P_{E_1}\) denote orthogonal projection onto \(E_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonconvex Euclidean trust-region subproblems, including repeated leftmost eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algebraic hard case occurs when \[P_{E_1}g=0.\] Define the critical shifted solution \[s_{\mathrm{cri}}:=-(H-\theta_1I)^\dagger g,\] which is orthogonal to \(E_1\). The active hard case occurs when additionally \(\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|<\Delta\). Then the optimal multiplier is \(\lambda_*=-\theta_1\), and every hard-case global solution has the form \[s_*=s_{\mathrm{cri}}+z,	 z\in E_1,	 \|s_*\|=\Delta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hard case is the spectrally degenerate situation in which the gradient has no component in the eigenspace of the most negative eigenvalue. The usual shifted-solution norm therefore need not diverge at the limiting admissible shift. If its limiting pseudoinverse solution lies strictly inside the trust region, the multiplier equals the negative leftmost eigenvalue and an eigenspace component must be added to reach the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_{E_1}g=0,	\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|<\Delta\Longrightarrow \lambda_*=-\theta_1,	s_*=s_{\mathrm{cri}}+z,	z\in E_1,	\|s_*\|=\Delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Q_1\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(E_1\), the hard-case orthogonality condition is \(Q_1^Tg=0\).
The spectral norm function has no pole at \(\lambda=-\theta_1\) precisely because all coefficients associated with \(E_1\) vanish.
special_cases_latex: If \(E_1=\operatorname{span}\{v_1\}\), then \(z=\pm\sqrt{\Delta^2-\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|^2}\,v_1\).
If \(g=0\) and \(H\) is indefinite, then \(s_{\mathrm{cri}}=0\) and every boundary vector in \(E_1\) is a global solution.
immediate_consequences_latex: The shifted matrix \(H+\lambda_*I=H-\theta_1I\) is positive semidefinite and singular.
Nonuniqueness occurs whenever more than one eigenspace completion satisfies the boundary equation.
boundary_notes: Orthogonality alone identifies the algebraic hard case; completion is needed only when the limiting shifted solution does not already exceed the radius.
A small but nonzero value of \(\|P_{E_1}g\|\) is a near-hard case, not the exact hard case.

notation.meaning: Eigenspace associated with the smallest eigenvalue of \(H\).

children.title: Hard-Case Recognition System
children.top_down_role: Spectral signatures and numerical recognition of hard-case behavior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral diagnostics for exact and near hard cases
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=H^T\), \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq0\), \(E_1=\ker(H-\theta_1I)\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\). Let \(Q_1\) have orthonormal columns spanning \(E_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact arithmetic recognition and its tolerance-based finite-precision relaxation for Euclidean subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hard-case recognition system is the diagnostic tuple \[\mathcal R(H,g,\Delta)=\left(\theta_1,	\eta_E:=\|Q_1^Tg\|,	s_{\mathrm{cri}}:=-(H-\theta_1I)^\dagger g,	\delta_{\mathrm{cri}}:=\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|\right).\] It recognizes the active exact hard case when \(\theta_1<0\), \(\eta_E=0\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{cri}}<\Delta\). Given tolerances \(\varepsilon_E,\varepsilon_\Delta\geq0\), it recognizes a near-hard case when \(\eta_E\leq\varepsilon_E\|g\|\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{cri}}\leq(1+\varepsilon_\Delta)\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recognition system combines the leftmost eigenvalue, the gradient component in its eigenspace, and the norm of the limiting pseudoinverse solution. Exact hard-case behavior requires a negative leftmost eigenvalue, zero projected gradient, and a limiting shifted solution lying inside the trust-region boundary. Numerical recognition replaces the exact equalities by stated tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\theta_1<0,	\|Q_1^Tg\|=0,	\|(H-\theta_1I)^\dagger g\|<\Delta\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal R\text{ declares the active exact hard case}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The condition \(Q_1^Tg=0\) is equivalent to \(g\in\operatorname{Range}(H-\theta_1I)\).
A missing pole of \(\|(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g\|\) at \(\lambda=-\theta_1\) is the same spectral signature.
special_cases_latex: For a simple \(\theta_1\) with unit eigenvector \(q_1\), the projection diagnostic reduces to \(\eta_E=|q_1^Tg|\).
If \(\theta_1\geq0\), this system does not declare the nonconvex hard case.
immediate_consequences_latex: When the exact active conditions hold, ordinary root finding on the open positive-definite shift interval cannot generate the required boundary step.
A small projection diagnostic warns that the secular root may lie extremely close to the singular shift and be ill-conditioned numerically.
boundary_notes: The numerical thresholds are algorithm parameters and do not redefine the exact hard case.
An approximate eigenvector may underestimate \(\eta_E\); reliable numerical recognition requires an adequately resolved leftmost invariant subspace.

notation.meaning: Magnitude of the gradient component in the leftmost eigenspace.
Norm of the limiting pseudoinverse shifted solution.

children.title: Hard-Case Spectral Structure
children.top_down_role: Eigenspace and curvature configurations associated with the trust-region hard case.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Spectral Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral predicate and solution structure for the classical trust-region hard case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=B^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), \(E_1=\ker(B-\theta_1I)\), \(g\perp E_1\), and \(\Delta>0\). Set \(\lambda_*=-\theta_1\) and \(p_0=-(B+\lambda_*I)^\dagger g\). The singular endpoint \(\lambda_*\) yields a global trust-region minimizer if and only if \(\|p_0\|_2\leq\Delta\). In that case, every global minimizer associated with this endpoint has the form \(p_*=p_0+z\), where \(z\in E_1\) and \(\|p_0+z\|_2=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the hard case, the gradient is orthogonal to the leftmost eigenspace and the optimal shift makes the shifted Hessian singular. The pseudoinverse step can be completed by a leftmost-eigenspace component exactly when its norm does not exceed the trust-region radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The endpoint \(\lambda_*=-\theta_1\) yields a global minimizer iff \(\|p_0\|_2\leq\Delta\); then \(p_*=-(B-\theta_1I)^\dagger g+z\), where \(z\in\ker(B-\theta_1I)\) and \(\|p_*\|_2=\Delta\).

children.title: Hard-Case Detection
children.top_down_role: Numerical diagnostics used to recognize hard-case behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact spectral test for the Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider 
\[
\min_{\|s\|\leq\Delta}m(s):=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs,
\]
where \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(\alpha=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\). Let \(E=\ker(B-\alpha I)\) and \(p=-(B-\alpha I)^{\dagger}g\). The hard case is detected exactly when
\[
g\perp E\quad\text{and}\quad \|p\|\leq\Delta.
\]
Equivalently, the optimal multiplier may equal \(\lambda_*=-\alpha\), making \(B+\lambda_*I\) singular. Every associated global solution has the form \(s_*=p+z\), where \(z\in E\) and \(\|p+z\|=\Delta\), except that \(z=0\) is permitted when \(\lambda_*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hard case occurs when the gradient misses the leftmost eigenspace and the pseudoinverse solution fits inside the trust region, requiring an eigenspace component for completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\perp E\) and \(\|p\|\leq\Delta\) characterize the hard case.

notation.meaning: Eigenspace associated with the smallest eigenvalue of B.
Minimum-norm solution of the singular shifted stationarity equation.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Hard Detection Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discontinuity of exact hard-case classification under vanishing spectral coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\), \(g_\varepsilon=(\varepsilon,0)^{\mathsf T}\), and \(\Delta>0\). At \(\varepsilon=0\), the problem is in the hard case: the optimal multiplier is \(\lambda_0=1\), and both \((\Delta,0)^{\mathsf T}\) and \((-\Delta,0)^{\mathsf T}\) are global minimizers. For every \(\varepsilon\neq0\), the shifted matrix is nonsingular and the unique minimizer satisfies
\[
\lambda_\varepsilon>1,\qquad s_{\varepsilon,1}=-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda_\varepsilon-1},\qquad \|s_\varepsilon\|=\Delta.
\]
Consequently, \(s_\varepsilon\to(-\operatorname{sign}\varepsilon\,\Delta,0)^{\mathsf T}\), so arbitrarily small gradient perturbations change the classification and select different limiting solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an exact hard case, arbitrarily small gradient components in the leftmost eigendirection remove singularity and select different boundary solutions according to perturbation sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact hard-case detection is discontinuous at \(\varepsilon=0\).

notation.meaning: Gradient coupling to the smallest-eigenvalue eigenspace.

children.top_down_role: Completion, perturbation, and eigenspace-based treatment of hard-case subproblems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completion, eigenspace, and perturbation resolutions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Assume the active hard-case data \(H=H^T\), \(\theta_1<0\), \(E_1=\ker(H-\theta_1I)\), \(P_{E_1}g=0\), and \(s_{\mathrm{cri}}=-(H-\theta_1I)^\dagger g\) with \(\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|<\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean hard-case subproblems; both exact completion and near-hard perturbative implementations are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hard-case resolution algorithm belongs to the family if it returns \(s_*\) by one of the following mathematically equivalent limiting mechanisms: \[(a)\quad s_*=s_{\mathrm{cri}}+z,	z\in E_1,	\|z\|^2=\Delta^2-\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|^2;\] \[(b)\quad z=Q_1w,	\|w\|^2=\Delta^2-\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|^2;\] or by a perturbation \(g_\varepsilon=g+\varepsilon v\), \(v\in E_1\), followed by easy-case shifted solves whose selected limit as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) satisfies (a). In every case the returned multiplier is \(\lambda_*=-\theta_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolution family completes the limiting pseudoinverse solution with a component from the most-negative eigenspace so that the trust-region boundary is reached. The completion may be computed directly in that eigenspace or obtained as the selected limit of perturbed easy-case problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(H-\theta_1I)s_*=-g,	\|s_*\|=\Delta,	H-\theta_1I\succeq0,	\lambda_*=-\theta_1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(s_{\mathrm{cri}}\perp E_1\), the boundary equation is equivalent to \(\|z\|^2=\Delta^2-\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|^2\).
For a simple leftmost eigenvalue, completion reduces to choosing one of two scalar roots along its unit eigenvector.
special_cases_latex: If \(g=0\), the method returns any \(s_*\in E_1\) with \(\|s_*\|=\Delta\).
If \(\|s_{\mathrm{cri}}\|=\Delta\), the zero completion \(z=0\) is sufficient.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exact completion satisfies the global trust-region optimality conditions.
Different completion vectors can produce multiple global minimizers with the same model value.
boundary_notes: A perturbation method must control the selected limiting branch; an arbitrary easy-case limit need not converge to the desired completion.
The family presupposes access to the leftmost eigenspace or an adequate approximation to it.

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis matrix for the leftmost eigenspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-Tridiagonal Construction of a Hard-Case Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The block notation and equation references are retained from the extract; the terminal component denoted by the source's alpha notation is determined using the stated eigenvector and norm equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hard case occurs for (7.5.1), T_k has the block form (7.5.64), and its last block T_{k_\ell} is the first block yielding the leftmost eigenvalue -\theta of M^{-1}H. If \theta\leq\lambda_{k_1}, then s_k=Q_{k_1}h_{k_1} solves (7.5.1), where (T_{k_1}+\lambda_{k_1}I_{k_1+1})h_{k_1}=-\gamma_0e_1 and the coefficient matrix is positive definite. If \theta>\lambda_{k_1}, then s_k=Q_kh_k solves (7.5.1), where h_k has leading block h, zero intermediate blocks, and the stated terminal \alpha-component; (T_{k_1}+\theta I_{k_1+1})h=-\gamma_0e_1 is nonsingular, u is an eigenvector of T_{k_\ell} for -\theta, and \alpha is chosen so that \|h\|_2^2+\alpha^2\|u\|_2^2=\Delta^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the hard case, when the last block is the first block attaining the leftmost eigenvalue, a solution is constructed by two cases. If theta is no larger than lambda_{k1}, solve the indicated positive-definite shifted first-block system and set s_k=Q_{k1}h_{k1}. If theta is larger, solve the indicated nonsingular first-block system, add a component along a leftmost-eigenvalue eigenvector of the last block, choose its magnitude to meet the trust-region boundary, and set s_k=Q_kh_k.
assumptions_latex: T_k\text{ has the block form specified in }(7.5.64).
T_{k_\ell}\text{ is the first block yielding the leftmost eigenvalue }-\theta\text{ of }M^{-1}H.

children.title: Hard-Case Eigenspace Completion
children.top_down_role: Resolution strategies using components from critical curvature eigenspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Eigenspace Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a global solution after the singular shifted solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input symmetric \(B\), gradient \(g\), radius \(\Delta>0\), smallest eigenvalue \(\alpha<0\), and a unit vector \(u\in\ker(B-\alpha I)\), with \(g\perp\ker(B-\alpha I)\). Compute
\[
p=-(B-\alpha I)^\dagger g,
\]
choosing the minimum-norm solution, hence \(p\perp u\). If \(\|p\|>\Delta\), report that hard-case completion is inapplicable. Otherwise set \(\rho=(\Delta^2-\|p\|^2)^{1/2}\), evaluate \(m(p+\rho u)\) and \(m(p-\rho u)\), and output the lower-valued candidate. The output \(s_*=p\pm\rho u\) satisfies \(\|s_*\|=\Delta\), \((B-\alpha I)s_*=-g\), and \(B-\alpha I\succeq0\), hence is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the singular shifted system in the orthogonal complement, then add a smallest-eigenvector component of the exact length needed to reach the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(s_*\) is a global trust-region subproblem minimizer.

children.title: Hard-Case Perturbation Families
children.top_down_role: Perturbative treatments of degenerate or nearly degenerate hard-case subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Perturbation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient perturbations regularize singular hard cases and select completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), choose a unit \(u\in E:=\ker(B-\alpha I)\), and suppose \(g\perp E\). Define \(p=-(B-\alpha I)^\dagger g\), assume \(\|p\|<\Delta\), and perturb the gradient by \(g_\varepsilon=g+\varepsilon u\). For every \(\varepsilon\neq0\), the corresponding global solution has a multiplier \(\lambda_\varepsilon>-\alpha\) and satisfies
\[
s_\varepsilon=-(B+\lambda_\varepsilon I)^{-1}g_\varepsilon,\qquad \|s_\varepsilon\|=\Delta.
\]
Writing \(\rho=(\Delta^2-\|p\|^2)^{1/2}\), the regular solutions select the hard-case completions according to
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^\pm}s_\varepsilon=p\mp\rho u.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a vanishing gradient component along a smallest eigenvector makes the shifted system regular and selects one of two hard-case completions according to its sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_\varepsilon=g+\varepsilon u\) regularizes the hard case and selects \(p\mp\rho u\).

notation.meaning: Norm of the limiting eigenspace completion.
