children.title: Hard-Case Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity regimes affecting completion and perturbation reliability.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies where shifted-solve conditioning and solution continuity fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a regular trust-region solution \((s,\lambda)\), define the shifted spectral gap \(\gamma=\lambda+\lambda_{\min}(B)>0\). Since
\[
\|(B+\lambda I)^{-1}\|_2=\gamma^{-1},
\]
a gradient perturbation \(\delta g\), with \(B\) and \(\lambda\) fixed, produces \(\|\delta s\|_2\leq\gamma^{-1}\|\delta g\|_2\). Thus uniform stability requires \(\gamma\) bounded away from zero. The hard-case boundary is \(\gamma=0\) together with gradient orthogonality to the nullspace of \(B+\lambda I\). As this boundary is approached, the shifted solve becomes arbitrarily ill-conditioned; at the boundary, eigenspace completion may be nonunique, and no uniform Lipschitz bound for the selected solution persists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stability is lost as the shifted matrix’s smallest eigenvalue approaches zero; at exact orthogonality, singularity and nonunique eigenspace completion can occur.
assumptions_latex: The multiplier is held fixed for the displayed perturbation estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform shifted-solve stability fails as \(\gamma\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of the shifted matrix.

children.top_down_role: Model-decrease, curvature, residual, and relative-optimality families used to qualify approximate trial steps.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite certificates for approximate trust-region steps
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), where \(H=H^T\), and let \(\mathcal B_\Delta=\{s:\|s\|\leq\Delta\}\). For feasible \(s\), define the model decrease \(D(s)=m(0)-m(s)\), let \(s_C\) be the Cauchy point, and let \(s_*\) be a global subproblem minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic quadratic subproblems; individual algorithms may require only a selected subset of the certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subproblem quality certificate system is a tuple \[\mathcal C(s,\lambda)=\bigl(C_C,C_N,C_R,C_O\bigr)\] whose components are: \[C_C:\ D(s)\geq\kappa_C D(s_C);\qquad C_O:\ D(s)\geq\kappa_O D(s_*);\] \[C_R:\ \|(H+\lambda I)s+g\|\leq\varepsilon_R,	|\lambda(\Delta-\|s\|)|\leq\varepsilon_K,	\lambda\geq0;\] and, when \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\), \[C_N:\ D(s)\geq\kappa_ND(s_E),\] where \(s_E\) is a boundary eigenpoint along a direction representing the negative curvature. Here \(\kappa_C,\kappa_O,\kappa_N\in(0,1]\) and \(\varepsilon_R,\varepsilon_K\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The certificate system qualifies a feasible approximate step by model decrease relative to the Cauchy point, exploitation of negative curvature, approximate shifted-system stationarity and complementarity, or decrease relative to the global model minimizer. A solver may report one or several components, but each reported component has an explicit inequality and tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C(s,\lambda)\text{ records explicit first-order, second-order, residual, and relative-optimality predicates for }s\in\mathcal B_\Delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The relative-optimality predicate is equivalent to \(m(s)-m(s_*)\leq(1-\kappa_O)D(s_*)\).
Exact KKT certification is recovered from \(\varepsilon_R=\varepsilon_K=0\) together with \(H+\lambda I\succeq0\) and feasibility.
special_cases_latex: A Cauchy-only solver can certify \(C_C\) without estimating the smallest eigenvalue.
When \(g=0\) and \(H\) is indefinite, \(C_N\) remains informative while the Cauchy decrease is zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: The system separates inexpensive global-convergence quality from stronger second-order or near-exact quality.
Certificate thresholds make the accepted inexactness explicit and reproducible.
boundary_notes: No single component is asserted to imply all the others.
Residual and complementarity bounds require an accompanying semidefiniteness check if they are used as an approximate global-optimality certificate.

notation.meaning: Predicted reduction in the quadratic model.
Cauchy, negative-curvature, residual, and relative-optimality certificate predicates.

children.title: Cauchy-Decrease Quality
children.top_down_role: First-order model-decrease quality relative to the canonical reference step.

knowledge_statements.title: Cauchy-Decrease Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order decrease certificate relative to the Cauchy step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\) on \(\|s\|\leq\Delta\), let \(s_C\) minimize \(m(-tg)\) over \(0\leq t\leq\Delta/\|g\|\), with \(s_C=0\) when \(g=0\). A feasible step \(s\) has Cauchy-decrease quality \(\kappa_C\in(0,1]\) when
\[
m(0)-m(s)\geq\kappa_C\bigl(m(0)-m(s_C)\bigr).
\]
For \(g\neq0\), the reference decrease obeys
\[
m(0)-m(s_C)\geq\tfrac12\|g\|\min\left\{\Delta,\frac{\|g\|}{\|B\|_2}\right\},
\]
where \(\|g\|/\|B\|_2:=+\infty\) when \(B=0\). Hence feasibility and the first displayed inequality provide a directly checkable first-order model-decrease certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible step is Cauchy-quality if its predicted decrease is at least a fixed fraction of the decrease obtained by exact minimization along the negative gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(s)\geq\kappa_C[m(0)-m(s_C)]\) certifies Cauchy decrease.

notation.meaning: Cauchy step minimizing the model along the negative-gradient ray.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fraction-of-Cauchy model-decrease quality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), with \(H=H^T\), and let \(\Delta>0\). Assume \(g\neq0\). Define \(D(s)=m(0)-m(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic trust-region models and feasible approximate steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Cauchy point is \[s_C=-\alpha_Cg,	\alpha_C=\begin{cases}\min\{\|g\|^2/(g^THg),\Delta/\|g\|\},&g^THg>0,\\\Delta/\|g\|,&g^THg\leq0.\end{cases}\] A feasible step \(s\) has Cauchy-decrease quality \(\kappa_C\in(0,1]\) when \[\|s\|\leq\Delta,	D(s)\geq\kappa_CD(s_C).\] Its realized Cauchy-quality ratio is \(\eta_C(s)=D(s)/D(s_C)\) whenever \(D(s_C)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cauchy-decrease quality compares the predicted reduction of an approximate feasible step with the reduction obtained by exactly minimizing the model along the negative-gradient ray, truncated by the trust-region boundary. A step meets quality level \(\kappa_C\) when it attains at least that fixed fraction of the Cauchy reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s\text{ is }\kappa_C\text{-Cauchy-quality}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|s\|\leq\Delta\text{ and }m(0)-m(s)\geq\kappa_C[m(0)-m(s_C)].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[m(s)\leq(1-\kappa_C)m(0)+\kappa_Cm(s_C).\]
For Euclidean models, the standard sufficient-decrease bound has the scale \(D(s)\geq c\|g\|\min\{\|g\|/\|H\|,\Delta\}\) for a fixed positive constant \(c\).
special_cases_latex: The Cauchy step itself has \(\eta_C(s_C)=1\).
If \(g^THg\leq0\), then \(s_C=-\Delta g/\|g\|\) lies on the boundary.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any step improving the model beyond the Cauchy point has \(\eta_C(s)\geq1\).
The certificate is computable using one Hessian-vector product and does not require a matrix factorization.
boundary_notes: When \(g=0\), \(D(s_C)=0\) and the ratio is undefined; negative-curvature quality is then the appropriate second-order certificate.
Cauchy quality is a first-order decrease standard and need not detect unexploited negative curvature.

notation.meaning: Cauchy point of the quadratic trust-region model.
Ratio of trial-step decrease to Cauchy decrease.

children.title: Negative-Curvature Quality
children.top_down_role: Second-order quality based on identifying and exploiting nonconvex curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order decrease certificate from an admissible negative-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+	frac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), where \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), and let \(v\) be a unit vector satisfying \(v^{\mathsf T}Bv<0\). Replace \(v\) by \(-v\) if necessary so that \(g^{\mathsf T}v\leq0\). The boundary step \(s_N=\Delta v\) then satisfies
\[
m(0)-m(s_N)=-\Delta g^{\mathsf T}v-	frac12\Delta^2v^{\mathsf T}Bv
\geq\tfrac12\Delta^2(-v^{\mathsf T}Bv).
\]
A feasible trial step \(s\) has negative-curvature quality \(\kappa_N\in(0,1]\) if its model decrease is at least \(\kappa_N[m(0)-m(s_N)]\). The displayed direction and inequality form a verifiable second-order decrease certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step has negative-curvature quality when it achieves a fixed fraction of the decrease obtained by moving to the boundary along a detected negative-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(s)\geq\kappa_N[m(0)-m(s_N)]\) certifies negative-curvature quality.

notation.meaning: Boundary step along the signed curvature direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eigenpoint-based negative-curvature quality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), where \(H=H^T\) has \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\), and let \(\Delta>0\). Define \(D(s)=m(0)-m(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonconvex Euclidean quadratic models; scaled-norm variants require corresponding metric factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direction \(u\) is a \(\kappa_{\mathrm{nc}}\)-negative-curvature direction when \[\|u\|=\Delta,	g^Tu\leq0,	u^THu\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{nc}}\theta_1\Delta^2,	\kappa_{\mathrm{nc}}\in(0,1].\] Its eigenpoint is \(s_E=u\), which satisfies \[D(s_E)\geq-\tfrac12\kappa_{\mathrm{nc}}\theta_1\Delta^2.\] A feasible trial step \(s\) has negative-curvature quality \(\kappa_N\in(0,1]\) if \[D(s)\geq\kappa_ND(s_E).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative-curvature quality requires a trial step to capture a fixed fraction of the decrease obtained at a boundary eigenpoint. The eigenpoint direction has a nonpositive linear contribution and a Rayleigh quotient representing a fixed fraction of the most negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D(s)\geq\kappa_ND(s_E)\geq-\frac12\kappa_N\kappa_{\mathrm{nc}}\theta_1\Delta^2.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The curvature condition is \(u^THu/\|u\|^2\leq\kappa_{\mathrm{nc}}\theta_1<0\).
Combined first- and second-order quality may be stated as \(D(s)\geq\kappa\max\{D(s_C),D(s_E)\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a unit leftmost eigenvector \(v_1\), choose \(u=\pm\Delta v_1\) with the sign making \(g^Tu\leq0\); then \(\kappa_{\mathrm{nc}}=1\).
If \(g=0\), the eigenpoint still guarantees decrease \(-\tfrac12\theta_1\Delta^2>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate prevents a zero-gradient step from being accepted at a strict saddle solely because its Cauchy decrease is zero.
An approximate eigenvector suffices when its Rayleigh quotient meets the stated curvature fraction.
boundary_notes: The definition applies only when negative curvature is present.
A direction with merely \(u^THu<0\) may be too weak unless its curvature is quantitatively related to \(\theta_1\).

notation.meaning: Fraction of leftmost curvature represented by the chosen direction.

children.title: Stationarity-Residual Certificate Pair
children.top_down_role: Accuracy families based on approximate subproblem stationarity or linear-solve residuals.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-stationarity and shifted-system residuals
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), \(H=H^T\), and \(\mathcal B_\Delta=\{s:\|s\|\leq\Delta\}\). Let \(P_{\mathcal B_\Delta}\) be Euclidean projection onto this ball.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic subproblems; the pair measures first-order stationarity and consistency with a candidate trust-region multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible step \(s\) and candidate multiplier \(\lambda\geq0\), define the stationarity-residual certificate pair \[\chi(s):=\left\|s-P_{\mathcal B_\Delta}\bigl(s-(g+Hs)\bigr)\right\|,\] \[R(s,\lambda):=\left(\|(H+\lambda I)s+g\|^2+\lambda^2(\Delta-\|s\|)^2\right)^{1/2}.\] The pair certifies tolerances \((\varepsilon_S,\varepsilon_R)\) when \(\chi(s)\leq\varepsilon_S\) and \(R(s,\lambda)\leq\varepsilon_R\). Exact first-order KKT stationarity is represented by \(\chi(s)=0\), equivalently by the existence of \(\lambda\geq0\) with \(R(s,\lambda)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first residual is a projected-gradient fixed-point residual for minimizing the model over the trust-region ball. The second combines the shifted linear-system residual with complementarity for an explicit multiplier. Both vanish at an exact KKT pair; global trust-region optimality additionally requires the shifted Hessian to be positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R(s,\lambda)=0\Longleftrightarrow (H+\lambda I)s=-g	\text{and}	\lambda(\Delta-\|s\|)=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\chi(s)=0\) is equivalent to \(0\in g+Hs+N_{\mathcal B_\Delta}(s)\), where \(N_{\mathcal B_\Delta}(s)\) is the normal cone.
For an interior feasible point, exact stationarity reduces to \(g+Hs=0\) and \(\lambda=0\).
special_cases_latex: On the boundary with \(s\neq0\), the KKT multiplier makes \(g+Hs=-\lambda s\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The shifted residual can be monitored directly by linear-system solvers.
The projected residual avoids requiring a multiplier estimate.
boundary_notes: Small residuals alone do not exclude convergence to a nonglobal stationary point when \(H+\lambda I\) is indefinite.
Relative residuals may be preferable under severe scaling; their normalization must be stated separately.

children.title: Subproblem Stationarity Quality
children.top_down_role: Approximate-solution quality assessed through subproblem stationarity information.

knowledge_statements.title: Subproblem Stationarity Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled residual certificate for trust-region KKT stationarity and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible step \(s\) and multiplier estimate \(\lambda\geq0\), define
\[
\eta_{\mathrm{KKT}}(s,\lambda)=\max\left\{
\frac{\|(B+\lambda I)s+g\|}{\max\{1,\|g\|,\|B\|_2\Delta\}},
\frac{\lambda\,|\Delta-\|s\||}{\max\{1,\lambda\Delta\}},
\frac{\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B+\lambda I)\}}{\max\{1,\|B\|_2,\lambda\}}
\right\}.
\]
The pair \((s,\lambda)\) has stationarity quality \(\varepsilon\) when \(\eta_{\mathrm{KKT}}(s,\lambda)\leq\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon=0\), feasibility, stationarity, complementary slackness, dual nonnegativity, and shifted positive semidefiniteness hold, so \(s\) is a global minimizer of the quadratic trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible step and nonnegative multiplier are certified by scaled stationarity, complementarity, and shifted-curvature residuals; zero residual gives the exact global optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_{\mathrm{KKT}}(s,\lambda)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies subproblem stationarity quality \(\varepsilon\).

children.title: Linear-Solve Residual Quality
children.top_down_role: Approximate-solution quality assessed through residual information from inner linear solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Solve Residual Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward-error certificate for the shifted stationarity equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a feasible step \(s\) and multiplier estimate \(\lambda\geq0\), define the shifted-system residual
\[
r=(B+\lambda I)s+g
\]
and its scaled value
\[
\eta_{\mathrm{lin}}=\frac{\|r\|}{\|B+\lambda I\|_2\|s\|+\|g\|},
\]
with \(\eta_{\mathrm{lin}}=0\) when numerator and denominator both vanish. If \(\eta_{\mathrm{lin}}\leq\varepsilon\), then \(s\) exactly solves \((B+\lambda I)s=-(g+\delta g)\) for \(\delta g=-r\), where
\[
\|\delta g\|\leq\varepsilon\bigl(\|B+\lambda I\|_2\|s\|+\|g\|\bigr).
\]
Thus \((r,\eta_{\mathrm{lin}})\) certifies normwise backward quality of the shifted linear solve, but not complementarity or shifted positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled shifted-system residual certifies that the computed step exactly solves a nearby linear system, but alone does not certify trust-region optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_{\mathrm{lin}}\leq\varepsilon\) is a normwise backward-error certificate.

notation.meaning: Residual of the shifted stationarity equation.
Gradient perturbation realizing the backward error.

children.title: Certificate Mismatch Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where stationarity and residual assessments indicate different quality levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Mismatch Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A zero shifted-solve residual need not certify subproblem optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the one-dimensional problem
\[
\min_{|s|\leq1}m(s)=-\tfrac12s^2.
\]
Take \(s=0\) and \(\lambda=1\). Then \(B=-1\), \(g=0\), and
\[
(B+\lambda)s+g=0,\qquad B+\lambda=0\succeq0,
\]
so the linear-solve residual vanishes and the shifted-curvature condition holds. Nevertheless,
\[
\lambda(1-|s|)=1\neq0,
\]
so complementary slackness fails; moreover, \(m(0)=0\) while \(m(1)=m(-1)=-1/2\). Thus a perfect linear-solve certificate can coexist with maximal failure to exploit the trust-region boundary and does not imply subproblem stationarity quality or model optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shifted system can be solved exactly while complementarity fails: the zero step for a concave quadratic has zero linear residual but is not optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_{\mathrm{lin}}=0\) does not imply the complete trust-region optimality conditions.

children.title: Relative Model-Optimality Quality

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Model-Optimality Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-decrease ratio relative to the globally optimal trust-region step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
m_*:=\min_{\|z\|\leq\Delta}m(z),qquad D_*:=m(0)-m_*.
\]
For a feasible trial step \(s\) and \(\kappa_M\in(0,1]\), relative model-optimality quality is certified by
\[
m(0)-m(s)\geq\kappa_M D_*.
\]
When \(D_*>0\), this is equivalent to the ratio \([m(0)-m(s)]/D_*\geq\kappa_M\), or to the objective-gap bound
\[
m(s)-m_*\leq(1-\kappa_M)D_*.
\]
When \(D_*=0\), the model is already minimized at the origin and the certificate requires \(m(s)=m_*=m(0)\). Any rigorous lower bound on \(m_*\) may replace its exact value to produce a conservative, computable certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible step has relative model-optimality quality when it realizes a prescribed fraction of the largest model decrease available inside the trust region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(s)\geq\kappa_M[m(0)-m_*]\) certifies relative model-optimality quality.

notation.meaning: Required fraction of optimal model decrease.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fraction of globally optimal model decrease
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a quadratic model, let \(\mathcal B_\Delta=\{s:\|s\|\leq\Delta\}\), and let \(s_*\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal B_\Delta}m(s)\). Define \(D(s)=m(0)-m(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional trust-region models with a global subproblem minimizer; the definition is independent of how the benchmark is computed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\kappa_O\in(0,1]\), a feasible step \(s\) has relative model-optimality quality \(\kappa_O\) if \[D(s)\geq\kappa_OD(s_*).\] When \(D(s_*)>0\), its relative quality ratio and relative model gap are \[\eta_O(s):=\frac{D(s)}{D(s_*)},	\gamma_O(s):=\frac{m(s)-m(s_*)}{D(s_*)}=1-\eta_O(s).\] Thus the certificate is equivalently \(\eta_O(s)\geq\kappa_O\) or \(\gamma_O(s)\leq1-\kappa_O\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative model-optimality quality compares the trial step with the strongest benchmark: a global minimizer of the trust-region model. A quality level of \(\kappa_O\) means that the step realizes at least that fraction of the maximum available predicted reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[m(0)-m(s)\geq\kappa_O[m(0)-m(s_*)]\Longleftrightarrow m(s)-m(s_*)\leq(1-\kappa_O)[m(0)-m(s_*)].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact model minimizer has \(\eta_O(s_*)=1\) and \(\gamma_O(s_*)=0\).
The condition is invariant under adding a constant to \(m\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\kappa_O=1\), any certified step is itself a global subproblem minimizer.
Since \(D(s_*)\geq D(s_C)\), relative-optimality quality implies a fraction-of-Cauchy bound with the same fraction.
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate remains informative when \(g=0\) but negative curvature yields positive optimal decrease.
It provides a solver-independent accuracy scale tied to the best attainable model value.
boundary_notes: The ratio is undefined when \(D(s_*)=0\); in that case every feasible step with \(m(s)=m(0)\) is already model-optimal.
Computing the benchmark exactly may be as expensive as solving the original subproblem, so practical stopping tests often use bounds that imply this condition.

notation.meaning: Fraction of optimal model decrease achieved.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Families of maps for quadratic trust-region subproblems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal D_n=\{(g,H,\Delta):g\in\mathbb R^n,	H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},	\Delta>0\}\), and let \(m_{g,H}(s)=g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic quadratic subproblems; solvers may return exact or certificate-qualified approximate steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region subproblem solver is a map \[\mathscr S:\mathcal D_n\to\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+,	(g,H,\Delta)\mapsto(s,\lambda),\] with \(\|s\|\leq\Delta\). The principal solver families are defined by their search representation: path solvers minimize over a prescribed low-dimensional curve; dense nearly-exact solvers determine \(\lambda\) from shifted factorizations or a secular equation; projected or subspace solvers minimize over \(\mathcal U\cap\mathcal B_\Delta\); Krylov solvers use \(\mathcal K_j(H,g)\cap\mathcal B_\Delta\); and matrix-free solvers access \(H\) only through products \(Hv\). An exact solver additionally returns a pair satisfying \[(H+\lambda I)s=-g,	H+\lambda I\succeq0,	\lambda(\Delta-\|s\|)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver family is a class of mappings from quadratic model data and a radius to a feasible step, optionally with a multiplier. Families are distinguished by whether they search a fixed path, perform dense shifted factorizations, optimize in a low-dimensional subspace, build Krylov spaces, or use only Hessian-vector products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathscr S(g,H,\Delta)=(s,\lambda)\Longrightarrow\|s\|\leq\Delta;\quad\text{exactness adds the global KKT conditions.}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A subspace method is matrix-free when its basis and reduced matrix can be generated solely from products with \(H\).
A path method is a one-dimensional constrained minimization over the image of a parameterized curve.
special_cases_latex: The Cauchy and dogleg methods are low-dimensional path solvers.
Newton–CG and Lanczos trust-region methods are large-scale Krylov or matrix-free solvers.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different solver families can be compared through common feasibility and quality certificates.
The classification separates the mathematical search domain from the requested solution accuracy.
boundary_notes: The family definition does not assert equal cost, accuracy, or suitability for indefinite models.
A particular implementation may belong to more than one family, such as a matrix-free Krylov solver.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Safeguarded trust-region multiplier update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Case-based selection of the secular-equation multiplier using a Newton candidate, classification sets, and bracket bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda\), \(\lambda^{\mathrm L}\), \(\lambda^{\mathrm U}\), and the solver-defined sets \(\mathcal L,\mathcal G,\mathcal N\) be given. Apply the following update:
1. If \(\lambda\in\mathcal L\) and \(g\neq0\), compute \(\lambda^+\) by the associated Newton secular step and replace \(\lambda\) by \(\lambda^+\).
2. If \(\lambda\in\mathcal G\), compute \(\lambda^+\). If \(\lambda^+\in\mathcal L\), replace \(\lambda\) by \(\lambda^+\). If \(\lambda^+\in\mathcal N\) and \(\lambda^+\leq\lambda^{\mathrm L}\), choose \(\lambda\in[\lambda^{\mathrm L},\lambda^{\mathrm U})\). If \(\lambda^+\in\mathcal N\) and \(\lambda^+>\lambda^{\mathrm L}\), set \(\lambda^{\mathrm L}:=\lambda^+\) and choose \(\lambda\in(\lambda^{\mathrm L},\lambda^{\mathrm U})\).
3. If \(\lambda\in\mathcal N\) or \(g=0\), choose \(\lambda\in(\lambda^{\mathrm L},\lambda^{\mathrm U})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the Newton secular step when its classification permits; otherwise select a multiplier from the current bracket, updating the lower bound when the rejected Newton candidate improves it.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal L,\mathcal G,\mathcal N\text{ and }\lambda^{\mathrm L},\lambda^{\mathrm U}\text{ are defined by the safeguarded solver}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda\text{ is updated by the stated Newton-or-bracketing case distinction}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path and small-subspace trust-region solvers
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), \(H=H^T\), and \(\Delta>0\). Let \(s_C\) denote the Cauchy point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional approximate subproblem solvers whose search domain has dimension independent of the ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A low-dimensional path solver selects either a continuous curve \(\Gamma=\{\gamma(t):t\in T\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) or a subspace \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) with \(\dim\mathcal U\leq2\), requires \(0,s_C\in\Gamma\) or \(s_C\in\mathcal U\), and returns \[s\in\arg\min\{m(z):z\in\Gamma,	\|z\|\leq\Delta\}\] or \[s\in\arg\min\{m(z):z\in\mathcal U,	\|z\|\leq\Delta\}.\] The inclusion of \(s_C\) ensures \(m(s)\leq m(s_C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family replaces minimization over the full trust-region ball by minimization along a canonical curve or within a subspace of dimension at most two. The search set contains the Cauchy point, so its minimizer achieves at least the Cauchy reduction while requiring only a small reduced problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s_C\in\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal B_\Delta,	s\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal F}m(z)\Longrightarrow m(s)\leq m(s_C),\] where \(\mathcal F\) is the feasible path or small-subspace search set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A parameterized path solver solves a scalar constrained minimization in \(t\).
A two-dimensional subspace solver reduces the subproblem to a trust-region problem in at most two coordinates.
special_cases_latex: The negative-gradient ray gives the Cauchy-step solver.
The two-segment path through the unconstrained steepest-descent point and Newton point gives classical dogleg.
The space \(\operatorname{span}\{g,H^{-1}g\}\) gives two-dimensional subspace minimization when \(H\succ0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exact minimizer on such a search set has Cauchy-decrease quality at least one.
The reduced problem can be solved without exploring all \(n\) directions.
boundary_notes: For indefinite \(H\), a path omitting negative-curvature directions may provide only first-order quality.
The definition does not include growing Krylov spaces whose dimension is not uniformly bounded by two.

knowledge_statements.title: Cauchy-Step Solver
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization of a quadratic model along the negative-gradient ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), symmetric \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\) for the model \(m(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\). If \(g=0\), output \(s_C=0\). Otherwise compute \(c=g^{\mathsf T}Bg\) and set
\[
t_C=
\begin{cases}
\min\left\{\dfrac{\|g\|^2}{c},\dfrac{\Delta}{\|g\|}\right\},&c>0,\\[6pt]
\dfrac{\Delta}{\|g\|},&c\leq0.
\end{cases}
\qquad s_C=-t_Cg.
\]
For \(g\neq0\), output \(s_C\); it is feasible and satisfies
\[
s_C\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\leq t\leq\Delta/\|g\|}m(-tg).
\]
For \(g=0\), the prescribed output is the feasible zero step. Thus the solver uses one curvature scalar and exact one-dimensional minimization on the truncated steepest-descent ray whenever that ray is nontrivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonzero gradient, the Cauchy solver minimizes the quadratic model exactly along the truncated negative-gradient ray; for a zero gradient, it returns the feasible zero step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(g\neq0\), the output \(s_C\) minimizes \(m\) over the truncated negative-gradient ray; for \(g=0\), the output is \(s_C=0\).

notation.meaning: Optimal ray parameter for a nonzero gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact minimization on the negative-gradient ray
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\), where \(H=H^T\), and let \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic trust-region models; this is a first-order baseline solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Cauchy-step solver is the map returning \[s_C\in\arg\min_{\alpha\geq0,	\alpha\|g\|\leq\Delta}m(-\alpha g).\] For \(g\neq0\), \[s_C=-\alpha_Cg,	\alpha_C=\begin{cases}\min\{\|g\|^2/(g^THg),\Delta/\|g\|\},&g^THg>0,\\\Delta/\|g\|,&g^THg\leq0.\end{cases}\] For \(g=0\), the solver returns \(s_C=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Cauchy-step solver minimizes the quadratic model exactly along the feasible portion of the negative-gradient ray. Positive curvature along that ray may produce an interior minimizer; nonpositive curvature sends the step to the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[m(s_C)=\min\{m(-\alpha g):\alpha\geq0,	\alpha\|g\|\leq\Delta\},	\|s_C\|\leq\Delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(p^s=-\Delta g/\|g\|\), then \(s_C=\tau_Cp^s\), with \(\tau_C\in[0,1]\) minimizing \(m(\tau p^s)\).
The solver is one-dimensional exact minimization over \(\operatorname{span}\{-g\}\cap\mathcal B_\Delta\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g^THg\leq0\), then \(s_C=-\Delta g/\|g\|\).
If \(H\succ0\) and \(\|g\|^3\leq\Delta g^THg\), then \(s_C=-(\|g\|^2/(g^THg))g\) is interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: The solver requires no factorization of \(H\).
Its output defines the reference decrease used in fraction-of-Cauchy acceptance tests.
boundary_notes: When \(g=0\), the solver returns zero and does not exploit negative curvature.
The Cauchy step generally differs from the global subproblem minimizer unless the relevant solution direction is parallel to \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polygonal-path dogleg solver family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^TBs\), where \(B\succ0\), and let \(\Delta>0\). Define the Newton point \(p_B=-B^{-1}g\) and the unconstrained steepest-descent minimizer \(p_U=-(g^Tg)/(g^TBg)\,g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite quadratic models; modified-Hessian variants replace \(B\) by a positive-definite approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dogleg path is a continuous piecewise-affine curve \(\gamma:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^n\) with \[\gamma(0)=0,	\gamma(t_U)=p_U,	\gamma(T)=p_B,\] such that \(\|\gamma(t)\|\) is nondecreasing and \(m(\gamma(t))\) is nonincreasing. A dogleg solver returns the last feasible path point, equivalently \[s_{DL}=\gamma(t_*),	t_*:=\max\{t\in[0,T]:\|\gamma(t)\|\leq\Delta\}.\] If \(\|p_B\|\leq\Delta\), then \(s_{DL}=p_B\); otherwise \(s_{DL}\) is the unique intersection of the path with \(\|s\|=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dogleg family approximates the curved exact trust-region solution trajectory by a polygonal path joining the origin, an unconstrained steepest-descent point, and the Newton point. The selected step advances as far as feasibility permits because the model decreases and the norm increases along the path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s_{DL}=p_B\text{ if }\|p_B\|\leq\Delta;	\text{otherwise }\|s_{DL}\|=\Delta\text{ at the unique path-boundary intersection}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The step minimizes \(m\) over the feasible portion of the monotone dogleg path.
Classical dogleg uses exactly two segments; double-dogleg variants insert additional vertices while retaining the endpoint and monotonicity properties.
special_cases_latex: For sufficiently small \(\Delta\), the selected step lies on the first segment and equals the Cauchy point.
If the Newton point is feasible, the trust-region constraint is inactive along the path endpoint.
immediate_consequences_latex: The path contains the Cauchy point, so the selected step achieves at least the Cauchy decrease.
Only a scalar boundary-intersection equation is required after the path vertices are known.
boundary_notes: For indefinite \(B\), \(p_B\) need not minimize the model, and the standard dogleg construction is not directly applicable.
Monotonicity is part of the mathematical family definition; an arbitrary polygonal path through the stated vertices is not necessarily a dogleg path.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Dogleg
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean classical dogleg step for a positive-definite quadratic trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\), define the Cauchy point \(p_U=-\frac{g^{\mathsf T}g}{g^{\mathsf T}Bg}g\) and Newton point \(p_N=-B^{-1}g\). If \(\lVert p_N\rVert\leq\Delta\), return \(p=p_N\). If \(\lVert p_U\rVert\geq\Delta\), return \(p=-\Delta g/\lVert g\rVert\). Otherwise return \(p=p_U+\tau(p_N-p_U)\), where \(\tau\in(0,1)\) is the unique value satisfying \(\lVert p\rVert=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Follow steepest descent to the Cauchy point, then turn toward the Newton point, stopping where the path first reaches the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step satisfies \(\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta\) and lies on the classical two-segment dogleg path from \(0\) through \(p_U\) to \(p_N\).

unconstrained minimizer along the negative-gradient ray

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical two-segment dogleg step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=m(0)+g^Ts+\tfrac12s^TBs\), where \(B\succ0\), \(g\neq0\), and \(\Delta>0\). Define \(p_U=-(g^Tg)/(g^TBg)\,g\) and \(p_B=-B^{-1}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite quadratic models with a Euclidean trust region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical dogleg path is \[\widetilde p(\tau)=\begin{cases}\tau p_U,&0\leq\tau\leq1,\\p_U+(\tau-1)(p_B-p_U),&1\leq\tau\leq2.\end{cases}\] The classical dogleg step is \[p_{DL}=\widetilde p(\tau_*),	\tau_*:=\max\{\tau\in[0,2]:\|\widetilde p(\tau)\|\leq\Delta\}.\] Hence \(p_{DL}=p_B\) if \(\|p_B\|\leq\Delta\); otherwise \(\tau_*\) is the unique boundary-intersection parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical dogleg follows two line segments: first from the origin to the exact unconstrained minimizer along the negative-gradient direction, then from that point to the Newton point. It returns the Newton point when feasible and otherwise the unique point where this path first reaches the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|p_B\|>\Delta\Longrightarrow\|\widetilde p(\tau_*)\|=\Delta,	p_{DL}=\widetilde p(\tau_*);\qquad \|p_B\|\leq\Delta\Longrightarrow p_{DL}=p_B.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: On the second segment, \(\tau_*\) is determined by \(\|p_U+(\tau_*-1)(p_B-p_U)\|^2=\Delta^2\).
The step is the minimizer of \(m\) over the feasible portion of the two-segment path because the model decreases along that path.
special_cases_latex: If \(\Delta\leq\|p_U\|\), then \(p_{DL}=-(\Delta/\|g\|)g\), the boundary Cauchy point.
If \(\|p_U\|<\Delta<\|p_B\|\), the step lies on the second segment.
immediate_consequences_latex: The classical dogleg step attains at least the Cauchy decrease.
After computing \(p_U\) and \(p_B\), only a scalar quadratic equation is needed for a boundary step.
boundary_notes: The assumption \(B\succ0\) ensures that \(p_B\) is the unique unconstrained minimizer and that path norm and model value are monotone in the required directions.
The definition is the two-segment classical method, not generalized or double-dogleg variants.

notation.meaning: Unconstrained minimizer along the negative-gradient line.
Largest feasible parameter on the classical dogleg path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Newton-dogleg selection and indefinite-curvature boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step selection for the classical Newton-dogleg method, recovery of a feasible Newton step, and failure of the classical endpoint interpretation under indefinite curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m_k(p)=f_k+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), with \(B\succ0\), \(p^{\mathrm B}=-B^{-1}g_k\), and classical dogleg path \(\widetilde p\). For \(\Delta>0\), the path has exactly one intersection with \(\|p\|=\Delta\) when \(\|p^{\mathrm B}\|\ge\Delta\), and no intersection when \(\|p^{\mathrm B}\|<\Delta\). Consequently, \[p_{\mathrm D}=\begin{cases}p^{\mathrm B},&\|p^{\mathrm B}\|\le\Delta,\\\widetilde p(\tau_\Delta),&\|p^{\mathrm B}\|>\Delta,\end{cases}\qquad \|\widetilde p(\tau_\Delta)\|=\Delta.\] If the intersection is on the second segment, \(\tau_\Delta\) satisfies \[\|p^{\mathrm U}+(\tau_\Delta-1)(p^{\mathrm B}-p^{\mathrm U})\|^2=\Delta^2.\] When \(H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\succ0\), one may take \(B=H_k\), so \(p^{\mathrm B}\) is the Newton step; otherwise a positive-definite modified Hessian may be used. Near a solution satisfying second-order sufficient conditions, a feasible full step can recover Newton behavior. If \(B\) is indefinite, however, \(-B^{-1}g_k\) is not in general an unconstrained minimizer of \(m_k\), so the defining endpoint premise of the classical dogleg construction fails and a negative-curvature-aware trust-region strategy is preferable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite dogleg model, the step is the full quadratic minimizer when that point is inside the trust region and otherwise the unique boundary point on the dogleg path. An exact positive-definite Hessian makes the full endpoint the Newton step, permitting Newton behavior near a suitable solution. With indefinite curvature, the full linear-system step is not generally a model minimizer, so the classical dogleg endpoint interpretation breaks down.
assumptions_latex: B\succ0\text{ for the classical dogleg construction}
H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\text{ when the exact Hessian is used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_{\mathrm D}=p^{\mathrm B}\ \text{if }\|p^{\mathrm B}\|\le\Delta,\quad \|p_{\mathrm D}\|=\Delta\ \text{otherwise};\qquad B\not\succ0\Longrightarrow -B^{-1}g_k\text{ need not minimize }m_k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized dogleg path and step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(p)=m(0)+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(g\ne0\), \(B\succ0\), and let \(\Delta>0\). Set \(p^U=-(g^Tg)/(g^TBg)\,g\) and \(p^B=-B^{-1}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, deterministic, smooth trust-region models with a positive-definite model Hessian. The definition covers double-dogleg and other polygonal path-shaping variants, rather than the classical two-segment dogleg alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized dogleg path is a continuous polygonal map \(d:[0,1]\to\operatorname{span}\{g,B^{-1}g\}\) having vertices \(d(0)=0\), \(p^U\), zero or more path-shaping points, and \(d(1)=p^B\), such that \(t\mapsto\|d(t)\|_2\) is nondecreasing and \(t\mapsto m(d(t))\) is nonincreasing. Its trust-region step is \[p_{\mathrm{GD}}=d(t_\Delta),\qquad t_\Delta=\max\{t\in[0,1]:\|d(t)\|_2\le\Delta\}.\] If \(\|p^B\|_2\le\Delta\), then \(p_{\mathrm{GD}}=p^B\); otherwise it is the unique outward intersection of the path with \(\|p\|_2=\Delta\), provided norm growth is strict on the intersected segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized dogleg method replaces the exact curved trust-region solution trajectory by a polygonal path from the origin through the steepest-descent minimizer \(p^U\), optionally through additional shaped points, and finally to the full Newton or quasi-Newton step \(p^B\). The admissible path must move monotonically outward and must not increase the quadratic model. The selected step is the farthest feasible point on that path. Thus it equals \(p^B\) when the full step is feasible and otherwise is the path’s boundary intersection.
assumptions_latex: Every added path-shaping vertex lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{g,B^{-1}g\}\) and preserves nondecreasing radius and nonincreasing model value along adjacent segments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{\mathrm{GD}}=d(1)=p^B\) if \(\|p^B\|_2\le\Delta\); otherwise \(\|p_{\mathrm{GD}}\|_2=\Delta\) and \(p_{\mathrm{GD}}\) lies on the prescribed generalized dogleg path.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The step solves \(\min\{m(d(t)):t\in[0,1],\ \|d(t)\|_2\le\Delta\}\) because the model is nonincreasing along the path.
special_cases_latex: With no added path-shaping point, the vertices \(0,p^U,p^B\) give the classical dogleg.
Adding a point on the segment toward \(p^B\) gives a double-dogleg-type path.
immediate_consequences_latex: Since the initial segment contains the Cauchy point, the selected generalized dogleg step attains at least its model decrease whenever the path conditions hold.
boundary_notes: Indefinite \(B\) is excluded because \(p^B\) need not minimize the unconstrained model.
A polygonal path that turns inward or increases the model is not a generalized dogleg under this definition.

notation.meaning: Unconstrained minimizer of the model along the negative-gradient ray.
Full Newton or quasi-Newton model step.

knowledge_statements.title: Double-Dogleg Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized three-segment extensions of the classical Euclidean dogleg path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) and form the polygonal path with vertices \(0\), \(p_U\), \(\gamma p_N\), and \(p_N\), retaining only an ordering for which model values decrease along successive vertices. Return \(p_N\) when \(\lVert p_N\rVert\leq\Delta\); otherwise return the first point on this path satisfying \(\lVert p\rVert=\Delta\). Each intersected segment is parameterized as \(v_i+t(v_{i+1}-v_i)\), with \(t\in[0,1]\) obtained from the scalar boundary equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A double-dogleg inserts a scaled Newton point between the Cauchy and Newton points, then takes the first trust-region boundary intersection along the resulting path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is feasible and belongs to \([0,p_U]\cup[p_U,\gamma p_N]\cup[\gamma p_N,p_N]\).

notation.meaning: closed line segment joining two vectors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No evidence is cited for this particular three-segment construction or for the admissible rule governing the intermediate scaling parameter. Double-dogleg definitions vary, so authoritative support is needed before this algorithmic formulation can be assessed reliably.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity along the double-dogleg path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance and quadratic-model monotonicity along the ordered double-dogleg construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the double-dogleg method, the distance from x_k increases monotonically along x_k\to\mathrm{C.P.}\to\widehat N. The model value q^{(k)}(x_k+s) decreases monotonically along x_k\to\mathrm{C.P.}\to\widehat N\to x_{k+1}^N.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along the double-dogleg path, the Cauchy point and intermediate Newton-oriented point lie at successively nondecreasing distances from the current iterate, while the quadratic model decreases as the path proceeds through those points to the Newton point.
assumptions_latex: \text{The points }\mathrm{C.P.},\widehat N,\text{ and }x_{k+1}^N\text{ are those of the double-dogleg construction.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\mathrm{C.P.}-x_k\|_2\leq\|\widehat N-x_k\|_2,\qquad q^{(k)}\text{ decreases monotonically along }x_k\to\mathrm{C.P.}\to\widehat N\to x_{k+1}^N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Double-dogleg boundary step and acceptance rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intermediate-point construction, boundary intersection, and sufficient-decrease acceptance in the double-dogleg method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \widehat N=x_k+\eta s_k^N with \eta\in[\gamma,1], with the stated practical choice \eta=0.8\gamma+0.2. Choose \lambda from
\left\|s_k^c+\lambda(\eta s_k^N-s_k^c)\right\|_2^2=\Delta_k^2
and set x_{k+1}(\lambda)=x_k+s_k^c+\lambda(\eta s_k^N-s_k^c). Accept x_{k+1}=x_{k+1}(\lambda) if
f(x_{k+1}(\lambda))\leq f(x_k)+\rho g_k^T(x_{k+1}(\lambda)-x_k),\qquad \rho\in(0,\tfrac12);
otherwise set x_{k+1}=x_k. When \eta=1, \widehat N is the Newton point and the construction reduces to the classical dogleg step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method selects an intermediate scaled-Newton point, finds the trust-region boundary intersection on the segment from the Cauchy point to that intermediate point by a scalar root solve, and accepts it only when the stated sufficient-decrease condition holds. Otherwise the iterate is unchanged. Setting the scale to one recovers classical dogleg.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}x_{k+1}(\lambda),&f(x_{k+1}(\lambda))\leq f(x_k)+\rho g_k^T(x_{k+1}(\lambda)-x_k),\\x_k,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Dogleg Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polygonal dogleg paths incorporating additional model-reducing trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select vertices \(v_0=0,v_1,\ldots,v_r=p_N\) such that \(\lVert v_i\rVert\) is nondecreasing and \(q(v_{i+1})<q(v_i)\) for every retained segment. If \(\lVert p_N\rVert\leq\Delta\), return \(p_N\). Otherwise find the least index \(i\) with \(\lVert v_{i+1}\rVert\geq\Delta\), and return \(p=v_i+t(v_{i+1}-v_i)\), where the first \(t\in[0,1]\) satisfying \(\lVert p\rVert=\Delta\) is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended doglegs use additional model-reducing vertices and stop at the first boundary crossing of the resulting polygonal path.
assumptions_latex: \(\Delta>0\), and the selected path reaches a vertex of norm at least \(\Delta\) whenever \(p_N\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step satisfies \(\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta\) and lies on a model-decreasing extended-dogleg path.

notation.meaning: ordered vertices of the extended path

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a generic model-decreasing polygonal-path procedure, but no source establishes that this is the intended mathematical meaning of the extended-dogleg family. The admissible vertices and crossing rule require authoritative specification.

knowledge_statements.title: Dogleg Variant Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection criterion for competing feasible dogleg-family trial steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a finite collection of dogleg variants, and let each variant produce a feasible step \(p_d\) with \(\lVert p_d\rVert\leq\Delta\). Select \(d_*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{d\in\mathcal D}\{q(0)-q(p_d)\}\), subject to the safeguard \(q(0)-q(p_{d_*})\geq\kappa\,[q(0)-q(p_C)]\), where \(p_C\) is the Cauchy step and \(\kappa\in(0,1]\). Reject or replace any variant that fails feasibility or the safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among feasible dogleg candidates, select the largest predicted reduction while requiring at least a fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is the current quadratic model and \(\Delta>0\).
\(\mathcal D\) is finite and contains at least one candidate satisfying the safeguard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected step is feasible and achieves at least \(\kappa\) times the Cauchy predicted reduction.

notation.meaning: Cauchy step for the current model and radius

knowledge_statements.title: Hook-Step Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region least-squares step for globalizing Newton iterations on nonlinear equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an iterate \(x\), given residual \(F(x)\), Jacobian \(J(x)\), and radius \(\Delta>0\), compute a hook step as any solution of \[\min_{\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta}\ \tfrac12\lVert F(x)+J(x)p\rVert^2.\] Equivalently, solve the quadratic trust-region model with \(g=J(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)\) and \(B=J(x)^{\mathsf T}J(x)\). Return the unconstrained Newton or Gauss–Newton step when feasible; otherwise return a boundary solution characterized by \((B+\lambda I)p=-g\), \(\lambda\geq0\), and \(\lVert p\rVert=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hook step minimizes the linearized residual within a trust region, using the Newton step when feasible and a multiplier-controlled boundary step otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output minimizes the linearized least-squares model over \(\{p:\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally constrained optimal hook step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(s)=f_c+g_c^Ts+\tfrac12s^TH_cs\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), with \(H_c=H_c^T\succ0\), \(g_c\ne0\), and radius \(\delta_c>0\). Define \(s(\mu)=-(H_c+\mu I)^{-1}g_c\) for \(\mu\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean trust regions with a positive-definite local quadratic model. Both the exact locally constrained optimum and the usual inexact hook-step acceptance interval are identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The hook-step family consists of steps \(s(\mu)\) obtained from shifted positive-definite systems. If \(\|s(0)\|_2\le\delta_c\), the hook step is \(s_H=s(0)\). Otherwise the exact hook step is \[s_H=s(\mu_*),\qquad \mu_*>0,\qquad \|s(\mu_*)\|_2=\delta_c.\] An inexact hook step with radial tolerances \(0<\ell\le1\le u\) is any \(s(\widehat\mu)\) satisfying \(\ell\delta_c\le\|s(\widehat\mu)\|_2\le u\delta_c\), with \(H_c+\widehat\mu I\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hook step is a shifted Newton step. The multiplier \(\mu\) is zero when the full step fits in the trust region. Otherwise it is chosen so that the shifted-system solution lies on, or within an accepted radial band around, the trust-region boundary. The family is therefore the curve \(s(\mu)=-(H_c+\mu I)^{-1}g_c\), not a polygonal approximation to that curve.
assumptions_latex: For an inexact member, \(0<\ell\le1\le u\) and \(H_c+\widehat\mu I\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected step has the representation \((H_c+\mu I)s_H=-g_c\); it is the full step when feasible and otherwise satisfies the prescribed boundary equation or radial tolerance.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact boundary multiplier is the root of \(\Phi(\mu)=\|s(\mu)\|_2-\delta_c=0\).
The exact step minimizes \(m(s)\) subject to \(\|s\|_2\le\delta_c\).
special_cases_latex: Dennis–Schnabel’s loose practical band is \(\tfrac34\delta_c\le\|s(\widehat\mu)\|_2\le\tfrac32\delta_c\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(g_c\ne0\), \(\|s(\mu)\|_2\) decreases strictly with \(\mu\ge0\), so the exact positive boundary multiplier is unique.
boundary_notes: The positive-definite formulation does not include the spectral hard case of an indefinite model.
The hook step is distinct from dogleg steps, which approximate the shifted-step curve by line segments.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Dimensional Subspace Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact trust-region minimization restricted to the gradient–Newton plane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\), form \(p_N=-B^{-1}g\) and the subspace \(\mathcal S=\operatorname{span}\{g,p_N\}\), deleting a dependent generator if necessary. Choose an orthonormal basis matrix \(Z\) for \(\mathcal S\), solve \[\min_{y}\ g^{\mathsf T}Zy+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}(Z^{\mathsf T}BZ)y\quad\text{subject to}\quad\lVert y\rVert\leq\Delta,\] and return \(p=Zy\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict the quadratic model to the plane spanned by the gradient and Newton step, solve that small trust-region problem exactly, and lift the result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step solves \(\min\{q(p):p\in\mathcal S,\ \lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-dimensional trust-region subspace minimization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(p)=m(0)+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), where \(B=B^T\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\). Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a subspace of dimension at most two.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean quadratic trust-region subproblems. Positive-definite and negative-curvature-aware two-dimensional choices are distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A two-dimensional subspace trust-region step is any global solution \[p_S\in\arg\min_{p\in S,\ \|p\|_2\le\Delta}\left(g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\right).\] For \(B\succ0\), the canonical subspace is \(S=\operatorname{span}\{g,B^{-1}g\}\). If \(B\) has smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1<0\), a standard shifted choice is \(S=\operatorname{span}\{g,(B+\alpha I)^{-1}g\}\), where \(-\lambda_1<\alpha\le-2\lambda_1\), with explicit negative-curvature augmentation when the shifted step lies inside the ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method minimizes the full quadratic model exactly over the intersection of the trust-region ball with a subspace of dimension no greater than two. For a positive-definite model, the canonical subspace is generated by the gradient and full Newton direction. For an indefinite model, the second generator is obtained from a positive-definite shifted system or is supplemented by a negative-curvature direction.
assumptions_latex: In the shifted indefinite form, \(\lambda_1=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\) and \(-\lambda_1<\alpha\le-2\lambda_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_S\in S\), \(\|p_S\|_2\le\Delta\), and \(m(p_S)\le m(p)\) for every \(p\in S\) with \(\|p\|_2\le\Delta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(S\), then \(p_S=Zy_*\), where \(y_*\) solves \(\min_{\|y\|_2\le\Delta}(Z^Tg)^Ty+\tfrac12y^T(Z^TBZ)y\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\dim S=1\) and \(S=\operatorname{span}\{g\}\), the method reduces to the Cauchy-step solve.
For \(B\succ0\), the complete classical dogleg path lies in the canonical two-dimensional subspace.
immediate_consequences_latex: Because the Cauchy point belongs to the canonical subspace, exact subspace minimization produces at least the Cauchy model decrease.
boundary_notes: The method is a restricted minimization; it need not solve the full \(n\)-dimensional trust-region problem.
A negative-curvature-aware construction is required when \(B\) is indefinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearly exact dense trust-region solver family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(p)=m(0)+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\) with dense \(B=B^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), radius \(\Delta>0\), and exact minimizer \(p^*\) over \(\|p\|_2\le\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional dense Euclidean trust-region subproblems for which factorizations or spectral decompositions are affordable. High accuracy is expressed by a fixed fraction of optimal model decrease and controlled radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constants \(c\in(0,1]\) and \(\gamma\ge1\), a high-accuracy dense trust-region solver is a procedure returning \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[m(0)-m(p)\ge c\bigl(m(0)-m(p^*)\bigr),\qquad \|p\|_2\le\gamma\Delta.\] The family comprises dense shifted-factorization, secular-equation, and spectral procedures that exploit \(B\) beyond a single Cauchy or low-dimensional path calculation to meet these nearly exact conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-accuracy dense solver uses dense curvature information to return a nearly exact trust-region step. Its defining quality conditions require a prescribed fraction of the best possible quadratic-model decrease and a uniform bound on the step relative to the trust-region radius. Typical members repeatedly factor shifted matrices, solve a safeguarded multiplier equation, or use a full spectral representation.
assumptions_latex: The full subproblem has exact global minimizer \(p^*\), as it does on the compact Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(p\) captures at least the fraction \(c\) of optimal model reduction and satisfies \(\|p\|_2\le\gamma\Delta\).
special_cases_latex: The exact dense solve corresponds to \(c=1\) and \(\gamma=1\).
Moré–Sorensen shifted-factorization iterations are canonical nearly exact members.
immediate_consequences_latex: Unlike a Cauchy-only condition, the optimal-reduction condition remains informative when \(g=0\) and \(B\) has negative eigenvalues.
boundary_notes: The definition concerns solution quality, not a particular factorization implementation.
Matrix-free Krylov solvers belong to the large-scale family even when they attain comparable accuracy.

notation.meaning: Exact global minimizer of the dense trust-region subproblem.
Required fraction of optimal model reduction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton secular step from the positive side
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step behavior of the scalar Newton iteration used in a high-accuracy dense trust-region subproblem solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\lambda>-\lambda_1\) and \(\phi(\lambda)>0\). The next Newton iterate satisfies \(\lambda^+\leq\lambda^{\mathrm M}\), and either
\[
\lambda^+>-\lambda_1\quad\text{and}\quad\phi(\lambda^+)\leq0,
\]
or \(\lambda^+\leq-\lambda_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From an admissible multiplier with positive secular-function value, the next Newton iterate does not exceed the required root. It either remains above the spectral threshold with a nonpositive function value or crosses that threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda^+\leq\lambda^{\mathrm M}\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl[(\lambda^+>-\lambda_1\land\phi(\lambda^+)\leq0)\lor\lambda^+\leq-\lambda_1\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Newton secular iterates from the negative side
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of the scalar Newton iteration used in a high-accuracy dense trust-region subproblem solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\lambda>-\lambda_1\) and \(\phi(\lambda)<0\). All Newton iterates initialized at \(\lambda\) remain greater than \(-\lambda_1\), retain a negative value of \(\phi\), and converge monotonically to the required root \(\lambda^{\mathrm M}\). The convergence is globally Q-linear with factor at least
\[
\gamma_\lambda:=1-\frac{\phi'(\lambda^{\mathrm M})}{\phi'(\lambda)}<1,
\]
and is ultimately Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting to the right of the spectral threshold with a negative secular-function value, every Newton iterate preserves those properties and converges monotonically to the required multiplier. The convergence is globally Q-linear with factor at least the stated gamma_lambda and eventually Q-quadratic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moré–Sorensen multiplier solver
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|p\|_2\le\Delta}q(p)\), where \(q(p)=g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), \(B=B^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean trust-region subproblems, including indefinite models and the singular hard case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Moré–Sorensen solver seeks a pair \((p,\lambda)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \[(B+\lambda I)p=-g,\qquad B+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad \|p\|_2\le\Delta,\qquad \lambda(\Delta-\|p\|_2)=0.\] In the regular boundary case it defines \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) for \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\) and determines \(\lambda\) from \(\|p(\lambda)\|_2=\Delta\), normally by safeguarded scalar iteration and repeated shifted factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moré–Sorensen family solves a Euclidean quadratic trust-region problem through its multiplier characterization. It searches for a nonnegative shift that makes the shifted Hessian positive semidefinite, solves the shifted linear system, and enforces complementarity between the multiplier and the trust-region boundary. In the ordinary boundary case, this becomes a one-dimensional root problem for the norm of the shifted-system solution.
assumptions_latex: Regular iterations use shifts for which \(B+\lambda I\succ0\); a singular positive-semidefinite endpoint is permitted in the hard case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any returned pair satisfying the four displayed conditions has \(p\) as a global trust-region minimizer; the solver family constructs or approximates such a pair.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a regular active boundary, solve \(\phi(\lambda)=1/\Delta-1/\|p(\lambda)\|_2=0\).
With \(B=Q\operatorname{diag}(\theta_i)Q^T\), \(\|p(\lambda)\|_2^2=\sum_i(q_i^Tg)^2/(\theta_i+\lambda)^2\).
special_cases_latex: If \(B\succeq0\) and an unconstrained solution \(p\) of \(Bp=-g\) satisfies \(\|p\|_2\le\Delta\), then \(\lambda=0\).
If the regular root does not exist because of spectral orthogonality, the hard-case endpoint \(\lambda=-\lambda_{\min}(B)\) is used.
immediate_consequences_latex: The family handles negative curvature by shifting the entire spectrum rather than replacing \(B\) by an unrelated positive-definite approximation.
boundary_notes: Inexact implementations require explicit stopping tolerances and safeguards; these are variants of the defining exact conditions.
The Euclidean identity shift is replaced by a generalized shift for ellipsoidal trust regions.

notation.meaning: Trust-region Lagrange multiplier or spectral shift.
Smallest eigenvalue of the model Hessian.

children.top_down_role: Root-finding, bracketing, and safeguarding families for the multiplier representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Safeguarded Secular Root Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bracketed multiplier iteration for the regular case of the Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the Euclidean trust-region model \(q(p)=g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp\), set \(\ell=\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\). If \(B\succ0\) and \(p(0)=-B^{-1}g\) satisfies \(\lVert p(0)\rVert\leq\Delta\), return \(p(0)\). Otherwise, in the regular boundary case, solve \((B+\lambda I)p(\lambda)=-g\) for \(\lambda>\ell\) and define \(\phi(\lambda)=1/\lVert p(\lambda)\rVert-1/\Delta\). Maintain a bracket \([\lambda_L,\lambda_U]\subset(\ell,\infty)\) satisfying \(\phi(\lambda_L)\leq0\leq\phi(\lambda_U)\). Accept a Newton or interpolation update only when it remains inside the bracket and satisfies the prescribed contraction safeguard; otherwise bisect. Update the bracket according to the sign of \(\phi\), and stop when \(\lvert\lVert p(\lambda)\rVert-\Delta\rvert\leq\varepsilon\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return the unconstrained minimizer only when the Hessian is positive definite and that minimizer is feasible. Otherwise bracket the regular multiplier root, use safeguarded Newton or interpolation updates, and fall back to bisection until the boundary norm meets the requested tolerance.
assumptions_latex: For the boundary branch, the regular case holds: its optimal multiplier satisfies \(\lambda_*>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\).
\(\varepsilon>0\) is the prescribed relative boundary tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step satisfies the shifted equation \((B+\lambda I)p=-g\); in the interior branch it is the feasible unconstrained minimizer, and in the regular boundary branch it satisfies \(\lvert\lVert p\rVert-\Delta\rvert\leq\varepsilon\Delta\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Safeguarded secular-equation root solver
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(B=B^T\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) on the regular domain \(\mathcal D=(\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\},\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular, non-hard-case Euclidean trust-region multiplier computation. The bracket must remain in the positive-definite shifted domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A safeguarded secular root solver generates \(\lambda_j\in[L_j,U_j]\subset\mathcal D\) for the equation \[\phi(\lambda)=\frac1\Delta-\frac1{\|p(\lambda)\|_2}=0.\] Each trial shift is obtained from a Newton or rational-interpolation proposal and then projected or replaced so that \(\lambda_{j+1}\in[L_j,U_j]\) and \(B+\lambda_{j+1}I\succ0\). After evaluating \(\|p(\lambda_{j+1})\|_2-\Delta\), the bracket is reduced while retaining a root. The returned multiplier satisfies a stated secular residual or radial tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeguarded secular solver computes the trust-region multiplier as a bracketed scalar root. It combines a fast local update with bounds that prevent a shift for which the Cholesky factorization fails. Every accepted iterate remains in the positive-definite shifted domain, and the bracket is updated from whether the corresponding step is longer or shorter than the target radius.
assumptions_latex: The regular secular equation has a root in an initial bracket \([L_0,U_0]\subset\mathcal D\).
Shifted systems are solved sufficiently accurately to evaluate the radial residual.
A termination tolerance is prescribed for \(|\phi(\lambda)|\) or \(|\|p(\lambda)\|_2-\Delta|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solver returns \(\widehat\lambda\in\mathcal D\) with \(B+\widehat\lambda I\succ0\) and the prescribed secular or radial residual tolerance satisfied.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The same root may be written as \(\|p(\lambda)\|_2-\Delta=0\); the reciprocal form is typically closer to linear near the left spectral endpoint.
special_cases_latex: Without activation of a safeguard, the update is the Newton iteration applied to the reciprocal-norm secular function.
immediate_consequences_latex: All shifted Cholesky factorizations requested by the safeguarded iteration are well-defined.
boundary_notes: The hard case may have no root in the open regular domain and requires a spectral endpoint construction.
Safeguarding specifies admissibility and bracketing, not a unique interpolation formula.

notation.meaning: Domain on which shifted matrices are positive definite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Repeated shifted-factorization trust-region solver
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(p)=g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\), with dense symmetric \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense Euclidean trust-region solvers whose principal operation is factorization of a sequence of scalar shifts of the model Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shifted factorization solver generates admissible shifts \(\lambda_j\) satisfying \(B+\lambda_jI\succ0\), factors \[B+\lambda_jI=R_j^TR_j,\] and computes \(p_j\) and optionally \(w_j\) from \[R_j^TR_jp_j=-g,\qquad R_j^Tw_j=p_j.\] The factorization-derived quantities determine a new shift, for example \[\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j+\left(\frac{\|p_j\|_2}{\|w_j\|_2}\right)^2\frac{\|p_j\|_2-\Delta}{\Delta},\] subject to safeguards. The returned step is the final \(p_j\) meeting the chosen radial or optimality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family solves the trust-region multiplier problem by repeatedly factoring matrices of the form \(B+\lambda I\). Each factorization supplies both the shifted-system step and derivative information for updating the shift. Admissible shifts keep the factorization positive definite, and iteration stops when the step has the required relation to the trust-region radius.
assumptions_latex: The update is safeguarded whenever its raw value leaves the positive-definite shift interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output has the form \(p=-(B+\widehat\lambda I)^{-1}g\) and satisfies the solver’s stated trust-region radial or multiplier tolerance.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The auxiliary solve gives derivative information for Newton iteration on \(1/\Delta-1/\|p(\lambda)\|_2\).
special_cases_latex: If \(B\succ0\) and \(\|B^{-1}g\|_2\le\Delta\), a single unshifted factorization with \(\lambda=0\) suffices.
immediate_consequences_latex: The method avoids forming \((B+\lambda I)^{-1}\) explicitly; triangular solves determine the step.
boundary_notes: A singular endpoint in the hard case requires a modified factorization or eigenvector construction.
The definition does not require reusing factors across distinct shifts, although implementations may exploit structure.

notation.meaning: Cholesky factor of the current shifted Hessian.
Auxiliary vector used to evaluate the secular derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Shifted Factorization Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense multiplier iteration using factorizations of shifted model Hessians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a safeguarded multiplier \(\lambda\geq\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\). At each regular iteration, factor \(B+\lambda I=LL^{\mathsf T}\), solve \(LL^{\mathsf T}p=-g\), and test \(\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta\) together with complementarity. If the boundary is active, use the factorization to evaluate a secular Newton correction, safeguard the new multiplier inside a valid bracket, and refactor at the new shift. Stop when \(B+\lambda I\succeq0\), \(\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta\), and \(|\lambda(\Delta-\lVert p\rVert)|\) is within tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly factor the shifted Hessian, solve for the trial step, and update the multiplier until feasibility, positive semidefiniteness, and complementarity hold.
assumptions_latex: A separate hard-case correction is invoked if the shifted matrix becomes singular at the solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \((B+\lambda I)p=-g\) and the trust-region optimality conditions hold to the prescribed tolerances.

notation.meaning: Cholesky factor of the shifted Hessian

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Modification Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shift selection through positive-definiteness tests and stable matrix modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a trial shift \(\lambda\geq0\), attempt a stable factorization of \(B+\lambda I\). If a nonpositive or inadequately small pivot is encountered, increase \(\lambda\) or apply a symmetric modification \(E\succeq0\) so that \(B+\lambda I+E\succ0\). Solve \((B+\lambda I+E)p=-g\), use \(\lVert p\rVert-\Delta\) to update a safeguarded shift interval, and reduce the modification as regularity is approached. Return an unmodified step only after \(E=0\) and the trust-region optimality residuals meet tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modify an indefinite shifted Hessian until it factors stably, then adjust the shift using the step norm and remove the modification before accepting the solution.
assumptions_latex: The factorization reports loss of positive definiteness or unsafe pivots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance with \(E=0\) yields a step satisfying the original, rather than modified, shifted trust-region equations to tolerance.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Reuse Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid and limited forms of reuse across shifted dense solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(B\), a numerical factorization of \(B+\lambda I\) may be reused without alteration for multiple right-hand sides at the same \(\lambda\). Its elimination ordering and symbolic structure may also be reused when \(\lambda\) changes. In general, however, a factorization at \(\lambda_1\) is not an exact factorization at \(\lambda_2\neq\lambda_1\), because \((\lambda_2-\lambda_1)I\) is a full-rank update. Thus shifted iterations require numerical refactorization, a specialized diagonal-shift update, or a previously computed eigendecomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact numerical factors are reusable at the same shift; changing the shift generally requires refactorization or a specialized update, although symbolic structure remains reusable.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric and fixed across the compared solves.
The statement concerns exact arithmetic identities; numerical stability may impose additional refactorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary factor reuse is exact for equal shifts, while unequal shifts require additional numerical work unless a shift-aware representation is maintained.

knowledge_statements.title: Moré-Sorensen Hard-Case Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral correction when the secular equation misses the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d_1=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), set \(\lambda_*=-d_1\), and suppose \(g\) is orthogonal to \(\mathcal E_1=\ker(B-d_1I)\). Compute the minimum-norm solution \(\widehat p=-(B-d_1I)^{\dagger}g\). If \(\lVert\widehat p\rVert<\Delta\), choose a unit vector \(z\in\mathcal E_1\) and a scalar \(\alpha\) satisfying \(\lVert\widehat p+\alpha z\rVert=\Delta\), selecting the sign that minimizes the model, and return \(p_*=
\widehat p+\alpha z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the hard case, solve with the singular optimal shift and add a minimum-eigenvector component that reaches the trust-region boundary.
assumptions_latex: The minimum-norm singular solution satisfies \(\lVert\widehat p\rVert<\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corrected step satisfies \((B+\lambda_*I)p_*=-g\), \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\), and \(\lVert p_*\rVert=\Delta\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hard-case spectral endpoint construction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(B=Q\operatorname{diag}(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)Q^T\), where \(\theta_1=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), and let \(E_1=\ker(B-\theta_1I)\). Consider \(\min_{\|p\|_2\le\Delta}g^Tp+\tfrac12p^TBp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exact Euclidean hard case caused by orthogonality of the gradient to the leftmost eigenspace; numerical near-hard variants replace exact tests by tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Moré–Sorensen hard case occurs when \(Q_1^Tg=0\), where the columns of \(Q_1\) span \(E_1\), and the regular shifted solution at the spectral endpoint has norm below \(\Delta\). Set \(\lambda_*=-\theta_1\) and let \[p_0=-(B-\theta_1I)^\dagger g.\] Choose a unit \(z\in E_1\) and a scalar \(\tau\) satisfying \[\|p_0+\tau z\|_2=\Delta.\] A hard-case step is \(p_*=p_0+\tau z\), with the sign of \(\tau\) chosen to minimize the model if the two boundary choices differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the hard case, the gradient has no component in the eigenspace of the most negative eigenvalue, so the regular secular equation may never reach the trust-region boundary. The multiplier is fixed at the singular spectral endpoint. A minimum-norm shifted-system solution is then augmented by a component in the leftmost eigenspace until the step reaches the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a suitable \(\tau\), \((B+\lambda_*I)p_*=-g\), \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\), and \(\|p_*\|_2=\Delta\), where \(\lambda_*=-\theta_1\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In an eigenbasis, \(p_0=-\sum_{i:\theta_i\ne\theta_1}(q_i^Tg)/(\theta_i-\theta_1)\,q_i\), followed by an eigenspace component \(\tau z\).
special_cases_latex: If \(E_1\) is one-dimensional, \(|\tau|=\sqrt{\Delta^2-\|p_0\|_2^2}\).
For a multiple leftmost eigenvalue, any unit \(z\in E_1\) may be used subject to the model-minimizing choice.
immediate_consequences_latex: The completed step satisfies the global trust-region optimality conditions despite singularity of the shifted Hessian.
boundary_notes: If \(Q_1^Tg\ne0\), the ordinary regular secular root is used instead.
Near-hard numerical cases require tolerances for eigenspace orthogonality and singularity.

notation.meaning: Eigenspace associated with the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian.
Unit hard-case direction in the leftmost eigenspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue-Based Subproblem Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense trust-region solution using a spectral decomposition and scalar multiplier search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute \(B=Q\operatorname{diag}(d_i)Q^{\mathsf T}\) and \(h=Q^{\mathsf T}g\). In the regular case, find \(\lambda\geq\max\{0,-\min_i d_i\}\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{h_i^2}{(d_i+\lambda)^2}=\Delta^2,\] unless the unshifted minimizer is feasible. Set \(p=-Q\operatorname{diag}((d_i+\lambda)^{-1})h\). If a denominator vanishes and the corresponding \(h_i=0\), use the pseudoinverse components and add a vector from the minimum-eigenvalue eigenspace to attain norm \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonalize the Hessian, solve a scalar secular equation for the shift, reconstruct the step, and apply an eigenspace correction in the hard case.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean trust-region subproblem is solved in exact spectral coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstructed step and multiplier satisfy the global optimality conditions \((B+\lambda I)p=-g\), \(B+\lambda I\succeq0\), \(\lVert p\rVert\leq\Delta\), and \(\lambda(\lVert p\rVert-\Delta)=0\).
