knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-control subsequential criticality family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and let \(x_k\) be generated by a trust-region method. Let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), let \(B_k\) be the model Hessian, and let \(p_k\) satisfy a fraction-of-Cauchy decrease condition and \(\|p_k\|\le\gamma\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional unconstrained trust-region methods with weak acceptance control, typified by accepting any strictly decreasing trial step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weak-control criticality theorem family consists of global results whose acceptance rule permits \(\eta=0\) and whose canonical conclusion is only \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|g_k\|=0.\] Its standard hypotheses include bounded \(\|B_k\|\), a lower bound for \(f\) on the initial level set, Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla f\) on a neighborhood of that set, and uniform constants in the step-length and model-decrease conditions. The defining distinction is that the conclusion guarantees a subsequence approaching first-order criticality, not convergence of the complete criticality sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-control criticality results cover trust-region schemes whose acceptance test imposes only objective decrease. Under standard model-decrease, step-length, bounded-curvature, lower-boundedness, and gradient-Lipschitz conditions, they guarantee that gradient norms become arbitrarily small along some subsequence. They do not guarantee that all later gradient norms remain small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\text{ is an accumulation point of }\{\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a subsequence \(k_j\to\infty\) such that \(\|\nabla f(x_{k_j})\|\to0\).
If the corresponding subsequence of iterates converges to \(x_*\), then \(x_*\) is stationary.
special_cases_latex: The standard trust-region acceptance rule with \(\eta=0\) is the canonical weak-control case.
If extra controls imply \(\lim_k\|g_k\|=0\), the result belongs to the full-sequence family instead.
immediate_consequences_latex: At least one stationary accumulation point exists when the relevant subsequence is bounded.
Nonstationary accumulation points are not excluded by the defining conclusion alone.
boundary_notes: The family is defined by its \(\liminf\) strength, not merely by weak wording of assumptions.
The result does not assert convergence of \(x_k\) or second-order criticality.

notation.meaning: The required fraction of predicted reduction in the acceptance test.

knowledge_statements.title: Liminf Criticality Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak first-order convergence for an unconstrained trust-region method with Cauchy decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and bounded below on the initial level set. Suppose \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz continuous there, the symmetric model matrices satisfy \(\|B_k\|\leq\kappa_B\), and every trial step obeys \(\|s_k\|\leq\Delta_k\) and achieves at least a fixed positive fraction of Cauchy decrease. Assume trial acceptance and radius updates use fixed standard trust-region ratio thresholds, with the radius not decreased after a sufficiently successful iteration. Then the generated criticality sequence satisfies \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard smoothness, bounded-model, Cauchy-decrease, acceptance, and radius-update conditions, gradient norms have a subsequence converging to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz continuous on the relevant level set.
Each step supplies uniform fractional Cauchy decrease under standard ratio-based updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Control Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary separating liminf criticality from full-sequence and all-cluster-point conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), and define \(x_{2j}=0\) and \(x_{2j+1}=1\) for every integer \(j\geq0\). Then \(f'(x)=2x\), so \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}|f'(x_k)|=0,\qquad \limsup_{k\to\infty}|f'(x_k)|=2.\] The sequence has cluster points \(0\) and \(1\), but only \(0\) is stationary. Therefore a liminf criticality guarantee alone implies neither \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\) nor stationarity of every cluster point; additional algorithmic control is indispensable for either stronger conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating sequence for a smooth quadratic has liminf gradient zero while its gradients do not converge and one cluster point is nonstationary.
assumptions_latex: Only the weak conclusion \(\liminf_k\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0\) is imposed.
No asymptotic regularity or full-sequence criticality control is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Liminf criticality alone does not imply full-sequence criticality or criticality of every cluster point.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Sequence Criticality Results
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong first-order convergence under uniform model accuracy and standard trust-region safeguards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and bounded below on the initial level set, with Lipschitz-continuous gradient there. Suppose \(B_k=B_k^{\mathsf T}\), \(\sup_k\|B_k\|<\infty\), every feasible trial step achieves a uniform positive fraction of Cauchy decrease, and the actual-to-predicted reduction test uses fixed thresholds \(0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1\). Assume unsuccessful iterations reduce \(\Delta_k\), sufficiently successful iterations do not reduce it, and the model error is uniformly first-order accurate on each trust region. Then \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform model accuracy and standard radius safeguards strengthen subsequential gradient convergence to convergence of the entire criticality sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and has Lipschitz-continuous gradient on the relevant level set.
The symmetric model matrices are uniformly bounded and steps give fractional Cauchy decrease.
Ratio acceptance, radius safeguards, and first-order model accuracy hold uniformly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\) as \(k\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-sequence first-order criticality family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(x_k\) be generated by a trust-region method with gradient \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional unconstrained trust-region methods with sufficient acceptance control strong enough to govern the complete gradient sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The full-sequence criticality result family consists of global convergence statements with conclusion \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\|g_k\|=0.\] In the standard trust-region framework this conclusion is associated with a strictly positive acceptance parameter \(\eta\), uniformly bounded model Hessians, a lower-bounded initial level set, Lipschitz-continuous gradients on a neighborhood of that set, and uniform fraction-of-Cauchy and step-length conditions. Full-sequence criticality means that for every \(\epsilon>0\) there exists \(K\) such that \(\|g_k\|<\epsilon\) for every \(k\ge K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-sequence criticality result guarantees that every sufficiently late iterate has a small first-order criticality measure. For smooth unconstrained problems this means the entire sequence of gradient norms converges to zero, which is strictly stronger than merely having a subsequence with vanishing gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists K\ \forall k\ge K:\ \|\nabla f(x_k)\|<\epsilon.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The defining limit is \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0\).
If \(\{x_k\}\) is bounded, every accumulation point is stationary.
special_cases_latex: A standard ratio test requiring actual reduction to be at least \(\eta>0\) times predicted reduction supports this family under the cited hypotheses.
If \(x_k\to x_*\), continuity yields \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: No subsequence can have gradient norm bounded away from zero.
The criticality conclusion remains compatible with several distinct stationary accumulation points.
boundary_notes: Full-sequence criticality does not imply that \(x_k\) itself converges.
The definition does not include second-order stationarity or a worst-case iteration bound.

notation.meaning: An index after which every criticality measure is below a prescribed tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists $\delta_1>0$ such that, for every iteration $k$, defining $\bar g_k=g_k+B_k\hat d_k$, $\hat d_k=d_k-\bar P_kd_k=d_k-\bar d_k$, and $\bar\Delta_k=(\Delta_k^2-\|\hat d_k\|_2^2)^{1/2}$,\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Pred}_k&-\frac12\sigma_k\bigl(\|c_k\|_2^2-\|c_k+A_k^Td_k\|_2^2\bigr)-\delta_1\|d_k\|_2\|c_k\|_2\\&\geq \frac14\|\bar P_k\bar g_k\|_2\min\left\{\bar\Delta_k,\frac{\|\bar P_k\bar g_k\|_2}{2\|B_k\|_2}\right\}+\frac12\sigma_k\|c_k\|_2\min\left\{\|c_k\|_2,\frac{b_2\Delta_k}{\|A_k^+\|_2}\right\}.\end{aligned}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive constant exists such that, at every Powell–Yuan iteration, predicted reduction after subtracting the stated feasibility and coupling terms is bounded below by the sum of a projected-gradient trust-region decrease term and a penalty-weighted constraint-reduction term.
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is an iteration of the Powell--Yuan algorithm}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order global convergence of trust-region iterates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. Define \(\chi_{2,g}(x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|\), \(\chi_{2,H}(x)=\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\}\), and \(\chi_2(x)=\max\{\chi_{2,g}(x),\chi_{2,H}(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional unconstrained nonconvex optimization; the definition concerns necessary second-order criticality, not positive-definite sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region method is second-order globally convergent if, from every admitted start and under its stated global assumptions, its generated sequence satisfies a declared global mode implying \[\nabla f(x_*)=0,\qquad \nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\] for the covered limit points \(x_*\). A full limit-point result requires every accumulation point to satisfy these conditions; a weaker result may assert existence of at least one such accumulation point or \(\liminf_k\chi_2(x_k)=0\). The algorithmic assumptions must ensure that significant negative curvature is detected or exploited when it is present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order global convergence strengthens first-order stationarity by also excluding negative Hessian curvature at the limit points covered by the result. Its target is a point with zero gradient and positive-semidefinite Hessian. Different results may cover one limit point, isolated limit points, or every limit point, so the convergence mode is part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_*\text{ covered by the result}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\nabla f(x_*)=0\ \text{ and }\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_*))\ge0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Second-order criticality is \(\chi_2(x_*)=0\).
An \((\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\)-approximate target satisfies \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge-\epsilon_H\).
special_cases_latex: If every limit point is covered, all accumulation points satisfy the second-order necessary conditions.
At a point with positive-definite Hessian, the second-order critical point is an isolated strict local minimizer under standard smoothness assumptions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict saddles with \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f)<0\) are excluded as covered limit points.
Positive semidefiniteness permits degenerate saddles or flat nonminimizing stationary points.
boundary_notes: First-order global convergence alone is insufficient for this definition.
The condition \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\) is necessary but not sufficient for a strict local minimum.

notation.meaning: Combined first- and second-order criticality measure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete convergence and radius stability near a positive-definite critical point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order convergence guarantee for iterates generated by the basic trust-region algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathrm{AF.1--AF.3}\), \(\mathrm{AN.1}\), \(\mathrm{AM.1--AM.5}\), and \(\mathrm{AA.1}\) hold. Let \(\{x_k\}\) be generated by Algorithm BTR, and suppose a subsequence \(\{x_{k_i}\}\) converges to a first-order critical point \(x_*\). If \(s_k\ne0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\) and \(\nabla_{xx}f(x_*)\) is positive definite, then \(x_k\to x_*\), every sufficiently late iteration is very successful, and \(\Delta_k\) is bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under AF.1–AF.3, AN.1, AM.1–AM.5, and AA.1, if basic trust-region iterates have a subsequence converging to a first-order critical point, late steps are nonzero, and the objective Hessian at that point is positive definite, then the full sequence converges there, all late iterations are very successful, and the trust-region radius has a positive lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\to x_*,\qquad \exists K'\ \forall k\ge K',\ k\text{ is very successful},\qquad \liminf_{k\to\infty}\Delta_k>0

abla^2f(x_*)\succeq0.\] Thus vanishing convexification supplies a second-order criticality route, whereas a shift bounded away from zero cannot by itself certify nonnegative curvature of the unshifted Hessian.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convexified-model route is a trust-region construction satisfying \[\widehat B_k\succeq0,\qquad \widehat m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^Ts+	frac12s^T\widehat B_ks,\] together with a consistency condition strong enough that, along any convergent subsequence \(x_{k_j}	o x_*\) to which the second-order conclusion is applied, \[\|\widehat B_{k_j}-

abla f(x_*)=0\) and \(

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convexified-model route replaces the local quadratic curvature by a positive-semidefinite modification so that the subproblem is convex. Convexification alone is not a second-order guarantee: the modified curvature must also converge to the true Hessian along the relevant subsequence. With first-order convergence and this consistency, positive semidefiniteness transfers to the limiting Hessian.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-curvature exploitation route
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TB_ks\), where \(B_k=B_k^T\), and let \(\Delta_k>0\). Define the negative-curvature magnitude \(\nu_k=\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B_k)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonconvex trust-region methods that retain and exploit negative curvature rather than convexifying it away.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A negative-curvature convergence route requires that whenever \(\nu_k>0\) is significant and first-order criticality is sufficiently small, the computed feasible step captures a uniform fraction of the decrease available from a most-negative-curvature direction. One canonical condition is \[m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)\ge\kappa_{nc}\nu_k\Delta_k^2,\qquad \|s_k\|\le\Delta_k,\qquad \kappa_{nc}>0,\] possibly with the right side replaced by the decrease at an eigenpoint. Coupled with model-Hessian consistency, this condition prevents a covered limit point from retaining strictly negative true-Hessian curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-curvature route explicitly uses a direction associated with a negative eigenvalue of the model Hessian and requires a model decrease proportional to the negative-curvature magnitude times the squared radius. With first-order convergence and consistent second-order models, persistent negative curvature would therefore trigger nonvanishing model progress and cannot remain at a covered limit point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_{k_j}\to x_*,\ \|g_{k_j}\|\to0,\ B_{k_j}\to\nabla^2f(x_*),\ \text{and negative curvature is uniformly exploited}\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_*))\ge0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: An eigenpoint may be defined by minimizing the model along a direction \(u_k\) satisfying \(u_k^TB_ku_k\le-\kappa\nu_k\|u_k\|^2\).
A global reduced trust-region minimizer exploits negative curvature when the relevant eigendirection is represented in its subspace.
special_cases_latex: Following a most-negative eigenvector to the trust-region boundary is the exact eigenpoint case.
A Lanczos Ritz vector can provide an approximate negative-curvature direction for large-scale problems.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict saddles are excluded as limit points covered by a full second-order convergence theorem.
The step may lie on the trust-region boundary even when the gradient is zero.
boundary_notes: Stopping a Krylov process before the negative eigenspace is represented can invalidate the required decrease.
Merely detecting negative curvature without using it in the step is insufficient.

notation.meaning: Magnitude of the negative part of the smallest model-Hessian eigenvalue.
Uniform fraction in the negative-curvature decrease condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Trust-Region Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic trust-region subproblems whose model Hessian has negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in\mathbb R\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), a symmetric matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and a radius \(0<\Delta<\infty\), a nonconvex quadratic trust-region model is \[m(s)=f+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs,\qquad s\in\mathbb R^n,\quad \|s\|\leq\Delta,\] with \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\). Equivalently, some nonzero direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(d^{\mathsf T}Bd<0\). The feasible ball is compact, so the subproblem possesses a global minimizer. An interior local minimizer would require \(B\succeq0\); consequently, every global minimizer of a model with \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\) satisfies \(\|s\|=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region quadratic is nonconvex when its symmetric Hessian has a negative eigenvalue. The compact feasible ball ensures existence of a global minimizer, and every global minimizer lies on the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subproblem has a global minimizer, and every global minimizer satisfies \(\|s\|=\Delta\).

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of the model Hessian

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenpoint Step Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary step generated by an approximate leftmost eigenvector of the model Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(\kappa_e\in(0,1]\). Compute a unit vector \(v\) satisfying \(v^{\mathsf T}Bv\leq-\kappa_e[-\lambda_{\min}(B)]\) whenever \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\). Replace \(v\) by \(-v\) if necessary so that \(g^{\mathsf T}v\leq0\), and set \(s_E=\Delta v\). If no negative curvature is detected, return a nonnegative-curvature status and defer to a gradient-based step. Otherwise output \(s_E\), which is feasible and satisfies \[m(0)-m(s_E)\geq\tfrac12\kappa_e[-\lambda_{\min}(B)]\Delta^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate leftmost eigenvector, oriented against the gradient and scaled to the boundary, produces a quantified negative-curvature model decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is unit length and captures a fraction \(\kappa_e\) of the leftmost curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step satisfies \(\|s_E\|=\Delta\) and the stated curvature-dependent decrease bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radius Collapse and Model Negative Curvature Near a Negative-Curvature Limit Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic lemma supporting the eigenpoint and negative-curvature route to second-order trust-region convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathrm{AF.1\text{--}AF.3}\), \(\mathrm{AN.1}\), \(\mathrm{AM.1\text{--}AM.6}\), \(\mathrm{AA.1}\), and \(\mathrm{AA.2}\) hold. Let \(x_*\) be a limit point of the BTR iterates with \(\lambda_*:=\lambda_{\min}(\nabla_{xx}f(x_*))<0\). For every subsequence \(\{x_{k_i}\}\) converging to \(x_*\), \(\Delta_{k_i}\to0\), and for all sufficiently large \(i\), \(\nabla_{xx}m_{k_i}(x_{k_i})\) has an eigenvalue \(\tau_{k_i}\leq\tfrac12\lambda_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a BTR limit point has a negative minimum objective-Hessian eigenvalue, then along every subsequence converging to it the trust-region radius tends to zero and the model Hessian eventually has an eigenvalue no greater than half that limiting eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\{k_i\}\text{ with }x_{k_i}\to x_*,\quad \Delta_{k_i}\to0\quad\text{and}\quad \exists i_0\ \forall i\ge i_0\ \exists\tau_{k_i}\in\sigma(\nabla_{xx}m_{k_i}(x_{k_i})):\ \tau_{k_i}\leq\tfrac12\lambda_*.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Exploitation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantified model reduction obtained by moving to the boundary along captured negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m(s)=f+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), let \(d\) be a unit vector with \(d^{\mathsf T}Bd\leq-\gamma<0\). Choose its sign so that \(g^{\mathsf T}d\leq0\), and take the boundary step \(s=\Delta d\). Then \[m(0)-m(s)=-\Delta g^{\mathsf T}d-\tfrac12\Delta^2d^{\mathsf T}Bd\geq\tfrac12\gamma\Delta^2.\] Hence a trust-region method that detects and exploits curvature bounded above by \(-\gamma\) obtains decrease proportional to \(\gamma\Delta^2\), independently of the gradient magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary step along a negatively curved direction, properly oriented, guarantees model reduction proportional to curvature magnitude times radius squared.
assumptions_latex: The sign of \(d\) is chosen so that \(g^{\mathsf T}d\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(\Delta d)\geq\tfrac12\gamma\Delta^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Capture Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-saddle failure when a trust-region step rule ignores model negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=-\tfrac12 x_1^2+\tfrac12\sum_{i=2}^n x_i^2\) and use its exact quadratic trust-region model at \(x_0=0\). Then \(g_0=0\), \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x_0))=-1\), and every radius \(\Delta_0>0\) permits a step \(s=t e_1\) with \(0<|t|\leq\Delta_0\) and \(m_0(0)-m_0(s)=t^2/2>0\). A step rule restricted to gradient-generated directions may instead return \(s_0=0\). Consequently, first-order sufficient-decrease conditions alone do not force departure from a strict saddle or convergence to second-order criticality; a negative-curvature capture condition is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient-only trust-region rule can stop at a strict saddle even though feasible negative-curvature steps yield positive model decrease.
assumptions_latex: The model equals the exact second-order Taylor model of \(f\) at \(x_0\).
The step rule may return zero whenever the model gradient is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule can satisfy first-order stationarity while violating \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x_0))\geq 0\); hence second-order convergence is not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Imperfect-model global-convergence regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), let \(x_k\) and \(\Delta_k>0\) be trust-region states, and let \(m_k\) be a possibly random or conditionally valid local model. Let \(\mathcal F_{k-1}\) denote the information available before constructing \(m_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Umbrella definition covering deterministic approximate derivatives, conditionally valid models, and random model-accuracy events; each subtype requires a separately stated convergence mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Global convergence with imperfect models is a family of trust-region guarantees in which exact Taylor agreement is replaced by quantified model-accuracy events. A representative event is \[\mathcal A_k=\left\{\sup_{\|s\|\le\Delta_k}|f(x_k+s)-m_k(s)|\le\kappa_f\Delta_k^2,\ \|\nabla f(x_k)-\nabla m_k(0)\|\le\kappa_g\Delta_k\right\}.\] The deterministic regime requires \(\mathcal A_k\) at all relevant iterations or after finitely many model-improvement steps. A probabilistic regime specifies a conditional bound such as \(\mathbb P(\mathcal A_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\ge p\). A result belongs to this family only when its conclusion and probability mode—deterministic, almost sure, in probability, or expected—are explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global convergence with imperfect models replaces exact derivatives or exact local models by scale-dependent error conditions. Deterministic variants enforce those conditions directly or through model-improvement steps. Probabilistic variants require sufficiently accurate models with a stated conditional probability. The convergence conclusion must identify both the criticality target and the stochastic mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{Quantified model accuracy at scale }\Delta_k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{a declared global criticality conclusion in a declared probability mode}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A fully linear deterministic model uses function error \(O(\Delta_k^2)\) and gradient error \(O(\Delta_k)\) on the trust region.
A conditional model is valid only when an explicit geometry or quality predicate holds and is repaired until that predicate is satisfied.
special_cases_latex: Approximate-gradient trust-region methods are deterministic imperfect-model methods.
Derivative-free interpolation models are conditional imperfect models when validity depends on interpolation geometry.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact-model theory is recovered when \(\kappa_f=\kappa_g=0\).
A probability lower bound without a specified filtration does not define a conditional model-accuracy statement.
boundary_notes: The inspected local sources support deterministic approximate derivatives and conditional models but do not support the stated probabilistic accuracy condition.
No universal value of \(p\) or universal stochastic conclusion is part of the definition.

notation.meaning: Event that the model has the required local accuracy at iteration \(k\).
Pre-model information sigma-field in a probabilistic regime.

review_flags: A precise authoritative source is required for the probabilistic-model component and its conditional-probability formulation.
The local source inspected covers deterministic approximate derivatives and conditional models only, so it is not cited as support for the complete umbrella definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic controlled-imperfection model family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, let \(m_k\) be a differentiable trust-region model centered at \(x_k\), and let \(\Delta_k>0\). Write \(g_k=\nabla m_k(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional trust-region methods with controlled approximate derivatives or conditionally repaired models; stochastic accuracy is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An imperfect-model convergence family is determined by constants \(\kappa_f,\kappa_g\ge0\) and a validity rule such that, at every iteration used by the convergence argument, \[m_k(0)=f(x_k),\qquad \sup_{\|s\|\le\Delta_k}|f(x_k+s)-m_k(s)|\le\kappa_f\Delta_k^2,\qquad \|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\kappa_g\Delta_k.\] The model may satisfy these bounds directly or become valid after finitely many model-improvement operations. Together with standard sufficient model decrease, radius updates, lower-boundedness, and smoothness, these scale-dependent errors define the deterministic imperfect-model regime in which first-order global convergence is studied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The deterministic imperfect-model family permits local models and model gradients to be inaccurate, provided their errors shrink with the trust-region radius at the rates needed for first-order agreement. A model can be accepted immediately when the bounds hold or repaired until a validity condition guarantees them. Fixed errors that do not decrease with the radius are outside this family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|f(x_k+s)-m_k(s)|=O(\Delta_k^2),\qquad \|\nabla f(x_k)-\nabla m_k(0)\|=O(\Delta_k)\quad\text{uniformly for }\|s\|\le\Delta_k.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: With exact function interpolation at the center, a controlled approximate gradient is sufficient when its error is proportional to \(\Delta_k\).
Conditional validity may be expressed by a predicate whose satisfaction implies the displayed function and gradient error bounds.
special_cases_latex: Finite-difference gradients with difference intervals proportional to \(\Delta_k\) can fit the approximate-gradient regime under suitable smoothness.
A fully linear derivative-free interpolation model is a conditional-model specialization.
immediate_consequences_latex: As \(\Delta_k\to0\), the model becomes first-order accurate at the trust-region scale.
The exact-model setting is the special case \(\kappa_f=\kappa_g=0\).
boundary_notes: Errors bounded only by fixed positive constants are not controlled imperfections in this sense.
Random model accuracy and noisy function values require probability or dynamic-accuracy conditions not included here.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Derivative Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order global convergence under radius-scaled deterministic derivative errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a standard trust-region method with model \(m_k(s)=f_k+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}B_ks\). Suppose each trial step gives a fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease, acceptance uses the ratio of actual to predicted reduction, and unsuccessful iterations contract \(\Delta_k\). If \(\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\kappa_g\Delta_k\), the matrices \(B_k\) are uniformly bounded, and function values used in the ratio have errors bounded by \(\kappa_f\Delta_k^2\), then the usual trust-region descent argument remains valid. In particular, unless the method terminates at a stationary point, \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radius-scaled gradient and function errors preserve the standard trust-region guarantee that true gradients approach zero along a subsequence.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is bounded below on the iterate level set and has Lipschitz-continuous gradient there.
\(\|B_k\|\leq\kappa_B\), and each step attains a uniform fraction of Cauchy decrease.
Derivative and function-value errors obey the displayed radius-scaled bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either some \(\nabla f(x_k)=0\), or \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0\).

children.title: Imperfection-Tolerance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Error regimes beyond which deterministic convergence guarantees cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Imperfection-Tolerance Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed derivative bias imposes a nonvanishing floor on certifiable true stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\), but suppose every model uses the biased derivative \(g(x)=x+b\) for a fixed \(b\neq0\). At \(x=-b\), the model gradient is zero, so any step rule that declares stationarity from \(g(x)\) may stop. Nevertheless, \(|f'(-b)|=|b|\). Thus a uniform derivative error bound \(|g(x)-f'(x)|\leq|b|\) permits, at best, convergence to an \(|b|\)-stationary neighborhood. Guaranteeing arbitrarily small true first-order residuals therefore requires the derivative error to vanish with the trust-region radius or requested tolerance; a fixed nonzero error cannot suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed gradient bias can make a model stationary where the true gradient is nonzero, imposing an unavoidable stationarity-error floor.
assumptions_latex: Termination or step generation relies on the approximate gradient \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No guarantee of \(|f'(x)|<\varepsilon\) is possible for every \(\varepsilon<|b|\) under the fixed error bound alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic-Model Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure first-order convergence with conditionally accurate random models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_{k-1}\) denote the information available before constructing the random model \(M_k\). Suppose that, conditionally on \(\mathcal F_{k-1}\), \(M_k\) is fully linear on \(B(x_k,\Delta_k)\) with probability at least \(p>1/2\). Assume model gradients and Hessians satisfy the standard boundedness conditions, trial steps give a fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease, and noisy function estimates are accurate enough to preserve the acceptance decision with the corresponding conditional probability. For standard trust-region acceptance and radius updates, the iterates then satisfy \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If sufficiently accurate random models occur conditionally with probability exceeding one half, standard trust-region safeguards yield almost-sure subsequential stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is bounded below on the iterate level set and has Lipschitz-continuous gradient.
\(\mathbb P(M_k\text{ is fully linear}\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\geq p>1/2\).
Steps, estimates, acceptance tests, and radius updates obey uniform trust-region safeguards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\!\left(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|=0\right)=1\).

notation.meaning: Random trust-region model at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probabilistically accurate trust-region model sequence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, and let \((X_k,\Delta_k,M_k)\) be random iterates, radii, and models. Write \(B_k=B(X_k,\Delta_k)\), and let \(\mathcal F_{k-1}\) contain all information available before \(M_k\) is generated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional stochastic trust-region models whose accuracy is measured conditionally on the algorithmic past; this definition does not itself assert convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constants \(\kappa_f,\kappa_g>0\) and \(p\in(0,1]\), define the event \(I_k=\{M_k\text{ is }(\kappa_f,\kappa_g)\text{-fully linear for }f\text{ on }B_k\}\), meaning that, almost surely on \(I_k\), \[|f(y)-M_k(y)|\leq\kappa_f\Delta_k^2,\qquad \|\nabla f(y)-\nabla M_k(y)\|\leq\kappa_g\Delta_k\quad(\forall y\in B_k).\] The model sequence is probabilistically fully linear with probability at least \(p\) when \[\mathbb P(I_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\geq p\quad\text{almost surely for every }k.\] A probabilistic-model convergence regime is an algorithmic regime in which these conditional accuracy events, together with specified acceptance and radius rules, are the model-quality hypotheses used to establish a stated mode of convergence of \((X_k)\), such as almost-sure first-order convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random trust-region model sequence is probabilistically fully linear when, conditionally on everything known before the current model is sampled, the probability is at least p that its function error is at most a constant times the squared radius and its gradient error is at most a constant times the radius throughout the current trust-region ball. A probabilistic-model convergence regime uses these conditional accuracy events, together with explicit trust-region update rules, as the information-quality condition for a separately stated stochastic convergence result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P\!\left(\left.\sup_{y\in B_k}|f(y)-M_k(y)|\leq\kappa_f\Delta_k^2,\ \sup_{y\in B_k}\|\nabla f(y)-\nabla M_k(y)\|\leq\kappa_g\Delta_k\ \right|\mathcal F_{k-1}\right)\geq p.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(\mathbf 1_{I_k}\) denoting the accuracy indicator, the conditional-probability condition is equivalently \(\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{I_k}\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\geq p\) almost surely.
special_cases_latex: If \(p=1\), the definition reduces to an almost-sure fully linear model at every iteration.

If the model-generation randomness is conditionally independent of \(\mathcal F_{k-1}\), the condition reduces to the corresponding unconditional accuracy probability for the current state and radius.
immediate_consequences_latex: The definition controls model accuracy without requiring every realized model to be accurate.
The conditioning prevents success probabilities from being averaged over favorable and unfavorable algorithmic histories.
boundary_notes: The threshold on \(p\) needed by a convergence theorem is theorem-dependent and is not fixed by this definition.
Independence of successive model events is not part of the definition.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convergence regime of a trust-region iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), let \(x_*\) be an isolated local minimizer, and consider accepted trust-region iterates \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), with quadratic models \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TB_ks\) and constraints \(\|s\|\leq\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth deterministic trust-region iterations near a nondegenerate minimizer; the definition classifies local behavior rather than supplying sufficient global hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region method has a local convergence regime of order \(q\geq1\) at \(x_*\) if there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\), constants \(C>0\) and \(K\), and, when \(q=1\), a constant \(C<1\), such that every run entering the regime with \(x_K\in U\) remains in \(U\), accepts its generated steps for all \(k\geq K\), satisfies \(x_k\to x_*\), and obeys \[\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\leq C\|x_k-x_*\|^q\quad(k\geq K).\] Superlinear local convergence means instead \[\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|}{\|x_k-x_*\|}\to0.\] The regime is Newton-inheriting when additionally \(\|s_k-s_k^N\|=o(\|s_k^N\|)\), where \(B_ks_k^N=-g_k\), and the trust-region constraint is eventually inactive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region method is locally convergent of order q at an isolated minimizer when all sufficiently late iterates remain near that minimizer, their trial steps are accepted, they converge to it, and the next error is bounded by a constant times the current error raised to q. Linear convergence requires a contraction constant below one; superlinear convergence means the ratio of consecutive errors tends to zero. A Newton-inheriting local regime additionally requires asymptotic agreement between the accepted and Newton steps and eventual inactivity of the radius constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\to x_*\quad\text{and}\quad \|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\leq C\|x_k-x_*\|^q\quad(k\geq K).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Quadratic local convergence is the case \(q=2\).
Q-superlinear convergence is equivalently \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|=o(\|x_k-x_*\|)\).
special_cases_latex: When \(s_k=s_k^N\) eventually and \(\nabla^2f\) is locally Lipschitz with \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succ0\), the inherited Newton rate is quadratic.
immediate_consequences_latex: Eventual inactivity separates local rate analysis from radius truncation.
Asymptotic Newton-step similarity permits superlinear behavior even when subproblems are not solved exactly.
boundary_notes: This definition does not claim that an arbitrary initial point enters the local neighborhood.
R-linear and R-superlinear rates are distinct classifications not covered here.

notation.meaning: Unconstrained Newton or model-Newton step satisfying the local linear system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-region standing assumption A0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained finite-dimensional methods using exact Hessian curvature near a strict local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An iteration belongs to the trust-region Newton local-convergence family at \(x_*\) when \(x_k\to x_*\), its accepted steps satisfy a standard sufficient model-decrease condition, and, whenever the unconstrained Newton step \[s_k^N=-\nabla^2f(x_k)^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\] lies safely inside the trust region, the computed step is asymptotically Newton-like: \[\|s_k-s_k^N\|=o(\|s_k^N\|).\] The defining local behavior is that there exists \(K\) such that \(\|s_k\|<\Delta_k\) for every \(k\geq K\), so the trust-region bound is inactive, and \[\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|}{\|x_k-x_*\|}\to0.\] The exact-step subclass additionally satisfies \(s_k=s_k^N\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), giving the ordinary Newton local regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact-curvature trust-region Newton family consists of smooth trust-region iterations near a positive-definite stationary point that use the true Hessian and compute steps asymptotically equal to the Newton step whenever that step comfortably fits inside the radius. Its defining local outcome is eventual inactivity of the radius and superlinear convergence. If the computed step eventually equals the Newton step, the method is in the exact-step subclass and inherits the usual Newton behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K\ \forall k\geq K:\ \|s_k\|<\Delta_k,\qquad \lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|}{\|x_k-x_*\|}=0.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The asymptotic-similarity condition can be written \(s_k=s_k^N+o(\|s_k^N\|)\).
special_cases_latex: Dogleg, two-dimensional subspace, and nearly exact solvers that eventually select \(s_k^N\) form an exact-step subclass.
With a locally Lipschitz Hessian, the exact-step subclass has quadratic local convergence.
immediate_consequences_latex: The trust-region safeguard does not change the late local iteration once the Newton step is selected.
Approximate subproblem solution is compatible with superlinear convergence when its relative Newton-step error vanishes.
boundary_notes: Positive definiteness at \(x_*\) excludes degenerate minimizers and saddle points.
The definition does not cover quasi-Newton curvature matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for eventual trust-region inactivity and superlinear convergence when trial steps are asymptotically similar to sufficiently interior Newton steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be twice Lipschitz continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $x^*$, where $x^*$ satisfies second-order sufficient conditions. Suppose $x_k\to x^*$ and that, for all sufficiently large $k$, a trust-region algorithm uses $B_k=\nabla^2 f(x_k)$ and chooses $p_k$ satisfying the Cauchy-point-based model-reduction criterion. Suppose also that whenever $\|p_k^{\mathrm N}\|\leq \tfrac12\Delta_k$, one has $\|p_k-p_k^{\mathrm N}\|=o(\|p_k^{\mathrm N}\|)$. Then the trust-region bound is inactive for all sufficiently large $k$, and $\{x_k\}$ converges superlinearly to $x^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the objective has the stated twice-Lipschitz continuous differentiability near a second-order sufficient solution, the iterates converge to that solution, and the trust-region models eventually use the exact Hessian, then Cauchy-decrease steps that become asymptotically equal to Newton steps whenever those Newton steps have norm at most half the radius eventually lie free of the trust-region bound, and the iterates converge superlinearly.

p_k\text{ satisfies the Cauchy-point-based model-reduction criterion for all sufficiently large }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K\;\forall k\geq K:\ \text{the trust-region bound is inactive},\qquad \{x_k\}\text{ converges superlinearly to }x^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eventual full Newton-step regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider a smooth trust-region method with accepted update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), radius \(\Delta_k>0\), positive-definite local model Hessian \(B_k\), and unconstrained model-Newton step \(s_k^N=-B_k^{-1}g_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local deterministic regime in which the trust-region constraint ceases to truncate a Newton-like step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The method is in an eventual full-step regime at \(x_*\) if there exists an index \(K\) such that, for every \(k\geq K\), the unconstrained model minimizer is feasible and accepted without truncation: \[\|s_k^N\|<\Delta_k,\qquad s_k=s_k^N,\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k^N.\] A weak eventual full-step regime replaces exact equality by \[\|s_k-s_k^N\|=o(\|s_k^N\|),\qquad \|s_k\|<\Delta_k,\] while still requiring acceptance of the unscaled trial step. Thus the term “full step” refers simultaneously to inactivity of the trust-region constraint and absence of an additional damping factor; it does not mean that the step has unit Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region method reaches the eventual full-step regime when, from some iteration onward, the unconstrained Newton or model-Newton step lies strictly inside the current trust region, is chosen without truncation, and is accepted as the complete update. The weak version permits a step whose relative difference from the Newton step tends to zero. Full refers to the absence of radius truncation or damping, not to the numerical length of the step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K\ \forall k\geq K:\quad \|s_k^N\|<\Delta_k,\quad s_k=s_k^N,\quad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k^N.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a quadratic model with \(B_k\succ0\), inactivity is equivalent to the unconstrained minimizer being the trust-region subproblem minimizer and satisfying \(\|s_k^N\|<\Delta_k\).
special_cases_latex: If \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), the full step is the ordinary Newton step.
Dogleg and two-dimensional subspace solvers select the full Newton step locally when it is their unconstrained model minimizer and lies inside the radius.
immediate_consequences_latex: Late iterations coincide with the corresponding undamped Newton-like method.
Any local convergence rate of the full-step iteration transfers once the regime begins.
boundary_notes: A boundary solution with \(\|s_k\|=\Delta_k\) is not an inactive full step.
Acceptance of a scaled step \(\alpha_ks_k^N\) with \(\alpha_k<1\) is excluded.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nondegenerate local minimization after the trust-region safeguard becomes inactive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region sequence has Newton-rate inheritance at \(x_*\) when it eventually accepts full steps \(s_k\) whose discrepancy from the Newton step is small enough to preserve a Newton rate. Superlinear inheritance is defined by \[\|s_k-s_k^N\|=o(\|s_k^N\|),\qquad \|s_k\|<\Delta_k\quad\text{eventually},\] together with \[\|e_{k+1}\|=o(\|e_k\|).\] Quadratic inheritance is defined by the stronger step-accuracy condition \[\|s_k-s_k^N\|=O(\|e_k\|^2)\] and the rate \[\|e_{k+1}\|\leq C\|e_k\|^2\quad\text{eventually}.\] Exact Newton-rate inheritance is the special case \(s_k=s_k^N\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton-rate inheritance means that the late trust-region steps are sufficiently close to full Newton steps that the iterates have the same local rate. A relative step error tending to zero defines superlinear inheritance. A step error of second order in the current iterate error, together with a locally Lipschitz Hessian, defines quadratic inheritance. Exact inheritance occurs when every sufficiently late step is the Newton step itself.

Exact eventual Newton steps imply exact coincidence with the local Newton iteration.
special_cases_latex: With a Lipschitz-continuous Hessian and exact eventual Newton steps, the inherited rate is quadratic.
Asymptotically similar but nonidentical steps may inherit only a superlinear rate.

Subproblem accuracy can be stated directly in terms of relative Newton-step error.

Singular Hessians require a different local theory.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inexact-subproblem local-rate class associated with a forcing sequence \((\eta_k)\) is defined by the following mutually nested accuracy regimes: \[\sup_k\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\quad\text{(linear class)},\] \[\eta_k\to0\quad\text{(superlinear class)},\] and \[\eta_k=O(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|)\quad\text{(quadratic class, with locally Lipschitz Hessian)}.\] The corresponding local rate is measured in the equivalent \(H_*\)-norm \(\|v\|_{H_*}:=\|H_*v\|\): linear convergence means \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_{H_*}\leq\widehat\eta\|x_k-x_*\|_{H_*}\) eventually for some \(\widehat\eta<1\); superlinear and quadratic convergence have their usual Q-rate definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact trust-region subproblem rates are classified by how accurately the accepted step solves the Newton equations after the radius becomes inactive. A forcing sequence bounded below one gives a linear local class. Forcing terms tending to zero give a superlinear class. Forcing terms no larger than a constant times the gradient norm give a quadratic class when the Hessian is Lipschitz. The linear estimate may be expressed in the norm induced by multiplying errors by the limiting Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\Rightarrow Q\text{-linear};\qquad \eta_k\to0\Rightarrow Q\text{-superlinear};\qquad \eta_k=O(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|)\Rightarrow Q\text{-quadratic}.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(H_*\) is nonsingular, \(\|H_*v\|\) and the Euclidean norm are locally equivalent for rate classification.
special_cases_latex: Exact subproblem solutions have \(r_k=0\) and therefore satisfy every forcing class.
A fixed \(\eta_k=\eta<1\) generally supports only the linear class.
immediate_consequences_latex: Tightening the inner stopping tolerance can improve the outer local rate.
Oversolving is unnecessary when only linear outer convergence is required.
boundary_notes: The quadratic class requires local Lipschitz continuity of the Hessian.
These classifications assume that the full computed step is accepted.

notation.meaning: Equivalent local norm defined as the Euclidean norm of H_*v.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-Newton trust-region local-rate interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable near \(x_*\), with \(H_*:=\nabla^2f(x_*)\succ0\). Let symmetric nonsingular matrices \(B_k\) define \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TB_ks\), and let \(s_k^Q=-B_k^{-1}g_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained trust-region methods using secant or quasi-Newton curvature approximations near a nondegenerate minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quasi-Newton trust-region sequence has a local rate interface at \(x_*\) when the trust-region constraint is eventually inactive, \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k^Q\) eventually, and the curvature approximations satisfy the stepwise Dennis–Moré condition \[\frac{\|(B_k-H_*)s_k^Q\|}{\|s_k^Q\|}\to0.\] The associated superlinear-rate class additionally satisfies \[\frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|}{\|x_k-x_*\|}\to0.\] A linear-rate class replaces the vanishing curvature error by a uniform local contraction estimate \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\leq q\|x_k-x_*\|\) for some \(q<1\). The definition concerns curvature quality along the steps, not convergence of the entire matrix sequence \(B_k\to H_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-Newton trust-region method enters its local rate regime when the radius stops truncating the quasi-Newton step and the curvature approximation becomes accurate along the computed steps. Stepwise accuracy is expressed by the Dennis–Moré ratio: the action of the curvature error on the step, divided by the step norm, tends to zero. The superlinear class also requires the ratio of consecutive iterate errors to tend to zero. Full matrix convergence is not required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\|(B_k-H_*)s_k^Q\|}{\|s_k^Q\|}\to0,\qquad \|s_k^Q\|<\Delta_k\ \text{eventually},\qquad \frac{\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|}{\|x_k-x_*\|}\to0.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Along nonzero steps, the Dennis–Moré condition is \((B_k-H_*)s_k^Q=o(\|s_k^Q\|)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(B_k=H_*+o(1)\) in operator norm, the stepwise curvature condition follows.
Secant updates may satisfy the stepwise condition without converging to \(H_*\) in every matrix direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: Eventual radius inactivity makes the local iteration identical to an undamped quasi-Newton iteration.
Only curvature accuracy in directions actually taken is required by the interface.
boundary_notes: Positive definiteness and boundedness conditions on \(B_k\) used by particular convergence results must be stated separately.
The inspected source hints did not support this exact trust-region formulation and Dennis–Moré condition together.
review_flags: The supplied quasi-Newton sources were not shown to support the exact trust-region-local interface stated here.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Taxonomy of trust-region worst-case complexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an algorithm generate iterates \((x_k)\) for minimizing \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). Let \(\chi_j(x)\geq0\) be an order-\(j\) criticality measure, and let \(\epsilon>0\) be a requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case iteration, evaluation, and information complexity; local asymptotic rates are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region complexity class is a tuple \[\mathfrak C=(j,\chi_j,\mathcal O,\mathcal I,N),\] where \(j\) is the criticality order, \(\chi_j\) is the termination measure, \(\mathcal O\) specifies the available exact or inexact oracle, \(\mathcal I\) specifies the required model-information class, and \(N(\epsilon)\) is a worst-case resource bound. Formally, \(N(\epsilon)\) is valid if, for every problem and admissible algorithmic run satisfying the class hypotheses, some index \(k\leq N(\epsilon)\) satisfies \(\chi_j(x_k)\leq\epsilon\). Iteration complexity counts outer iterations; evaluation complexity counts calls to designated oracles; information complexity counts derivative, sample, or model-building work according to an explicitly declared cost unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region complexity taxonomy class records five items: the order of criticality sought, the corresponding termination measure, the oracle or evaluation regime, the model-information regime, and a worst-case resource bound. A bound is valid when every admissible problem and run reaches the requested criticality tolerance within that many counted resources. Iteration, evaluation, and information complexity are separate classifications because one iteration may require different numbers or types of oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\epsilon>0\ \forall\text{ admissible runs}\ \exists k\leq N(\epsilon):\quad \chi_j(x_k)\leq\epsilon.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The stopping time \(T_\epsilon:=\inf\{k:\chi_j(x_k)\leq\epsilon\}\) satisfies \(T_\epsilon\leq N(\epsilon)\) in the deterministic iteration-complexity setting.
special_cases_latex: First-order classes use a gradient or projected-gradient criticality measure.
Second-order classes combine first-order criticality with a measure of negative curvature.
Probabilistic classes may bound \(\mathbb E[T_\epsilon]\) or a tail probability rather than every realized stopping time.
immediate_consequences_latex: Complexity claims are incomparable until their cost units and oracle assumptions are aligned.
An asymptotic local convergence rate does not by itself define a worst-case complexity class.
boundary_notes: The definition assigns no universal exponent to \(N(\epsilon)\).
The inspected sources did not provide a single authoritative formulation of this taxonomy.

notation.meaning: First index attaining the requested criticality tolerance.

review_flags: A source covering the complete iteration-evaluation-information taxonomy is required.

children.title: First-Order Complexity
children.top_down_role: Worst-case iteration and evaluation complexity for approximate first-order criticality.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical worst-case bound for reaching approximate first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a trust-region method whose quadratic models have uniformly bounded Hessians and whose trial steps attain a fixed fraction of Cauchy decrease. Suppose accepted iterations reduce \(f\) according to the usual actual-to-predicted reduction test and radius updates use fixed contraction and expansion factors. For any \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the number of iterations before producing an iterate with \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\) is at most \(C\varepsilon^{-2}\), where \(C\) is independent of \(\varepsilon\). With a uniformly bounded number of objective and derivative evaluations per iteration, the evaluation complexity is also \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeguarded trust-region method needs at most order epsilon to the minus two iterations and evaluations to make the gradient norm at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below on the relevant level set and has Lipschitz-continuous gradient there.
Model Hessians are uniformly bounded, and trial steps provide a uniform fraction of Cauchy decrease.
Acceptance and radius updates use fixed standard trust-region parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first index \(k\) satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\) obeys \(k=O(\varepsilon^{-2})\), with the same order for evaluations under bounded per-iteration cost.

notation.meaning: Problem- and algorithm-dependent constant independent of tolerance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fraction-of-Cauchy decrease yields the classical trust-region first-order complexity order
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound role and classical order are plausible, but a theorem locator is required to verify the assumptions used to bound unsuccessful iterations and to transfer iteration complexity to evaluation complexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order trust-region complexity bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and bounded below on the relevant level set. Define \(T_1(\epsilon)=\inf\{k\geq0:\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\epsilon\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case approximate first-order stationarity for smooth unconstrained finite-dimensional trust-region methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region method has first-order iteration complexity \(O(\epsilon^{-p})\) if there exist constants \(C_0,C_1\geq0\), independent of \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\), such that every admissible run satisfies \[T_1(\epsilon)\leq C_0+C_1\epsilon^{-p}.\] It has first-order evaluation complexity \(O(\epsilon^{-p})\) for a declared oracle if the total number \(E_1(\epsilon)\) of calls to that oracle made through iteration \(T_1(\epsilon)\) obeys the same form of bound. The definition requires the constants to be uniform over the declared problem class and algorithmic parameter range; merely proving \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\) does not establish a complexity order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First-order trust-region complexity measures the worst-case work required to produce an iterate whose gradient norm is at most epsilon. The iteration complexity is order epsilon to the minus p when the first such index is uniformly bounded by a constant plus another constant times epsilon to the minus p. Evaluation complexity uses the same definition but counts calls to a specified oracle. The constants may depend on the problem-class parameters and initial optimality gap, but not on epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_1(\epsilon)\leq C_0+C_1\epsilon^{-p}\quad\text{for every }\epsilon\in(0,1].
equivalent_formulations_latex: The bound is equivalently \(T_1(\epsilon)=O(\epsilon^{-p})\) as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\), with uniform hidden constants over the declared class.
special_cases_latex: For constrained problems, \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\) may be replaced by an explicitly defined projected-gradient or feasible-direction criticality measure.
When each iteration uses at most a fixed number of oracle calls, an iteration bound yields an evaluation bound of the same order.
immediate_consequences_latex: The stopping criterion is approximate first-order criticality, not proximity to a minimizer.
Oracle accounting must include rejected trial evaluations when they occur.
boundary_notes: No exponent is asserted without smoothness and model-decrease hypotheses.
The supplied inspected sources did not support a specific modern first-order trust-region complexity exponent.
review_flags: A source supporting the intended exponent and its exact trust-region hypotheses is required.
knowledge_statements.title: First-order trust-region complexity bound

children.title: Second-Order Complexity
children.top_down_role: Worst-case complexity incorporating curvature criticality.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical trust-region bound for joint gradient and negative-curvature tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a second-order trust-region method that obtains a uniform fraction of Cauchy decrease when the gradient is significant and a uniform fraction of eigenstep decrease when the model has negative curvature. Under standard acceptance and radius safeguards, for tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H\in(0,1)\), an iterate satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\geq-\varepsilon_H\) is obtained within \(O\!\left(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-2}\varepsilon_H^{-1},\varepsilon_H^{-3}\}\right)\) iterations and evaluations, assuming a uniformly bounded number of evaluations per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature-exploiting trust-region methods reach joint approximate first- and second-order criticality within a tolerance-dependent cubic-type worst-case bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below, twice continuously differentiable, and has Lipschitz-continuous Hessian on the relevant level set.
Trial steps capture uniform Cauchy and negative-curvature model decrease.
Model, acceptance, radius-update, and per-iteration evaluation safeguards are uniform.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joint \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-criticality is reached in \(O\!\left(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-2}\varepsilon_H^{-1},\varepsilon_H^{-3}\}\right)\) iterations and evaluations.

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric Hessian.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and leaf placement are correct, but the mixed tolerance bound depends on precise eigenstep decrease, Hessian accuracy, radius lower bounds, and counting conventions. An authoritative second-order trust-region complexity theorem with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order trust-region complexity bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable. For tolerances \(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H>0\), define \(T_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\) as the first index satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\geq-\epsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case approximate second-order stationarity for smooth unconstrained finite-dimensional methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region method has second-order complexity bounded by \(N_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\) when every admissible run satisfies \[T_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\leq N_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H).\] A polynomial order \(O(\epsilon_g^{-p}+\epsilon_H^{-q})\) means that constants \(C_0,C_1,C_2\geq0\), independent of both tolerances in \((0,1]\), satisfy \[T_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\leq C_0+C_1\epsilon_g^{-p}+C_2\epsilon_H^{-q}.\] Evaluation or information complexity is obtained by replacing the iteration index with the number of explicitly designated function, gradient, Hessian, Hessian-vector, or model-building operations used before this joint stopping condition is first met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order trust-region complexity counts worst-case work until both the gradient is small and the Hessian has no eigenvalue below minus the curvature tolerance. A two-tolerance polynomial order is a uniform bound by constants times inverse powers of the gradient and curvature tolerances. Evaluation complexity must state which calls are counted, especially whether a Hessian, a Hessian-vector product, or a negative-curvature certificate is the basic operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists k\leq N_2(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H):\quad \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\epsilon_g,\quad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\geq-\epsilon_H.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(\chi_2(x)=\max\{\|\nabla f(x)\|/\epsilon_g,[-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))]_+/\epsilon_H\}\), termination is \(\chi_2(x_k)\leq1\).
special_cases_latex: Setting \(\epsilon_H=\sqrt{\epsilon_g}\) yields a one-parameter second-order target often used for comparisons.
Exact second-order criticality is recovered formally as both tolerances tend to zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: A first-order complexity bound alone does not control escape from strict saddles.
Curvature-oracle costs can dominate iteration counts.
boundary_notes: Degenerate stationary points are permitted by approximate second-order criticality.
No particular exponents are asserted without an exact source and algorithmic hypotheses.
review_flags: A source supporting specific second-order trust-region exponents and oracle assumptions is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-order trust-region complexity bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complexity regimes under inexact evaluations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let available values satisfy \(\widetilde f_k=f(x_k)+e_k^f\), \(\widetilde g_k=\nabla f(x_k)+e_k^g\), and, when used, \(\widetilde H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)+E_k^H\). Let \(\Delta_k\) be the trust-region radius.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic controlled errors and irreducible bounded-noise floors; stochastic sampling costs require an additional probabilistic specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An imperfect-evaluation complexity regime is specified by error envelopes \[|e_k^f|\leq\delta_k^f,
0\qquad \|e_k^g\|\leq\delta_k^g,
0\qquad \|E_k^H\|\leq\delta_k^H\] and by a cost function for obtaining those envelopes. The regime is dynamically accurate of order \((2,1,0)\) when \(\delta_k^f=O(\Delta_k^2)\), \(\delta_k^g=O(\Delta_k)\), and \(\delta_k^H=O(1)\); stronger second-order regimes may require correspondingly tighter envelopes. It is an intrinsic-noise regime when fixed floors \((\bar\delta_f,ar\delta_g,ar\delta_H)\) prevent arbitrary tightening. A complexity statement must then specify both a bound \(N(\epsilon;\delta)
0\) and an attainable tolerance region, since requests below the induced criticality floor need not be achievable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An imperfect-evaluation complexity regime records bounds on errors in function, gradient, and Hessian information and the work required to achieve those bounds. Dynamically accurate regimes tighten errors relative to the current trust-region radius. Intrinsic-noise regimes have nonzero error floors. Their complexity statements must state not only the amount of work but also which stationarity tolerances remain attainable; a nominal bound below the noise-induced criticality floor is not meaningful.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\epsilon;\delta)<\infty\quad\text{is asserted only for }\epsilon\text{ in the declared attainable region determined by }(\delta_k^f,\delta_k^g,\delta_k^H).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A deterministic error envelope may be replaced by a high-probability or conditional-moment envelope, but the resulting complexity notion must state its probability mode.
special_cases_latex: Exact evaluation is the zero-envelope case.
Fixed bounded gradient error generally yields only convergence to a neighborhood measured at the scale of that error.
Adaptive sampling is represented by decreasing envelopes with an evaluation cost that increases as accuracy tightens.
immediate_consequences_latex: Evaluation accuracy and evaluation cost cannot be separated in a meaningful oracle-complexity comparison.
An algorithm may have finite complexity to a noise-dependent neighborhood but infinite complexity for smaller requested tolerances.
boundary_notes: The radius scalings given here define an information regime, not a universal convergence theorem.
No inspected source established the complete complexity-and-noise-floor interface.
review_flags: An authoritative source is required for exact attainable-accuracy and complexity bounds under each error model.

children.title: Inexact Evaluation Complexity
